answers_clean: The symptoms of adult acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) can vary depending on the individual patient and the specific type of ALL they have. However, some common symptoms include fatigue, weakness or weight loss, fever, infections, bruising or bleeding, pain in the joints, abdominal swelling or discomfort, enlarged spleen or liver, nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath, coughing, chest pain, bone pain, decreased appetite, difficulty eating, and headaches . It is important to note that these symptoms may also be caused by other conditions, so it is crucial for individuals experiencing any of them to consult with their healthcare provider to determine the underlying cause.

The treatment of adult acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and stem cell transplantation . First-line chemotherapeutic agents include glucocorticoids such as prednisone or dexamethasone, vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, teniposide, cytarabine, daunorubicin, and methotrexate . Targeted therapies may also be used in certain cases to improve outcomes, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib mesylate and dasatinib , monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab , and proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib . Stem cell transplantation is often recommended after remission has been achieved with chemotherapy alone, particularly if there was minimal residual disease at the end of induction therapy .

The prognosis of adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) depends on several factors, including age, cytogenetic abnormalities, molecular mutations, response to initial treatment, and relapse status. In general, AML has a poor prognosis with an overall 5-year survival rate of less than 20%. However, there have been recent advances in targeted therapies that have improved outcomes for certain subgroups of patients. For example, patients with FLT3-ITD mutations can be treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as midostaurin or gilteritinib, which have shown significant improvements in progression-free survival compared to standard chemotherapy alone . Similarly, IDH1/IDH2 mutant AMLs are now routinely treated with oral inhibitors targeting these specific mutations, resulting in improved survival rates . Additionally, venetoclax, a BCL-2 inhibitor, has demonstrated impressive results when combined with hypomethylating agents in elderly patients who are unfit for intensive chemotherapy .

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a type of cancer that affects white blood cells called B-lymphocytes or B-cells. It is characterized by an overproduction of these cells in the bone marrow, which then accumulate in the peripheral blood, spleen, and other organs .

The treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) depends on several factors such as age, overall health status, symptoms, white blood cell count, genetic abnormalities, and whether or not you have received previous treatment . For patients who have never been treated before, first-line therapy typically involves either chemotherapy with fludarabine plus cyclophosphamide (FC), bendamustine (BR), or chlorambucil (C) . If there is a high risk of progression due to certain genetic mutations, targeted therapies may be considered in combination with chemoimmunotherapy .

The outlook for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) has significantly improved with the use of targeted therapies such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Prior to TKI therapy, CML was considered an incurable disease associated with poor survival rates . However, patients treated with TKIs have shown significant improvements in overall survival, progression-free survival, hematologic remission, and cytogenetic response compared to those who did not receive these treatments .

Hairy cell leukemia (HCL) is a rare type of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia that affects adults aged 40 to 65 years old . The exact cause of HCL remains unknown; however, certain genetic factors have been identified as potential predisposing factors. These include mutations in genes involved in DNA repair pathways such as ATM, CHEK2, PMS1, and PMS2 . In addition, exposure to benzene or other chemicals has also been linked to an increased risk of developing HCL . Other possible risk factors include family history of hematologic malignancies, prior chemotherapy or radiation therapy, and autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus .

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials related to hairy cell leukemia (HCL). These include studies of new targeted therapies such as ibrutinib, venetoclax, idelalisib, and ruxolitinib, as well as combination treatments with these agents or other chemotherapeutic drugs .

The prognosis of childhood acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, white blood cell count, chromosomal abnormalities, response to initial treatment, and relapse status . Overall survival rates have improved significantly over time due to advances in chemotherapy regimens and supportive care measures.

The exact cause of childhood acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and other myeloid malignancies remains unknown. However, several factors have been identified that may increase the risk of developing these diseases in children. These include exposure to certain chemicals or radiation, inherited genetic disorders, family history of blood cancers, preterm birth, low birth weight, maternal smoking during pregnancy, and viral infections such as human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). Additionally, some environmental exposures such as pesticides and solvents may also be associated with an increased risk of AML and other myeloid malignancies in children.

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials related to childhood acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and other myeloid malignancies that are listed in ClinicalTrials.gov . Some of these include studies evaluating new targeted therapies such as FLT3 inhibitors or IDH1/2 inhibitors, as well as immunotherapies such as chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR-T). Diagnosis of soft tissue sarcomas typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT), and histopathological examination of biopsy specimens . The initial workup for suspected soft tissue tumors includes physical examination, radiographic assessment with X-rays, CT scans, MRI, and ultrasound. A biopsy is then performed by a surgeon under local anesthesia in which a small piece of tissue from the mass is removed using a needle and examined under a microscope. Histologic features of the cells can help determine whether they are cancerous or benign. Immunohistochemical staining may also be used to identify specific proteins that indicate the type of cell from which the tumor originated.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) refers to a type of mesenchymal tumor that originates from the interstitial cells of Cajal or their precursors in the gastrointestinal tract . These tumors can occur anywhere along the digestive system but most commonly arise from the stomach (60%) followed by the small intestine (25%), colon (10%), rectum (3-4%), esophagus (< 1%), and other sites such as the omentum or mesentery . The majority of GISTs are benign; however, approximately 85% of patients with GIST have mutations in either KIT or PDGFRA genes which may lead to malignant behavior .

The treatment of gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) depends on several factors such as the size and location of the tumor, whether it has spread to other parts of the body, and its genetic makeup. Surgery is usually recommended for most patients with localized or resectable disease, while systemic therapy is used in cases where surgery cannot be performed or when there is metastatic disease .

Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is a rare type of soft tissue sarcoma that can occur in children and adults. The exact cause of childhood rhabdomyosarcoma is unknown, but it has been linked to certain genetic conditions such as neurofibromatosis 1 and Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Other factors that may increase the risk of developing childhood rhabdomyosarcoma include exposure to radiation or certain chemicals, family history of cancer, and being male. Children under the age of 4 who develop rhabdomyosarcoma have an increased risk of developing other types of tumors later in life.

There have been several ongoing studies to investigate new treatments for childhood rhabdomyosarcoma. One such study is the Children's Oncology Group (COG) trial AEWS1221, which aims to compare two different chemotherapy regimens in treating children with intermediate-risk rhabdomyosarcomas . Another COG trial, ARST0831, is investigating whether adding irinotecan to standard chemotherapy can improve outcomes in patients with metastatic or high-risk localized rhabdomyosarcoma . The four stages of adult Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) according to the Ann Arbor staging system are as follows: Stage I: The disease is confined to one lymph node region or organ; Stage II: The disease involves two or more adjacent regions within the same organ or lymphoid structures on both sides of the diaphragm; Stage III: The disease extends beyond regional lymph nodes to areas outside the abdomen but not widely disseminated throughout the body; Stage IVA: Widespread disease involving the bone marrow, liver, spleen, lungs, or bone; Stage IVB: Disease with widespread skin involvement .

The most common symptom of adult non-Hodgkin lymphoma is painless swelling or lump in the neck (lymphadenopathy). Other symptoms include fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, coughing, shortness of breath, abdominal discomfort, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, difficulty passing urine, frequent urination, chest pain, bone pain, skin changes, and weakness.

These lymphomas include primary effusion lymphoma (PEL), body cavity lymphoma (BCL), Burkitt's lymphoma, diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), Hodgkin's disease, and Kaposi sarcoma . PEL and BCL are the most common types of AIDS-related lymphomas.

Overall, the 5-year survival rate for children with NHL is around 80%, but it can be lower in some specific types of NHL, such as Burkitt's lymphoma or anaplastic large cell lymphoma . It is important to note that while most patients with childhood NHL will achieve remission after initial therapy, many will experience a recurrence during their lifetime. Therefore, ongoing monitoring and follow-up care are essential for these individuals to detect any signs of recurrent disease early and initiate appropriate intervention when necessary.

It's believed that smoking increases the risk by damaging DNA and increasing inflammation throughout the body. 4) History of other cancers: Having had one type of cancer, such as cervical cancer, puts you at higher risk for anal cancer.

Radiation therapy may be used after surgical resection to reduce the risk of recurrence, especially if there was residual disease left behind .

The main types of childhood CNS embryonal tumors include medulloblastoma, primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET), atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor (ATRT), ependymoma, choroid plexus papilloma, retinoblastoma, pineocytoma, subependymoma, and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNT).

Treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination of these approaches . While the prognosis for patients with childhood craniopharyngiomas has improved over time due to advances in treatment, they still have a high recurrence rate and can lead to significant morbidity and mortality if not managed properly .

The stages of childhood craniopharyngioma include: 1) pre-tumor stage (when no tumors or symptoms are present), 2) early stage (the first signs of the disease appear as enlargement of head circumference in infants, or vision problems in children over age two years old), 3) intermediate stage (symptoms worsen due to increased pressure from the growing tumor, including hydrocephalus, seizures, endocrine dysfunction, and other neurological deficits), and 4) late stage (advanced neurological complications such as brain herniation may occur).

The most common symptom of childhood ependymoma is headache, which may be accompanied by vomiting or dizziness. Other possible symptoms include weakness in one arm or leg, difficulty walking, seizures, vision problems, back pain, and neck stiffness.

The treatment of childhood ependymomas typically involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. Chemotherapy may be used before or after surgery depending on the location and extent of the tumor. Radiation therapy may also be recommended if the tumor cannot be completely removed surgically or if there is evidence of residual disease.

Surgery is often the best treatment option for patients with early-stage liver cancer, while chemotherapy and radiation therapy may be used in combination with surgery to treat more advanced stages of liver cancer .

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), also known as liver cancer or hepatoma, is a type of primary liver cancer that originates from the epithelial cells of the liver called hepatocytes . It is one of the most common types of malignant tumors worldwide, with an estimated 841,080 new cases diagnosed in 2018 alone . The main risk factors for developing HCC include chronic infection with the hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV), exposure to dietary aflatoxin, heavy alcohol consumption, smoking, obesity, diabetes, and certain metabolic disorders such as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

The treatment of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors depends on various factors such as the location, size, grade, and stage of the tumor. MDS/MPN is a group of blood cancers that arise from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow. These disorders result in abnormal production of one or more types of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

The incidence rate of CMML in the general population is estimated to be between 1 and 2 cases per 100,000 people per year , but it may be underdiagnosed due to its similarity to other forms of chronic myeloid neoplasms such as essential thrombocythemia or polycythemia vera.

Patients with aCML typically have an indolent course compared to those with typical CML; however, they may experience disease progression or transformation into acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which can be associated with poor outcomes .

The four stages of endometrial cancer (EC) are as follows: Stage I: confined to uterus; Stage II: spread into cervix or upper two-thirds of vagina; Stage III: metastasis to regional lymph nodes; Stage IV: distant organ metastases .

However, patients with metastatic disease or seminoma have lower survival rates compared to those with nonmetastatic disease or other types of germ cell tumors.

Uveal melanoma can affect anyone but it most commonly occurs in adults between 50 and 70 years of age . It is more common among white people than black or Asian people. Risk factors include fair skin color, light eye color, and family history of uveal melanoma.

The treatment of intraocular melanoma typically involves a combination of approaches, including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy. Surgery is often used as an initial treatment to remove the tumor from the eye . Radiation therapy may be used after surgery or alone if the tumor cannot be removed completely by surgery. Chemotherapy can also be used either before or after surgery to help prevent recurrence. Immunotherapy such as interferon alpha-2b has been shown to improve progression-free survival when compared with observation only .

The most common presenting symptom is leukocoria (white intraocular opacity) followed by strabismus (eye misalignment), ocular inflammation or hyphema (blood within the eye). Other signs include nystagmus (rapid involuntary movement of eyes), proptosis (bulging of eyeball), phthisis bulbus (shrinkage of the globe due to scarring), buphthalmos (enlargement of the eyeball), lid edema, conjunctival injection, and iritis (inflammation of the iris).

The symptoms of ovarian epithelial cancer can include abdominal or pelvic pain, bloating, urinary urgency, frequent urination, menstrual irregularities, fatigue, weight loss, and changes in bowel habits . Symptoms of fallopian tube cancer may be similar to those of ovarian epithelial cancer, while primary peritoneal carcinoma typically presents with ascites, abdominal distension, and increased abdominal circumference . It is important for patients to seek medical attention if they experience any of these symptoms, especially if they persist or worsen over time, as early detection and treatment of these types of cancers can improve outcomes.

There have been several ongoing studies to investigate new treatments for ovarian epithelial cancer. One such study is the AGO-OVAR 12 trial, which aims to compare the efficacy of carboplatin plus bevacizumab versus carboplatin alone in patients with recurrent platinum-sensitive ovarian carcinoma . Another study, NRG Oncology Gynecologic Group 003, is evaluating the use of olaparib maintenance therapy after first or second line chemotherapy in patients with high grade serous ovarian cancer who were previously treated with bevacizumab .

The stages of ovarian germ cell tumor (OGCT) are classified according to the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO). There are four stages in total for epithelial OGCTs, while there is only one stage for non-epithelial OGCTs due to their rarity .

Diagnosis of ovarian low malignant potential tumors (LMPTs) typically involves a combination of imaging tests such as transvaginal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), along with blood markers such as cancer antigen 125 (CA-125). However, it is important to note that LMPTs can be challenging to detect due to their similarity in appearance to other types of benign ovarian cysts or early stage ovarian cancer . Therefore, a thorough evaluation by an experienced gynecologist is necessary for accurate diagnosis.

Ovarian cancer refers to malignant tumors that originate from cells in one or both ovaries. It can be divided into epithelial, germ cell, sex cord-stromal, and rare types of ovarian cancer . Epithelial ovarian cancer accounts for 85%–90% of all cases of ovarian cancer, with serous carcinoma being the most common subtype .

Gallbladder cancer (GBC) is a rare type of biliary tract cancer that develops in the epithelial cells lining the gallbladder. The incidence rate of GBC varies widely across different regions of the world, with higher rates reported in South America, Central Europe, India, Pakistan, and Japan .

The treatment of gallbladder cancer typically involves surgery to remove both the tumor and the gallbladder (a procedure known as cholecystectomy). In some cases, chemotherapy or radiation therapy may also be recommended depending on the stage of the disease and other factors such as whether the cancer has spread.

There have been several ongoing studies related to testicular cancer. One such study is the “Testis Specific Antigen Study” which aims to develop an early detection method for testicular cancer using serum markers. Another study is the “Germ Cell Tumour Consortium,” which seeks to identify new biomarkers and therapeutic targets for testicular cancer by analyzing genomic data from patients with different types of germ cell tumors. Additionally, there are also studies focusing on improving treatment outcomes for testicular cancer through the use of novel chemotherapy regimens or radiation therapy techniques.

The most common symptom of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) is vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy . Other possible signs include abnormal fetal heart rate patterns detected by ultrasound, excessive uterine enlargement, hyperemesis gravidarum, polyuria, dyspnea, and fatigue.

The prognosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, organ involvement, and genetic mutations. In general, children with single-organ disease have a good prognosis, while those with multisystem or disseminated disease may have a poorer outcome .

Risk factors associated with hypopharyngeal cancer include smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol consumption, exposure to secondhand smoke or other types of environmental tobacco smoke (ETS), human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, and occupational exposures such as nickel compounds, chromium salts, and strong acid mists .

The treatment of hypopharyngeal cancer typically involves a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy or chemoradiation depending upon the stage of disease at diagnosis . For early-stage disease (T1–2N0), endoscopic resection is often used as primary treatment modality with high rates of local control and preservation of swallowing function . However, this approach may not be suitable for all patients due to tumour size, location or other factors such as patient preference. In cases where surgical intervention is required, total laryngectomy with partial pharyngolaryngectomy remains the standard procedure but can result in significant functional impairment including dysphagia, aspiration, gastroesophageal reflux, and voice changes .

Laryngeal cancer can occur in both men and women of any age group but it is more common among middle-aged adults over 50 years old. Several factors have been identified as increasing the risk of laryngeal cancer including smoking tobacco (cigarettes or pipes), alcohol consumption, exposure to secondhand smoke, occupational exposures such as working in mining, textile, metal, ceramic, glass, chemical, rubber, plastics, coal, coke, iron, steel industries, and woodworking, certain dietary habits like pickled foods, hot beverages, spicy food, fried food, and salted meat products, human papillomavirus infection, chronic coughing from bronchial asthma, chronic sinusitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and family history of head and neck cancer .

The treatment of laryngeal cancer depends on various factors such as stage, location, size, type, grade, and overall health status of the patient. For early-stage cancers (I or II), surgery is often used to remove the tumor. Radiation therapy may also be used in combination with surgery or alone if the patient is not fit for surgery. In advanced stages (III or IV) when the cancer has spread into nearby tissues, chemotherapy and radiation therapy are typically recommended. Chemotherapy may be given before or after radiation therapy depending on the specific situation.

Diagnosis of lip and oral cavity cancer typically involves a combination of history taking, physical examination, imaging tests such as ultrasound or MRI, and biopsy for histopathological evaluation. The specific approach may vary depending on factors such as patient symptoms, risk factors, and suspected location of the tumor.

Metastatic squamous neck cancer with an occult primary (MSNCP) refers to the presence of metastases in the head and neck region that do not have an identifiable primary tumor site . The most common sites for MSNCP include the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, salivary glands, lymph nodes, and skin .

The treatment of metastatic squamous cell neck cancer (MSNC) is challenging due to its rarity and lack of standardized guidelines. However, there are several potential options that can be considered depending on various factors such as tumor location, patient's overall health status, and preference .

Diagnosis of nasopharyngeal cancer typically involves a combination of clinical examination, imaging tests such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT), and biopsy for histopathological evaluation. The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) recommends that all patients with suspected NPC undergo MRI of the head and neck region .

Oropharyngeal cancer refers to malignant tumors that occur in the oropharynx, which includes the base of the tongue, soft palate, tonsils, pharyngeal walls, and posterior pillar of the tongue . The most common type of oropharyngeal cancer is squamous cell carcinoma, accounting for approximately 90% of all cases . Other types include lymphomas, salivary gland cancers, sarcomas, neuroendocrine tumors, and melanomas .

The stages of oropharyngeal cancer are determined by the Tumor Node Metastasis (TNM) classification system . This system takes into account the size of the primary tumour (T), whether it has spread to nearby lymph nodes (N) and whether there is distant metastasis (M).

The most common symptom of paranasal sinus cancer is nasal obstruction or blockage, which can be unilateral or bilateral. Other symptoms include persistent nasal discharge, facial pain or pressure, headaches, loss of smell and taste, hoarseness, coughing, difficulty breathing through the nose, and recurrent ear infections .

There have been several ongoing studies related to paranasal sinus and nasal cavity cancer. One study is investigating the use of targeted therapy in patients with advanced head and neck cancers, including those affecting the paranasal sinuses . Another study is evaluating the effectiveness of immunotherapy using nivolumab in treating recurrent or metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the upper aerodigestive tract, which includes tumors originating from the paranasal sinuses .

The prognosis of salivary gland cancer depends on several factors such as tumor size, location, grade, histology, stage at diagnosis, and treatment received. Generally, patients with early-stage localized disease have a good prognosis, while those with advanced or metastatic disease have poorer outcomes .

There have been several ongoing studies related to oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancer. One such study is NCT03296147 which aims to evaluate the effectiveness of pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy as first-line treatment for patients with advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Another study, NCT05181803, is evaluating the efficacy of nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus nivolumab monotherapy in treating recurrent or metastatic HNSCC. Additionally, there is also an observational study, NCT04628702, that aims to assess the safety and feasibility of using anti-PD-L1 therapy in combination with cetuximab in patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC who have progressed after platinum-based chemotherapy.

The prognosis of pancreatic cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor location, and whether it has metastasized to other parts of the body. It is one of the most aggressive types of cancers with a 5-year survival rate of less than 10% . Early detection increases the chances of successful treatment and improves overall survival rates. However, due to its asymptomatic nature in early stages, many patients do not get diagnosed until later stages when treatment options become limited and less effective. Therefore, regular screening tests such as annual physical exams, blood work, imaging studies (CT scans), or endoscopies can help detect pancreatic cancer earlier when it's more treatable.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pNET) can occur in both sporadic and hereditary forms. The most common genetic condition associated with pNETs is multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1), which is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the MENIN gene that predisposes to tumors of the parathyroid gland, pituitary gland, and enteropancreatic system . Other rare syndromes such as Von Hippel Lindau disease, tuberous sclerosis complex, neurofibromatosis type I, familial adenomatous polyposis, and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome have also been linked to increased risk of developing pNETs . Sporadically, these tumors usually develop in individuals over the age of 50 years, with no family history of cancer or other known genetic conditions .

There have been several ongoing studies investigating pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs). Some of these include phase II clinical trials evaluating the efficacy of everolimus in patients with advanced PanNETs who progressed after first-line treatment with somatostatin analogues (NCT01493285), as well as phase III clinical trials assessing the effectiveness of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy using lutetium Lu 177 dotatate in patients with metastatic midgut NETs, including PanNETs (NCT02607773).

Transitional cell cancer (TCC), also known as urothelial carcinoma, is a type of cancer that arises from the transitional or uroepithelium, which covers the urinary tract from the renal pelvis to the bladder and down into the urethra . TCC can occur at any site along this region but most commonly presents in the bladder. It accounts for about 90% of all primary tumors found within the bladder.

Treatment options for transitional cell cancer (TCC) of the renal pelvis or ureter typically include surgery with nephroureterectomy being the standard surgical procedure. Depending on the stage at diagnosis, adjuvant chemotherapy may be recommended to reduce recurrence rates .

Wilms tumor is diagnosed through a combination of clinical symptoms, physical examination findings, imaging studies such as ultrasound or computed tomography (CT), and laboratory tests including urine analysis for microscopic hematuria and serum alpha-fetoprotein levels .

Breast cancer refers to any type of malignant tumor that develops in the breast tissue. It can be classified as invasive or non-invasive depending on whether it has spread beyond the ducts or lobules into surrounding tissues. The most common types of breast cancer include ductal carcinoma, which originates from milk ducts within the breast; lobular carcinoma, which arises from the lobules where milk fat is produced; and mixed ductal and lobular carcinomas, which contain elements of both these subtypes . Other less frequent forms of breast cancer include angiosarcoma, phyllodes tumors, and Paget’s disease.

Diagnosis of breast cancer typically involves a combination of clinical examination, mammography, ultrasound, and biopsy. Clinical examination includes palpation of the breasts and axillae, as well as inspection of the skin for any abnormalities such as dimpling or retraction. Mammography is used to detect early signs of breast cancer in asymptomatic women, while ultrasonography can help distinguish between benign and malignant masses. Biopsies may be performed using fine-needle aspiration (FNA), core needle biopsy, or open surgical biopsy depending on the size and location of the mass. The diagnosis of breast cancer is usually made by examining tissue samples under a microscope after they have been stained with dyes.

Male breast cancer is a rare type of cancer that affects men. It occurs when abnormal cells grow in the tissue of the breast. The exact cause of male breast cancer is unknown, but there may be some inherited genetic factors or environmental exposures that increase the risk of developing this disease.

The prognosis of male breast cancer depends on several factors such as tumor size, stage at diagnosis, hormone receptor status, lymph node involvement, and human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER-2) expression . Overall, men with breast cancer have worse survival rates than women with breast cancer due to later detection and more advanced disease at presentation . However, when diagnosed early through regular self-examination or screening mammography, the prognosis can be similar between men and women .

Diagnosis of skin cancer typically involves a combination of patient history, physical examination, and diagnostic testing such as biopsy with histopathological evaluation. A thorough patient history should include questions about sun exposure patterns, family history of skin cancer, personal history of moles or other pigmented lesions, and any changes in existing lesions.

Melanomas are malignant tumors that arise from melanocytes, which are specialized cells found in the skin, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, reproductive organs, and brain . The most common type of melanoma is cutaneous or skin melanoma, which can occur anywhere on the body but is more commonly found on areas exposed to sunlight such as the face, neck, scalp, arms, hands, legs, and feet . Other types of melanoma include ocular melanoma, which occurs in the eye; acral lentiginous melanoma, which affects the palms, soles, and subungual sites; mucosal melanoma, which arises in the oral cavity, genitals, vagina, anus, and other parts of the gastrointestinal tract; and leptomeningeal melanoma, which develops in the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord .

The stages of melanoma are as follows: Stage 0 (in situ): The cancer cells have not spread beyond the outer layer of skin that contains melanocytes.Stage I: The cancer has grown into the deeper layers of skin but has not yet spread to lymph nodes or other parts of the body.Stage IIA: There is no spread to lymph nodes, but there may be thickening or swelling in one area of the skin.Stage IIB: Cancerous tissue can be felt under the skin and there may be redness or swelling in more than one place.Stage III: The cancer has spread to small groups of lymph nodes near the primary tumor.Stage IV: The cancer has metastasized to distant sites such as the lungs, liver, brain, bone marrow, or skin.

The most common symptom of Merkel cell carcinoma is a rapidly growing skin nodule or mass that may be painless but often causes discomfort due to its size . Other symptoms include bleeding from the lesion, ulceration, inflammation, redness, swelling, itching, and tenderness in the area surrounding the tumor.

There have been several ongoing studies related to MCC in recent years. One such study is NCT03124879, which aims to evaluate the efficacy of pembrolizumab as a first-line treatment for patients with advanced or metastatic MCC. Another study, NCT03652936, is evaluating the safety and effectiveness of cemiplimab as a second-line treatment for patients with advanced or metastatic MCC who progressed after chemotherapy. Additionally, there are also phase I/II studies underway that aim to assess the safety and efficacy of other immunotherapies, including nivolumab (NCT03413735), ipilimumab plus nivolumab (NCT03490139), and durvalumab (NCT03708539).

The prognosis of plasma cell neoplasms depends on various factors such as the type of disease, stage at diagnosis, age, overall health status, and response to treatment. In general, multiple myeloma has a poor prognosis with an average survival time of 3-5 years . However, recent advances in treatments have led to improved outcomes, particularly when patients achieve complete or near-complete remission after initial therapy .

No, neuroblastoma is not considered to be an inheritable disease. However, there may be rare cases of familial clustering or syndromic associations with certain genetic mutations that increase the risk of developing neuroblastoma in children .

The treatment of neuroblastoma typically involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy (for localized disease), and sometimes stem cell transplantation (for high-risk disease). The specific treatment plan depends on several factors, including the stage and risk group of the tumor, as well as other patient characteristics such as age and overall health status.

The most common symptoms of non-small cell lung cancer include coughing, chest pain, weight loss, shortness of breath, hemoptysis (coughing up blood), fatigue or weakness, hoarseness, difficulty breathing, persistent pneumonia, wheezing, and coughing that doesn't go away .

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials related to non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Some of these trials aim to evaluate new treatments or combinations of existing therapies, while others focus on identifying biomarkers that can help predict response to specific treatments.

The stages of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) are determined using the tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) staging system developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). Staging is important because it helps to determine the best treatment approach for each patient's specific situation.

Lung cancer can affect anyone, but certain factors increase the likelihood of developing lung cancer. These include smoking tobacco products (cigarettes, cigars, pipes), secondhand smoke exposure, radon gas exposure, asbestos or other occupational exposures to carcinogens, family history of lung cancer, chronic inflammation from conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or bronchiectasis, long-term air pollution exposure, and a personal history of cancer.

The prognosis of parathyroid cancer depends on several factors, including tumor size, location, stage at diagnosis, and whether or not it has metastasized to other parts of the body. Generally speaking, patients with early-stage localized disease have a good chance of survival, while those with advanced or metastatic disease may have a poorer prognosis .

Penile cancer can affect any man regardless of age or ethnicity; however, it occurs more frequently in older men (usually between 50-80 years old) and those living in industrialized countries . Risk factors include phimosis, smoking, chronic inflammation due to poor hygiene, balanoposthitis, human papillomavirus infection, and other sexually transmitted diseases such as syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia .

The treatment of penile cancer depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor size, location within the penis, histologic grade, lymph node involvement, and patient preferences . For early-stage disease (Stage I), local excision with or without inguinal lymphadenectomy is recommended. For advanced-stage disease (Stages II–IVA), radical penectomy with or without pelvic lymphadenectomy may be performed depending on the extent of the disease. Chemotherapy can also be used in combination with surgery to treat locally advanced penile cancer .

Diagnosis of pituitary tumors typically involves a combination of clinical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and sometimes additional diagnostic procedures depending on the specific type of pituitary tumor being considered.

Prostate cancer is a type of cancer that develops in the prostate gland, which is located near the bladder and rectum. It is one of the most common types of cancer diagnosed in men worldwide, with an estimated 1.4 million new cases reported each year . The exact cause of prostate cancer is not known, but several factors have been identified as increasing the risk of developing it, including age, family history, race or ethnicity, certain dietary habits, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and exposure to radiation .

The treatment options for prostate cancer depend on various factors such as age, overall health status, stage of disease, and preferences of patients. For early-stage localized prostate cancer, the standard treatment is usually radical prostatectomy (surgical removal of the prostate) or radiation therapy using external beam radiotherapy or brachytherapy (internal radiation). Active surveillance may also be recommended for some men with low-risk prostate cancer who prefer to avoid immediate treatment but accept the risk that their cancer might progress during follow-up.

Risk factors for colon cancer include age (older than 50 years), family history of colorectal cancer or polyps, personal history of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, certain types of diets, obesity, smoking tobacco products, physical inactivity, high alcohol consumption, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and positive family history of first-degree relatives with colorectal cancer .

The treatment of colon cancer depends on various factors such as stage, location, grade, and whether it has spread to other parts of the body. For early-stage localized colon cancer (stages I or II), surgery is typically recommended. In more advanced stages of colon cancer (III or IV) chemotherapy may be used in addition to surgery .

Diagnosis of rectal cancer typically involves a combination of clinical symptoms, physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging studies such as colonoscopy with biopsy, and in some cases, genetic testing. The specific diagnostic approach may vary depending on various factors, including the patient's age, family history, risk factors for colorectal cancer, and other health conditions.

Colorectal cancer refers to any type of malignant tumor that arises from the colon or rectum. It can be divided into two types: colorectal adenocarcinoma and colorectal squamous cell carcinoma. The most common form of colorectal cancer is colorectal adenocarcinoma, which accounts for approximately 90% of all cases .

Risk factors associated with small intestinal cancer include smoking tobacco, alcohol consumption, certain dietary habits (such as high red meat or processed meat diets), family history of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) or Lynch syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, celiac disease, primary sclerosing cholangitis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, radiation exposure, and occupational exposure to nickel compounds or other carcinogens .

The treatment of small intestinal cancer typically involves surgical resection (removal) of the tumor along with nearby lymph nodes. Chemotherapy may also be used in some cases to help prevent recurrence after surgery or as palliative care for patients who cannot undergo surgery due to advanced disease stage.

The stages of thymomas and thymic carcinomas are classified according to the Masaoka staging system or the World Health Organization (WHO) classification system. The Masaoka staging system classifies thymomas into four stages based on tumor invasion and metastasis . Stage I is localized with no invasion beyond the capsule; stage II is invasive outside the capsule but without mediastinal invasion; stage III involves the mediastinum and/or great vessels; and stage IV includes any distant metastases.

The diagnosis of urethral cancer typically involves a combination of clinical history, physical examination, imaging tests such as ultrasound or MRI, and biopsy for histopathological evaluation. During the physical exam, doctors will look for signs of swelling, redness, bleeding, discharge, narrowed urinary stream, pain with urination, and difficulty voiding. Imaging tests can help determine if the tumor is confined to the urethra or has spread to other parts of the body. Biopsies are usually performed using endoscopy techniques such as cystourethroscopy, transurethral resection (TUR), or retrograde urethrography.

Vulvar cancer refers to any malignant tumor that arises from cells of the vulva. The vulva consists of the labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, urethra, vaginal introitus, perineum, and anorectal area . Most cases of vulvar cancer originate in the squamous epithelium lining the outer surface of the female genital organs.

No, abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) do not follow any specific pattern of inheritance. However, there is evidence that suggests genetic factors may play a role in their development. Studies have shown that people with AAA tend to have family members with high blood pressure or smoking history. Additionally, certain gene variants have been linked to increased risk for developing AAA. For example, mutations in genes such as SMAD3, TGFBR1, and TGFBR2 have been associated with familial thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections. Similarly, polymorphisms in genes like angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE), apolipoprotein E (APOE), and interleukin-6 receptor (IL6R) have also been implicated in the pathogenesis of AAAs.
Yes, abetalipoproteinemia is an autosomal recessive disorder. This means that both parents must have and transmit the same gene mutation to their child for them to develop the condition.

An absence or congenital absence of one or both tibias is known as tibial agenesis. It can occur in isolation or with other limb abnormalities such as fibular hypoplasia or absence, femoral deficiency, and foot deformity . The condition may be associated with various genetic syndromes including Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis, multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, and Fanconi anemia .

The symptoms of Acanthosis nigricans include velvety hyperpigmented skin lesions that typically appear on the axillae, neck, umbilicus, and other intertriginous areas. Muscle cramps and acral enlargement have not been reported as symptoms associated with this condition.

The accessory navicular bone is an extra ossicle located at the junction of the medial part of the navicular bone with the middle phalanx of the fifth digit in some people . It may be congenital or acquired due to repetitive stress from activities that involve overuse of the foot and toes such as ballet dancing, gymnastics, football, basketball, volleyball, running, hiking, weight lifting, and other sports involving jumping and sprinting .

Achalasia is a rare disorder of the esophagus characterized by impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter muscle and abnormal peristaltic contractions in the upper part of the esophagus. This results in failure to empty food from the stomach into the esophagus, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, regurgitation, chest pain, weight loss, and aspiration pneumonia .

The symptoms of Apert syndrome include craniofacial abnormalities such as hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes), exophthalmos (bulging eyes), midface hypoplasia, maxillary protrusion, micrognathia (small jaw), cleft palate, and dental malocclusion. Other features may include short stature, clubbed fingers or toes, syndactyly (fingers or toes fused together) in some individuals, and genital anomalies in males .

Achondrogenesis is a rare genetic disorder characterized by underdevelopment of cartilage during fetal development, leading to dwarfism and skeletal dysplasia. The diagnosis of this condition involves a combination of clinical features, imaging studies, and genetic testing.

Achondroplasia is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder that affects bone growth during childhood. It results from mutations in the FGFR3 gene located on chromosome 4p16. The most common symptoms of this condition include short stature, rhizomelia (shortening of limbs), frontal bossing, midface flattening, trident acetabular roofs, lumbar lordosis, kyphotic curvature of the spine, genu varum (bowlegs), and macrocephaly .

Achondroplasia is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects bone growth during childhood. It results in short stature due to abnormalities of cartilage development . The most common symptoms include disproportionate dwarfism with a normal head size relative to the body, rhizomelia or limb shortening, macrocephaly, midface hypoplasia, trident acetabular roofs, kyphosis, genu valgum, and lumbar lordosis .

Acquired hemophilia A (AHA), also known as acquired hemophilia B or autoimmune hemolytic anemia with factor VIII deficiency, is a rare bleeding disorder characterized by acquired factor VIII (FVIII) deficiency due to inhibitors of FVIII . It was first described in 1952 by Morris et al. , who reported cases of patients exhibiting spontaneous bleeding without any personal or family history of coagulation disorders. The incidence rate of AHA has been estimated at approximately one case per million people per year .

The symptoms of acrocephalopodysplastic syndrome include macrocephaly (large head), shortened trunk with narrow shoulders, abnormal limb development such as extra digits or fingers, and other skeletal anomalies including joint hypermobility, scoliosis, and hip dislocation .

The main features of acrofacial dysostosis-Catania (AFDC) include craniofacial malformations such as microcephaly, facial asymmetry with unilateral hypoplasia or absence of one ear, mandibular prognathism, and short nose with an upturned nasal tip . Other common findings include congenital heart defects , sensorineural hearing loss , ocular abnormalities including strabismus, ptosis, epiphora, and lacrimal duct obstruction , limb anomalies such as clubfoot, tarsal coalition, syndactyly, and hand and finger abnormalities , and dental abnormalities like missing teeth, supernumerary teeth, and enamel hypoplasia .

The most common symptom is enlargement of hands and feet due to swelling (acromegalic hands). Other symptoms include facial changes such as coarse features, prognathism (jaw protrusion), mandibular prognathism (enlarged lower jaw or chin) and macroglossia (enlarged tongue); skin changes including thickening, oily skin, seborrhea (increased oiliness in scalp, face, axillae, groins), carpal tunnel syndrome; cardiac complications like left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmias, heart failure; respiratory problems such as sleep apnea, difficulty breathing; headaches; high blood pressure; diabetes mellitus; menstrual irregularities; infertility; gallbladder disease; arthropathy (joint pain, stiffness, swelling); increased sweating; psychological disturbances like anxiety, depression, personality change, impaired judgment, sexual dysfunction; and social stigma .

The symptoms of acroosteolysis can vary depending on which bones or parts of the body are affected. In general, patients may experience pain, tenderness, numbness, tingling, swelling, and skin discoloration in the affected areas .

The symptoms of acute alcohol sensitivity typically occur within 30 to 90 minutes after consuming even small amounts of alcohol. They include facial flushing, rapid heartbeat (tachycardia), sweating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, shakiness, confusion, anxiety or panic attacks, diarrhea, fever, chills, thirst, and in severe cases, seizures and coma .

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), also known as variegate porphyria or type I porphyria, is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the hydroxymethylbilane synthase gene (HMBS). It results from deficiency of delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase, which catalyzes the third step in heme synthesis . AIP typically presents with acute attacks characterized by abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypertension, mental status changes, seizures, and autonomic instability. These symptoms can be triggered by various factors such as alcohol consumption, fasting, pregnancy, infection, exposure to certain drugs, hormonal therapy, and stress . The diagnosis of AIP involves measuring urinary levels of 1-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (1-HAA) and 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), as well as genetic testing for HMBS mutations . Treatment during acute attacks includes administration of glucose, hemin therapy, and avoidance of precipitating factors .

The treatment of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) typically involves a combination of hemin therapy, glucose infusion to suppress heme biosynthesis, and supportive care . Hemin is administered intravenously at a dose of 30 mg/kg per day in divided doses every 6 hours or continuously as a 5% solution over 24 hours via a central venous catheter if available; otherwise, an peripheral vein can be used . Glucose infusions should be initiated immediately upon diagnosis with a goal blood glucose level between 180–250 mg/dL . Intravenous fluids containing dextrose should not be given due to their ability to induce further oxidative stress .

The symptoms of ADCY5-related dyskinesia include involuntary movements such as chorea, athetosis, or dystonia that can affect any part of the body . These movements may be triggered by certain factors such as stress, fatigue, or physical activity and can occur in isolation or with other movement disorders. Other common features of this condition include cognitive impairment, psychiatric disturbances, and sleep abnormalities .

The most common symptom of adenocarcinoma of the appendix is acute or recurrent right lower quadrant (RLQ) pain that may be associated with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, weight loss, fever, chills, palpable abdominal mass, anorexia, and fatigue .

The term "HIV- or AIDS-related" in reference to cancers indicates that there is a causal relationship between human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection or acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), which results from advanced HIV infection, and the development of certain types of malignancies . This association was first recognized in 1982 with the occurrence of Kaposi's sarcoma among patients diagnosed with AIDS . Since then, numerous additional tumor types have been identified as being associated with HIV infection or AIDS, including non-Hodgkin's lymphomas (NHLs), cervical cancer, anal cancer, Hodgkin's disease, lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck region .

The usual treatment for HIV-related Kaposi sarcoma (KS) involves antiretroviral therapy to control HIV infection along with localized radiation therapy, surgical excision of lesions, cryosurgery, or systemic chemotherapy using doxorubicin, paclitaxel, cisplatin, vincristine, bleomycin, dacarbazine, cyclophosphamide, etoposide, ifosfamide, gemcitabine, docetaxel, vinblastine, vinorelbine, and topotecan .

As of August 2021, there were over 35 ongoing clinical trials listed in ClinicalTrials.gov database that focused specifically on cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCLs) such as mycosis fungoides (MF), Sézary syndrome (SS), and other CTCL subtypes. These included phase I to III trials evaluating various treatment modalities such as topical agents, systemic chemotherapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and cellular therapy approaches using CAR-T cells. Some examples include Nivolumab plus Relaxin in Patients With MF (NCT04687935); Axicabtagene ciloleucel in relapsed or refractory primary cutaneous CD30+ T-Cell Lymphoma (NCT03587447); and Pembrolizumab Plus Azacytidine in Participants With Previously Treated Mycosis Fungioides (NCT03642963). It is important to note that this list may not be exhaustive and more trials may have been initiated but not yet registered in the database.

Primary CNS lymphomas (PCNSL) can be diagnosed by biopsy of brain tissue obtained through surgery, cerebral spinal fluid analysis, MRI scan, PET-CT scan, and CT scan. The most common method is an MRI scan that shows abnormal masses in the brain. A biopsy is also necessary for confirmation.

Lymphomas can occur at any age but are more common among older adults. The incidence of childhood lymphoma varies by type of lymphoma; for example, Hodgkin's lymphoma is more common in adolescents while non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) is more common in younger children.

Recent studies have shown that treatment of pediatric patients with newly diagnosed B cell non-Hodgkin's lymphomas (NHL) has improved over time due to advances in chemotherapy regimens and supportive care measures. The current standard first line therapy is known as Rituximab, EPOCH-R, vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone (REOPCP). This combination has been found to be effective in treating pediatric patients with high risk NHL subtypes such as Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B cell lymphoma.

The long-term prognosis for childhood lymphoma and leukemia depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, type of cancer, stage of disease, response to treatment, and presence of genetic abnormalities. Overall, the cure rate for pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) has increased from 20% in the early 1970s to over 85% today due to advances in chemotherapy regimens, supportive care measures, and targeted therapies . However, some patients may still experience relapse after initial remission, which can be treated with additional cycles of chemotherapy, stem cell transplantation, or other therapeutic approaches.

Cancer of the cervix occurs when abnormal cells grow uncontrollably in the tissue that connects the uterus to the vagina. It can be caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection or other factors such as smoking, having multiple sexual partners, having a history of sexually transmitted diseases, family history of cervical cancer, long-term use of oral contraceptives, and early age at first intercourse .

There are several ongoing clinical trials for cancer of the bladder, prostate, kidney, testicles, ovaries, vagina, cervix, vulva, penis, urethra, fallopian tubes, endometrium (uterus), and other parts of the female reproductive system. These include phase I-III studies evaluating immunotherapy agents such as pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab, durvalumab, and tremelimumab; targeted therapies including olaparib, rucaparib, talazoparib, ribociclib, abemaciclib, palbociclib, and letrozole; hormonal therapy with goserelin acetate, bicalutamide, degarelix sodium, flutamide, leuprorelin acetate, and gosering acetate; chemotherapeutics such as carboplatin, gemcitabine hydrochloride, docetaxel, paclitaxel, vinflunine, irinotecan, and topotecan hydrochloride hydrate; combination regimens consisting of atezolizumab plus cobimetinib, cabozantinib plus everolimus, pembrolizumab plus lenvatin

The most common cause of adult brain and nervous system tumors is exposure to ionizing radiation. Other risk factors include family history of certain types of cancer, genetic syndromes such as neurofibromatosis, and lifestyle factors such as smoking tobacco products and drinking alcohol.

Doctors typically assess children with suspected central nervous system (CNS) tumors by conducting a thorough physical examination, including checking their vital signs such as temperature, pulse rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation levels. They also perform neurological examinations to check reflexes, coordination, balance, sensation, vision, hearing, speech, and swallowing abilities.

The most common cause of pediatric brain tumors is unknown (idiopathic). However, some cases have been linked to genetic syndromes such as neurofibromatosis 1 (NF-1), tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) and Li Fraumeni syndrome (LFS). Congenital brain tumors are rare but may be associated with these same genetic disorders. Most pediatric brain tumors occur after birth, although they can also arise during fetal development.

Pediatric brain tumors are typically classified using the World Health Organization (WHO) classification system, which categorizes tumors into four different grade groups based on histological features such as cellular atypia, mitotic activity, and microvascular proliferation . Grade I tumors are considered benign with low potential to recur after surgical resection; however, they may still have malignant transformation in rare cases. Grade II tumors are considered intermediate risk with a high rate of local recurrence but infrequent metastasis. Grade III tumors are considered high-risk with frequent local recurrences and distant metastases. Finally, grade IV tumors are considered highly aggressive with rapid growth rates and poor overall survival outcomes.

A child with an aggressive brain or spinal cord tumor may experience various signs and symptoms depending on the location of the tumor. Some common symptoms include persistent headache, dizziness, blurred vision, nausea, vomiting, weakness in arms or legs, seizures, difficulty walking, numbness, tingling sensations, back pain, neck stiffness, slurred speech, confusion, personality changes, irritability, depression, anxiety, fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss, and unexplained fever . These symptoms should raise concern for further evaluation to rule out a brain or spinal cord tumor. However, it is important to note that some children with brain or spinal cord tumors do not present with any specific symptoms at all. Therefore, if there is any suspicion of a brain or spinal cord tumor, even without any clear symptoms, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention.

Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (AT/RTs) are aggressive pediatric brain cancers with poor prognosis. The standard treatment regimen includes surgical resection followed by chemotherapy consisting of vincristine, carboplatin, and cyclophosphamide . Radiation therapy is not recommended due to its potential negative effects on neurocognitive development in young patients. In addition, targeted therapies such as mTOR inhibitors have shown promise in preclinical studies but require further investigation before they can be considered an effective option for AT/RT treatment .

Brainstem gliomas can be diagnosed through various methods such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT) scan, positron emission tomography (PET) scan, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and biopsy of tumor tissue. MRI is considered the gold standard for detecting brainstem gliomas due to its ability to provide detailed images of soft tissues without radiation exposure. CT scans may also be ordered in addition to an MRI to rule out other conditions that could cause similar symptoms. PET scans use radioactive tracers to help identify areas of increased metabolism within the brainstem, which can aid in identifying potential tumors. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis involves collecting fluid from around the spinal cord and testing it for abnormal cells or proteins. Biopsies involve removing small pieces of tissue from the suspected tumor site using a needle under image guidance. These samples are then examined by pathologists who look for specific features associated with brainstem gliomas, including high cellularity, nuclear atypia, mitotic figures, and necrosis.

Embryonal tumors of the central nervous system (ET CNS) refer to a group of rare malignant neoplasms that arise from undifferentiated cells during early fetal development . These tumors account for approximately 1% of all childhood cancers and occur most commonly in infants and young children under the age of five years old . The most common sites of origin include the posterior fossa region of the brain, followed by the supratentorial compartment and the spine .

There are several ongoing clinical trials for pediatric patients with rare embryonal brain or CNS tumors that may be found at ClinicalTrials.gov (https://clinicaltrials.gov). Families of such patients should consult their healthcare provider to determine which trial(s) would be most appropriate for them. In addition, they may also consider consulting with a pediatric oncology specialist who has experience treating rare embryonal brain or CNS tumors.

Germ cell tumors (GCTs) are rare malignant neoplasms that originate from primordial germ cells during embryonic development . They account for approximately 2% of all pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors and occur most commonly within the ovaries, testes, anterior mediastinum, retroperitoneal space, and pineal gland . GCTs arising in the posterior fossa or spine are extremely uncommon, accounting for less than 1% of CNS GCTs .

Craniopharyngiomas are benign (noncancerous) tumors that arise from remnants of embryonic tissue at the base of the brain near the hypothalamus . They account for approximately 1% to 3% of all primary intracranial neoplasms and typically affect children between the ages of 5 and 20 years old . The exact cause of these tumors remains unknown; however, they may be associated with genetic mutations or exposure to radiation .

Pediatric brain tumors can be classified into two main categories: benign and malignant. The most common type of benign tumor in children is called craniopharyngioma (CP), which arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch during embryogenesis . CP accounts for 5%-20% of all intracranial neoplasms in childhood and usually occurs between ages five to twelve years old. It has an incidence rate of one per million people annually worldwide .

The most common presenting symptom of pediatric brain tumors is an increase in intracranial pressure (ICP), which can manifest as persistent headache that wakes them up at night, nausea and vomiting, blurred vision, double vision, difficulty walking, dizziness, weakness in one arm or leg, numbness, seizures, and irritability .

The standard treatment of pediatric ependymomas involves surgical resection followed by radiation therapy (RT) with concurrent chemotherapy (CT). If surgery cannot be performed due to tumor location, RT alone may be used as primary treatment. For recurrent or progressive disease after initial treatment, second-line therapies include repeat surgery, CT, RT, and targeted molecular therapies such as mTOR inhibitors.

The prognosis of adult patients with a primary liver tumor depends on various factors such as the type of liver cancer, stage at diagnosis, age, overall health status, presence of comorbidities, and treatment received. Generally speaking, the 5-year survival rate for all types of liver cancers combined is approximately 18%, while the median life expectancy after diagnosis is typically less than one year . However, it should be noted that this varies greatly depending on the specific type of liver cancer. For example, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has a relatively better prognosis compared to other types of liver cancer, with a reported 5-year survival rate of up to 30% in some cases . On the other hand, cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer), which accounts for about 20% of all primary liver cancers, generally has a much worse prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of only around 5–10%.

Cholangiocarcinoma can occur anywhere within the biliary tree, including the hepatic ducts, common bile duct, cystic duct, and gall bladder. Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) refer to malignant tumors that arise from the epithelial cells lining the intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts. The most common type is cholangiocarcinoma, which arises from the extrahepatic bile ducts, including the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, right and left hepatic ducts, and the main bile duct.

Doctors may use several methods to diagnose pediatric hepatoblastoma (HB). These include physical examination, imaging tests such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET), blood tests for alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels, and biopsy of the liver tissue. AFP is a protein produced by HB cells that can be detected in the bloodstream. Elevated AFP levels suggest HB but cannot confirm it. Biopsies involve removing small pieces of liver tissue using a needle inserted through the skin and into the liver under CT guidance. The samples are then examined under a microscope to look for signs of cancerous cells.
The main type of primary liver cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

Doctors use several methods to diagnose bone and soft tissue cancers in children and teenagers. These include physical examination, imaging tests such as X-rays, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT) scans, positron emission tomography (PET) scans, ultrasound, and biopsy of the affected area. The results from these tests help rule out other conditions that may cause similar symptoms.

There have been several ongoing clinical trials in recent years that aim to improve treatment outcomes for patients with osteosarcoma. These include phase II and III trials of novel chemotherapy regimens such as olaparib (NCT03741256), pembrolizumab (NCT03890516) and nivolumab (NCT03905109). Other trials are evaluating the use of targeted agents such as mTOR inhibitors (NCT03259125) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (NCT03747024). Additionally, there is an ongoing trial investigating the efficacy of hyperthermic isolated limb perfusion combined with melphalan in treating high-grade soft tissue sarcomas including osteosarcoma (NCT03333354).
