Hormone-producing neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) can occur anywhere in the body but are most commonly found in the lungs, pancreas, small intestines, appendix, colon, rectum, and stomach . The exact cause is unknown, although certain factors may increase the risk of developing NETs. These include older age, male sex, smoking tobacco products, exposure to radiation, genetic predisposition, and some underlying medical conditions such as autoimmune disorders, celiac disease, and diabetes mellitus .

The usual treatment of GI neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) depends on various factors such as location, size, grade, stage, and symptoms. Surgery is typically the first line of treatment for resectable NENs to remove the primary tumor and any metastases. However, surgery may not be feasible or appropriate for all patients due to the extent of disease or associated risks. In these cases, other treatments may be considered depending on the type and stage of the tumor.

A chronic myeloproliferative disorder (MPD) can be diagnosed through a combination of clinical symptoms, physical examination findings, laboratory tests, and imaging studies such as ultrasound or CT scans to assess for splenomegaly. The diagnosis is confirmed by identifying specific genetic mutations associated with MPDs using molecular testing techniques such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Doctors use several methods to diagnose polycythemia vera (PV), including measuring hematocrit levels, performing peripheral blood smear examination, and testing for JAK2 V617F mutation. Patients with PV may also have enlarged spleen or liver, so abdominal ultrasound can be used as an imaging test.

Myelofibrosis is a chronic disease with no cure available at this time. Treatment options depend on several factors including age, overall health status, risk stratification (low-, intermediate-1, intermediate-2, high-risk), and symptoms. The goal of treatment is to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life.

The rare blood disorder you are referring to is called chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). It is characterized by an abnormal proliferation of immature cells derived from the bone marrow that accumulate in the peripheral bloodstream. CML is not typically classified as a type of leukemia because it does not exhibit the same degree of uncontrolled growth and spread as other types of leukemias. However, CML can be treated with similar therapies such as chemotherapy or targeted therapy using tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) .
The blood or bone marrow disorder in which cells both fail to mature normally and proliferate excessively is called myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN).

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) can occur at any age but is more common in people over 50 years old. It affects men and women equally. The exact cause of CLL is unknown, but certain genetic factors may increase the risk of developing this condition.

The most common sign of this condition is enlargement of lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy). Other possible signs include anemia, jaundice, petechial rash, hepatosplenomegaly, bleeding diathesis, thrombosis, and neurological manifestations.

The prognosis of MPN depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, type of MPN, risk stratification group, presence of certain genetic mutations, and treatment received. In general, patients with essential thrombocythemia (ET) have better survival rates than those with polycythemia vera (PV) or myelofibrosis (MF). Patients with PV tend to have lower survival rates compared to ET or primary myelofibrosis (PMF), while secondary myelofibrosis (SMF) has poorer outcomes than PMF.

The medical term for this condition is endometrial hyperplasia (EH). EH refers to an overgrowth of cells in the inner layer of the uterus, which may be benign or malignant. It is not always associated with abnormal uterine bleeding, but when it occurs, it can lead to heavy menstrual periods, irregular spotting between periods, and postmenopausal bleeding .

Uterine cancer is typically staged using the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) system. This involves taking into account tumor size, depth of invasion, lymph node involvement, and metastasis to other organs or tissues . The FIGO stage I indicates that the cancer has only invaded the inner layer of the uterus; while stages II-IV indicate increasing degrees of spread beyond the uterus.

The most common symptom of endometrial cancer is abnormal vaginal bleeding that occurs during or outside of menstruation in postmenopausal women. Other symptoms include pelvic pain, discharge with an unpleasant odor, weight loss, fatigue, dyspareunia (painful intercourse), diarrhea, constipation, and indigestion .

There have been several recent advances in the treatment of uterine sarcomas. The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is currently conducting a phase II trial to evaluate the efficacy of pembrolizumab as a second-line therapy for advanced uterine sarcomas (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03917458). Pembrolizumab is an anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) antibody that has shown promising results in other types of soft tissue sarcomas .

Germ cell tumors (GCTs) in children can occur anywhere in the body but most commonly arise from the gonads or extragonadal sites . The most common primary site of GCTs is the testis in males and ovaries in females during adolescence, accounting for 2–4% of all childhood malignancies . Extragonadal GCTs account for approximately 10-15% of pediatric GCTs and typically develop in midline structures such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, pineal region, and sacrococcygeal area .

There are several ongoing clinical trials that aim to improve outcomes for patients with relapsed or refractory solid extra-cranial germ cell tumors (GCTs). These include phase I/II trials evaluating the safety and efficacy of novel agents such as olaparib, rucaparib, niraparib, and irinotecan plus cisplatin combination therapy. Other trials are investigating the use of targeted therapies such as antiangiogenic drugs and immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The general prognosis of extragonadal germ cell tumor (EGCT) depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, primary site involvement, stage, histology, presence or absence of metastasis, and response to treatment. Overall, EGCT has an excellent prognosis with 5-year overall survival rates ranging from 80% to over 90%. However, patients with advanced disease have poorer outcomes compared to those with early-stage disease. For example, in one study, the 5-year overall survival rate was 72% for patients with stage III disease but increased to 100% for patients with stage I disease . Additionally, the type of histology can also affect the prognosis. Mixed germ cell tumors tend to be more aggressive than pure germ cell tumors and may require more intensive chemotherapy regimens .

Melanomas of the eye can occur anywhere in the ocular region including the conjunctiva (the mucous membrane that lines the inside of the eyelids), cornea (clear outer layer at the front of the eye), iris (colored part of the eye), ciliary body (tissue behind the iris), lens (transparent structure located behind the iris), vitreous humor (jelly-like substance that fills up the space between the lens and retina) or uvea (middle layer of the eyeball consisting of the iris, choroid, and retina).

Melanomas of the conjunctiva (the mucous membrane that lines the inner eyelids) and orbit are usually treated surgically by enucleation (removal of the entire globe), exenteration (complete removal of all ocular tissue), or orbital exenteration (partial removal of surrounding tissues). Radiation therapy may also be used as an adjuvant to surgery or as primary treatment when surgery is not possible due to tumor location or patient preference. Systemic chemotherapy and immunotherapy can be considered for advanced cases or metastatic disease.

There is no evidence that taking photographs can detect early ocular tumors. However, there may be other symptoms to look out for, such as a white pupil (leukocoria), squinting, redness, tearing, pain, or decreased visual acuity. If any of these symptoms occur, it is recommended to consult an ophthalmologist immediately.

There is ongoing research into novel treatments for retinoblastoma (RB) and other pediatric ocular tumors. Some of these include targeted therapies such as anti-VEGF agents, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and immunotherapies like CAR T cells . Clinical trials involving these approaches have shown promising results but further investigation is needed to determine their efficacy and safety profiles. Other areas of focus include developing better diagnostic tools and imaging techniques, improving surgical procedures, and exploring combination therapy strategies. It is important to note that while there has been significant progress made in recent years, more research is still required to develop effective treatments for RB and other rare childhood eye cancers.

There are several symptoms that may indicate a serious cancer of the lower abdomen or pelvis, such as persistent pain in the lower back, groin, rectum, or vagina; unexplained weight loss; bloating or swelling in the stomach or intestines; difficulty eating or feeling full quickly when eating; constipation or diarrhea; bleeding from the anus; discomfort during urination; and foul-smelling gas or stools. It is important to note that these symptoms could also be caused by less severe conditions, so it is crucial for individuals experiencing any of them to consult with their healthcare provider.

There are several ongoing clinical trials for ovarian cancer that aim to evaluate novel therapies in combination with standard chemotherapy regimens. One such trial is evaluating the addition of olaparib (a PARP inhibitor) to carboplatin-paclitaxel therapy as first-line treatment for patients with high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma . Another study is investigating the use of bevacizumab (an antiangiogenic agent) combined with platinum-based chemotherapy as maintenance therapy after response has been achieved with initial platinum-based chemotherapy .

The stage of an ovarian germ cell tumor determines how far the cancer cells have spread from where they started. Staging involves imaging tests such as ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, PET scan, blood test, and laparoscopy to determine if the cancer has spread outside of the ovary. Based on these results, the staging system classifies ovarian germ cell tumors into stages I–IV. Stage I indicates that the cancer is confined within one ovary; stage II means that the cancer has spread beyond one ovary but remains localized in the pelvis; stage III refers to metastasis to other parts of the abdomen, while stage IV describes distant organ involvement .

Doctors use various diagnostic tools to differentiate between a borderline ovarian tumor (BOT), a benign cytology, and malignant ovarian cancer. The most common method used by gynecologic oncologists for diagnosing BOTs is transvaginal ultrasound-guided needle aspiration biopsy of the mass. During this procedure, a small sample of tissue from inside the mass is removed using a thin needle under ultrasound guidance. This allows the doctor to examine the cells under a microscope to see if they look like normal cells or have any signs of being cancerous. Other tests that may be done include blood tests, laparoscopy with biopsy, and imaging such as CT scans or MRIs. It's important to note that while these tests can help in making a diagnosis, it's always best to consult with a healthcare provider who has experience in treating patients with ovarian masses or cysts.

Cancer that occurs in the ovary is called primary ovarian cancer (POC). POC accounts for 3% to 4% of all malignancies in women worldwide . The most common type of POC is epithelial carcinoma which includes serous, endometrioid, clear cell, and mucinous histology. Other rare subtypes include germ cell tumors, sex cord-stromal neoplasm, metastatic disease, and mixed histologies.

Cancer of the hepatobiliary region can occur at any age but is more common among individuals aged 50 years or older. The risk increases with advancing age. It occurs slightly more often in men than women. However, it may also be seen in children.

The standard treatments for gall bladder cancer include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy or a combination of these modalities depending upon the stage at diagnosis. For early stages (stage I), surgical resection is recommended while patients with advanced disease may be treated with palliative care.

There is ongoing research into several potential therapies for penile cancer, including immunotherapy with programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) inhibitors such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab, which have shown promise in early clinical trials . Other novel therapeutic approaches include targeted therapy using vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibition , photodynamic therapy , and gene therapy using viral vectors to deliver tumor suppressors like p53 . Additionally, there has been interest in developing more effective adjuvant chemotherapies for high-risk patients, particularly those with lymph node involvement at diagnosis .

Symptoms such as severe abdominal pain with fever, vaginal bleeding, prolonged labor (more than 12 hours), persistent headaches, blurred vision, convulsions, swelling of face, hands, or feet, shortness of breath, chest pain, high blood pressure (systolic BP > 140 mmHg and diastolic BP > 90 mmHg) can be indicative of a serious condition that requires immediate attention from a healthcare provider.

There have been several ongoing clinical trials in patients with GTD. One such trial is NCT03856149 (ClinicalTrials.gov), which aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of chemotherapy regimens using methotrexate and actinomycin D as first-line therapy in low-risk GTN. Another study, NCT02723003 (ClinicalTrials.gov) is evaluating the use of single-agent MTX maintenance therapy compared to observation alone in women who achieve complete remission after initial treatment for high-intermediate risk GTN.

The usual long-term prognosis for Langerhans Cell Histocytosis (LCH) depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, organ involvement, and genetic mutations. Most children with single-organ disease have an excellent prognosis after treatment, while those with multisystem disease may require more aggressive treatments and have a higher risk of relapse. Adults with LCH often have a poorer prognosis than children due to increased rates of multiorgan involvement and resistance to chemotherapy.

The highest risk of developing cancer in the lower throat or nearby areas (such as esophagus) includes individuals who smoke tobacco products, consume alcohol regularly, have human papillomavirus infection, and are exposed to radiation.

The usual treatments for cancer of the throat near the voice box and swallowing area include surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy depending upon the stage at diagnosis . Surgery is often used to remove early-stage tumors that have not spread to surrounding tissues. Chemotherapy may be given before or after surgery to help reduce the risk of recurrence. Radiation therapy uses high doses of radiation to kill cancer cells. Targeted therapy involves using drugs to target specific molecules involved in cell growth and survival.

The main factors that increase the likelihood of developing throat or laryngeal cancer include smoking tobacco (cigarettes, cigars, pipes), heavy alcohol consumption, exposure to secondhand smoke, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, poor oral hygiene, diet low in fruits and vegetables, occupational exposures such as wood dusts, textile industry dyes, formaldehydes, and other chemicals, radiation therapy for head and neck cancers, family history of upper aerodigestive tract cancers, chronic inflammatory conditions like reflux esophagitis, and long-term use of snuff or chewing tobacco.

The usual treatment options for cancer of the throat or voice box include medication (chemotherapy), surgery, radiation therapy, and targeted therapy. Treatment depends on several factors including stage at diagnosis, location of tumor within the head and neck region, size of the tumor, presence of lymph node involvement, and overall health status of patient. For early-stage cancers, chemotherapy alone may be used to treat small lesions that have not spread beyond the mucosal layer. Surgery with or without adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy is typically recommended for patients who present with moderate-to-advanced disease stages. Radiation therapy alone may also be considered depending on the specific type and extent of the cancer. Targeted therapy using monoclonal antibodies has shown promise in treating certain types of head and neck cancers but is still being evaluated for its effectiveness in clinical trials.

Doctors will typically examine any sore or lump in or around the mouth thoroughly by asking about its history (e.g., when did you first notice it, how long has it been present, does it hurt, etc.), physical examination of the area using visual inspection, palpation with fingers, and sometimes additional diagnostic testing such as biopsy or imaging studies like CT scans or MRIs. The appearance of the lesion can be helpful for diagnosis; for example, white patches may indicate oral thrush while red patches could suggest an ulcer caused by trauma or infection. A hard nodule that moves with swallowing might be indicative of a salivary gland tumor. If there is pain associated with the lesion, this could also help guide further evaluation. For instance, if the patient complains of severe pain out of proportion to the size of the lesion, this would raise suspicion for malignancy. In addition, doctors may order blood work to check for certain conditions that could cause swelling in the neck, such as mononucleosis. Ultimately, a biopsy is often necessary to make a definitive diagnosis.

This is known as metastatic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of unknown primary site or MSUP for short. It refers to the presence of SCC cells in a lymph node without an identifiable primary lesion elsewhere in the body. The diagnosis can be made by examining the pathology report from the biopsy of the affected lymph nodes.

The usual treatment for cancer that has spread to the neck lymph nodes with an unknown primary site involves imaging tests such as CT scans or PET scans to identify any suspicious lesions in other parts of the body. If a potential primary site is identified, surgical removal of the tumor may be performed along with chemotherapy and radiation therapy depending on the type of cancer. However, if no primary site can be identified, palliative treatments such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy may be used to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life.

Doctors use several methods to detect head and neck cancer (HNC). The most common method is by conducting physical examinations using an otoscope, which allows them to see into your ears and nose. They may also perform biopsies of suspicious areas and order imaging tests such as CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, and ultrasounds. These tests help determine if there are any signs of HNC that cannot be seen during the physical examination.

Cancer that develops at the back of the throat (oropharynx) can be referred to as an "oropharyngeal" or "throat" cancer. A sore in this area may also be described as a "mouth ulcer," but not all mouth ulcers indicate oral cancer. If someone mentions having a sore in their throat, you should ask them about other symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, pain with swallowing, cough, hoarseness, weight loss, etc., which could suggest a more serious condition like cancer. It's important for them to see a healthcare provider right away so they can get checked out.

The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system for oral cavity cancers includes TNM classification. T stage describes the depth of invasion of the primary tumor, N stage indicates regional lymph node involvement, and M stage represents distant metastasis. Stages I-IV range from localized to highly invasive disease with no evidence of metastases to locally advanced disease with extensive invasion and nodal involvement without distant metastatic disease. Stage IVB is reserved for patients who have distant metastasis .

Nasal or sinus cancer is a type of head and neck cancer that originates in the nose or paranasal sinuses. The most common symptom of this disease is persistent nasal congestion or obstruction, which may also occur with a severe sinus infection or other non-cancerous sinus conditions such as allergies or chronic rhinosinusitis. Other possible symptoms include facial pain or pressure, discharge from the nose or postnasal drainage, loss of smell, difficulty breathing through the nose, ear pain, hearing problems, and a sore throat. It is important to note that these symptoms alone do not necessarily indicate the presence of nasal or sinus cancer, but if they persist for several weeks without improvement despite treatment, further evaluation by a healthcare professional is recommended.

The National Cancer Institute (NCI) has identified several ongoing clinical trials related to cancers of the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and nearby head and neck areas. These include phase I-III studies evaluating targeted therapies such as immunotherapy or radiation therapy in combination with chemotherapeutic agents. Additionally, there are also several other clinical trials investigating novel treatment approaches using stem cells, gene therapy, and nanoparticles. However, none of these have been approved by the FDA yet. It is important to note that this information may change over time due to the rapidly evolving nature of cancer research. Therefore, it is recommended to check the NIH Clinical Trials website for the most up-to-date list of active clinical trials.

The prognosis of salivary gland tumors depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, histopathological subtype, grade, size, location, nodal status, and distant metastasis (1). Generally, the 5-year survival rate ranges from 30% to 84%, with an overall survival rate of approximately 67%. However, some types of salivary gland tumors have better outcomes than others. For example, pleomorphic adenomas have a high recurrence rate but low mortality, while mucoepidermoid carcinoma has both a high recurrence rate and high mortality (2).

There have been several ongoing clinical trials in head and neck cancer (HNC) treatment, which include oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). The National Cancer Institute has listed 154 active interventional clinical trials as of August 2021 . These include phase I to III trials that involve chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapies, vaccines, and other novel approaches such as gene-editing technology.

The prognosis of pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor size, lymph node involvement, distant metastasis, and resectability status . PDAC has an overall 5-year survival rate of less than 10% , with a median overall survival of approximately six months without treatment . However, patients who undergo complete surgical resection have been reported to have a five-year survival rate of up to 24%, while those with locally advanced disease treated with chemotherapy plus radiation therapy have a five-year survival rate of about 7% .

Rare hormone-producing pancreatic gland tumors can be caused by various factors including genetics, environmental exposures, lifestyle habits, and dietary intake. However, there is no clear evidence to suggest that any specific factor increases the risk of developing these types of tumors. It has been observed that some patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) have an increased risk for developing nonfunctioning neuroendocrine tumor (NET). Additionally, certain genetic syndromes like Von Hippel Lindau disease, Carney complex, and tuberous sclerosis may also lead to an elevated risk of NETs .

There have been several recent advances in the treatment of NETs, including targeted therapies such as somatostatin analogues (SSAs), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and mTOR inhibitors. These agents have shown promising results in preclinical models and early phase clinical trials.

Cancer of the renal pelvis (also known as ureteropelvic junction obstruction carcinoma) refers to malignant tumors arising from the renal pelvis or proximal ureters. It differs from kidney cancer because they originate from different parts of the urinary system. Renal cell carcinomas arise from the renal parenchyma, while urothelial carcinomas arise from the collecting tubules of the distal ureters.

The standard treatment for urothelial carcinoma (UC) of the upper urinary tract involves nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff excision. In addition to this surgical approach, adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy may be recommended depending on certain factors such as tumor stage, grade, and presence of high-risk features like lymphovascular invasion or positive margins. Radiation therapy may also be considered in select cases where complete surgical removal cannot be achieved due to concerns about preserving kidney function or other comorbidities.

Doctors typically perform an ultrasound examination of the child's abdomen first to identify any potential masses. If this initial test does not provide enough information for diagnosis, further testing may be recommended such as CT scans with contrast or MRI. These more detailed images can help differentiate between various types of tumors by looking at their size, shape, location within the body, how much blood flows into them from other parts of the body (perfusion), and if there is calcification inside them. In some cases, biopsies may also be needed to confirm the diagnosis.

A breast lump refers to an abnormal growth of cells in the breast tissue that can be felt as a painless mass or thickening under the skin of the breast. Breast cancer occurs when there is an uncontrolled division of normal cells resulting from changes (mutations) in the genetic material of these cells. These mutations may occur due to hereditary factors, exposure to certain hormones such as estrogen and progesterone, radiation therapy, alcohol consumption, smoking, lack of physical activity, obesity, early menarche, late menopause, family history of breast cancer, and age over 50 years old. The exact cause of breast cancer is not yet known but research suggests that it could be caused by a combination of several risk factors.

A new lump or an unusual change in the body can be concerning for patients and may require evaluation to rule out potential cancerous lesions. The first step would be to see a healthcare provider who will ask questions about the patient's history, physical examination findings, and recommend further testing if necessary.

The term for this condition is gynecomastia. It refers to an enlargement of male breasts that can occur due to hormonal imbalances, certain medications, alcohol consumption, obesity, liver disease, or genetic factors. Gynecomastia is not typically associated with breast cancer, although there may be some rare exceptions where both conditions coexist.

The prognosis of male breast cancer depends on various factors such as age, tumor size, grade, lymph node involvement, hormone receptor status, HER2 status, and treatment received. Generally speaking, men with breast cancer have worse overall survival rates than women. However, if the disease is caught early through regular screening or self-examination, the chances of survival can be quite high. If left untreated or detected at a later stage, the average 5-year relative survival rate drops to around 80%. This means that about 8 out of every 10 men who get treated will survive their breast cancer for at least five years after diagnosis. On the other hand, only about half (47%) of those who aren’t treated will still be alive in five years. It's important to note that these statistics vary widely depending on individual circumstances.

As a medical professional, I would recommend that individuals who notice any changes in their skin spots or moles consult with a healthcare provider for further evaluation. The ABCDE rule is an acronym commonly used by dermatologists to assess suspicious lesions (Table 1).

The medical term for this condition is melanocytic nevus (or simply “nevus”). It can appear as an abnormal growth of pigmented cells known as melanocytes. While most moles are benign, some can develop into melanoma, which is a type of skin cancer.

Doctors use several methods to classify the stages of skin cancer in both light-skinned individuals and people with darker complexions. The most commonly used method is the Clark level system, which takes into account various factors such as color, thickness, ulceration, and mitotic activity (the number of times that cells divide). In addition, there are other systems for staging skin cancers, including the Brodder classification system, which considers tumor size, depth, and histologic features; the TNM (tumor, node, metastasis) system, which assesses the extent of spread within the body; and the AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer), which combines these three systems.

The most common sign of melanoma is an abnormal mole or lesion that appears suddenly and grows rapidly without treatment. It may also be asymmetrical in shape, have irregular borders, and present with multiple colors. Other signs include bleeding, oozing, scaling, itching, pain, soreness, or a change in sensation around the area where the tumor is located. Melanomas can also appear as flat or raised areas of pigmented skin on normal-looking moles or birthmarks. They can develop anywhere on the body but are more likely to occur on the face, scalp, neck, arms, hands, feet, and legs. In addition to these visible signs, there may be internal changes such as swollen lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy) under the jaw, in the armpits, or behind the knees.

There have been several ongoing clinical trials related to rare aggressive skin cancers in the past few years. One of them is the phase II study evaluating the efficacy of pembrolizumab (Keytruda) as monotherapy treatment for patients with metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC). The results showed that 52% of participants had an objective response rate, including complete responses in 16%, partial responses in 34%, stable disease in 7%, and progressive disease in 9%. This trial was completed in June 2018 .

The prognosis of multiple myeloma (MM) depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, cytogenetic abnormalities, disease burden, response to initial therapy, and presence of extramedullary disease . In general, MM patients have an overall survival rate of 3–5 years from the time of diagnosis . However, some studies suggest that this may increase up to 10 years in certain patient populations due to advances in treatment options .

No, neuroblastoma is not typically inherited or passed down genetically from a parent. However, there may be some cases of familial neuroblastoma where multiple family members have been diagnosed with the condition. This could potentially suggest that certain genetic factors play a role in increasing susceptibility to developing neuroblastoma. It is important for parents who have had a child diagnosed with neuroblastoma to discuss their concerns about potential future pregnancies with a healthcare provider. Genetic counseling may also be recommended to help determine if any hereditary conditions were involved in the development of neuroblastoma.

The standard of care for low-risk neuroblastoma involves observation with serial imaging studies to monitor disease progression or regression. High-risk neuroblastoma typically requires multimodal therapy consisting of induction chemotherapy followed by surgical resection (if feasible), consolidation chemotherapy, radiation therapy, autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, immunotherapy, and targeted therapies. Treatment strategies may vary depending on tumor stage, age at diagnosis, histology, MYCN amplification status, ploidy, and other molecular markers.
The most common symptoms associated with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) include persistent cough, chest pain, dyspnea, weight loss, weakness, appetite loss, and recurrent infections .

There are several ongoing clinical trials that aim to improve outcomes in patients with NSCLC. One such trial is NCT03194568, which evaluates the efficacy of pembrolizumab (an anti-PD-L1 antibody) plus chemotherapy as first-line therapy for advanced NSCLC. Another study, NCT02773402, compares atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) versus docetaxel as second-line treatment for squamous NSCLC.

Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is typically classified into two stages at diagnosis: limited or extensive disease . Limited SCLC refers to tumors that involve one hemithorax with possible ipsilateral mediastinal lymph node involvement but without distant metastasis. Extensive SCLC involves bilateral pulmonary involvement, contralateral mediastinal lymph nodes, or distant extrathoracic organ sites .

Lung cancer can affect anyone; however, it is more common in men than women. The main risk factor for developing lung cancer is smoking tobacco products such as cigarettes, pipes, cigars, and hookahs. Other risk factors include secondhand smoke exposure, radon gas exposure, asbestos exposure, air pollution, family history of lung cancer, chronic inflammation due to conditions like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and lung diseases caused by long-term exposure to chemicals at work.

Parathyroid cancer is rare with an incidence of 0.5 to 1 cases per million persons annually in the United States . The overall survival rate for patients with parathyroid cancer varies depending on the stage at diagnosis. For localized disease (stage I), the five-year relative survival rates range from approximately 89% to 100%, while for regional spread (stages IIA and IIB) the five-year relative survival rates range from about 76% to 92%. However, these figures may be misleading because they include data from very small numbers of patients .

Penile cancer can be caused by various factors such as smoking tobacco, phimosis (inability to retract foreskin), chronic inflammation due to balanoposthitis (inflammation of the glans penis and foreskin) or lichen sclerosus (a skin condition that causes white patches and thickening of the skin). Poor genital hygiene may also contribute to an increased risk of penile cancer. Certain sexual practices like forceful circumcision without anesthesia, tight prepuce, multiple sex partners, and exposure to irritants have been associated with penile cancer but there is insufficient evidence to prove their causal relationship. Older men over 60 years old are at higher risk for developing penile cancer than younger men.

Male genitourinary (GU) malignancies include prostate, testicular, penile, bladder, renal pelvis, ureteral, and kidney cancers. Treatment of GU tumors depends on several factors including age, performance status, comorbidities, stage at diagnosis, histology, grade, and patient preference .

Doctors can use several methods to diagnose pituitary tumors, including physical examinations, blood tests, urine analysis, and imaging studies such as MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). Blood tests may reveal high levels of certain hormones that suggest a problem with the pituitary gland. Imaging studies using CT (computed tomography) or MRI can help identify any abnormalities in the size or shape of the pituitary gland. In addition, an endocrinologist will likely order additional testing to determine which specific hormones are affected by the tumor.

Prostate cancer is a type of cancer that affects the prostate gland, which produces fluid for semen. It usually grows slowly and may not cause any problems at first. However, if left untreated or unmanaged, it can spread to other parts of the body such as bones, lymph nodes, lungs, liver, etc., leading to metastasis. This condition can be life-threatening.

The usual treatment options for male genital cancers depend on various factors such as the type, stage, grade, location, size, and overall health status of the patient. Active surveillance may be recommended in some cases where the tumor is small (less than 1 cm), low-grade, and not causing any symptoms or functional impairment. In these cases, active surveillance involves regular monitoring through physical exams, imaging tests, and biopsies to check if there has been any change in the tumor over time. If no changes occur after several years of follow-up, then surgery or other treatments may not be necessary.

Bowel or colorectal cancer can affect anyone, but there are some factors that increase the likelihood of getting this disease. These include age (the risk increases after 50 years old), smoking tobacco products, having a diet high in fat and low in fiber, being overweight or obese, drinking alcoholic beverages regularly, not exercising enough, having a personal or family history of colon polyps or colorectal cancer, long-term inflammatory conditions like ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, type II diabetes mellitus, and radiation therapy to the pelvic area. Therefore, these individuals should take extra precautions to prevent the development of colorectal cancer by adopting healthy lifestyle choices and undergoing regular screening tests.

The usual treatment options for advanced-stage (Stage III) colorectal cancer include chemotherapy with or without targeted therapy, immunotherapy, radiation therapy, and surgical resection of the tumor. Treatment decisions may vary depending on the location of the primary tumor within the colon or rectum. For example, patients with Stage III colon cancer typically receive chemotherapy alone, while those with Stage III rectal cancer often undergo neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by surgery.

Rectal bleeding is one of the most common symptoms associated with colorectal cancer (CRC). Other symptoms include changes in bowel habits such as diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia, etc. The American Cancer Society recommends that people over 50 years old should get screened for CRC every ten years through either colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, stool test, or CT scan .

The correct term for this condition is colorectal cancer (CRC). It refers to any malignant tumor arising from the epithelial cells of the large intestine or rectum. CRC is one of the most common types of cancer worldwide, with approximately 1 million new cases diagnosed each year .

Small bowel cancer can occur in any individual regardless of their gender, race, or ethnicity. However, there are some known risk factors that may increase an individual's chance of developing this type of cancer. These include older age (most cases are diagnosed in people over 60 years old), smoking tobacco products, having a personal or family history of other types of gastrointestinal tumors, and exposure to radiation from sources like X-rays or atomic bomb. Certain genetic syndromes like Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, juvenile polyposis, neurofibromatosis type I, tuberous sclerosis, and Cowden disease have also been linked with increased risk of small bowel cancer. Additionally, individuals who have had inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis for many years may be more likely to develop small bowel cancer later in life.

Cancer in the small intestine can be treated with surgical resection (removal) followed by chemotherapy to kill any remaining cells that may have spread from the tumor. Radiation therapy may also be used as an alternative to surgery if the cancer cannot be removed completely. Targeted drug therapy such as monoclonal antibodies may also be used depending on the type of cancer.

Thymic carcinoma or thymic epithelial tumors are classified according to the World Health Organization classification of lung tumors . Doctors may use several methods to determine if there is an underlying cause of the symptoms beyond a simple UTI or irritant. These include physical examination, imaging studies (such as ultrasound, CT scan, MRI), cystoscopy (a procedure that uses a camera inserted into the bladder through the urethra) with biopsy (taking tissue samples for analysis under a microscope). The doctor will also consider factors such as age, family history, and other risk factors associated with certain conditions. It's important to note that while these tests can help identify potential causes of the symptoms, they cannot definitively diagnose cancer without further testing. If any concerning findings are detected during evaluation, it's crucial to follow up with additional diagnostic procedures to rule out potentially life-threatening conditions.

There could be several reasons why there might be an unusual sore or growth in the external genitals. Some of these include balanoposthitis (inflammation of the foreskin), lichen sclerosus, penile papilloma, condylomata acuminata (genital warts), psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, syphilis, herpes simplex virus 2 infection, human papillomavirus infection, actinomycosis, molluscum contagiosum, cutaneous lupus vulgaris, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, Bowen's disease, Paget's disease, Kaposi sarcoma, and penile cancer .

The National Cancer Institute (NCI) has reported that there were 132,600 new cases of female genital malignancies in the United States alone in 2020 . In addition to cervical cancer, endometrial carcinoma is also one of the most common types of cancer among women worldwide . Although surgery remains the primary treatment option for both diseases, chemotherapy and radiotherapy have been used as adjuvant therapies for decades . However, due to the high recurrence rate of these two tumors after conventional therapy, it is crucial to develop novel therapeutics with fewer side effects and higher efficacy.

Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) have been shown to be associated with genetic factors . A family history of AAA is one of the most important risk factors for developing this condition . The prevalence of AAAs among first-degree relatives of patients who underwent surgical repair was found to be 10%–25%, which is significantly higher than that observed in the general population .

The rare condition known as familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects the proper absorption of lipids and fat-soluble vitamins, leading to extremely low levels of serum cholesterol . It typically presents with retinal detachment during infancy or early childhood. FEVR can also be acquired due to other conditions such as trauma, inflammation, or infection.

If a baby is born with part of the lower leg bone, such as the shin bone, missing or underdeveloped, this condition may be called congenital absence or hypoplasia of the fibula (CAHF). This can occur either unilaterally or bilaterally. CAHF usually presents with painless swelling in the calf area during infancy. It often goes undiagnosed until an X-ray is performed for other reasons. The exact cause of CAHF is unknown but genetic factors have been implicated. Treatment typically involves physical therapy to improve range of motion and correct any resulting deformities. Surgery may also be required in severe cases. Prognosis is generally good, although some individuals with CAHF may develop complications later in life, including recurrent infections, compartment syndrome, and chronic venous insufficiency.

The condition you are referring to is likely scleroderma. Scleroderma is an autoimmune disease characterized by hardening and tightening of the skin due to excessive collagen production. It can cause dark, thickened skin in body folds such as the fingers, toes, face, and forearms. Other symptoms include enlargement of the joints (hand and foot swelling), muscle weakness, fatigue, and gastrointestinal issues. If a person has these symptoms, it's important for them to see their healthcare provider who may refer them to a rheumatologist for further evaluation. Treatment options vary depending on the severity of the disease but typically involve medications to reduce inflammation and manage pain. Lifestyle modifications such as exercise, physical therapy, and avoiding triggers like smoking can also help alleviate some symptoms.

An extra small bone or bump on the inner side of the foot (known as an os peroneum) may be present at birth or develop due to repetitive stresses caused by abnormal walking mechanics or injuries. The cause cannot always be determined.
The medical term for this condition is dysphagia due to esophageal achalasia. Yes, it can be classified as a type of swallowing disorder (dysphagia).

The rare hormonal or metabolic disorders that affect both hair growth and menstruation include polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), Turner Syndrome, Cushing’s disease, and Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS). PCOS is characterized by irregular menstruation, hirsutism, acne, obesity, insulin resistance, and infertility . CAH is an autosomal recessive genetic condition caused by mutations of the gene encoding 21-hydroxylase enzyme. It presents at birth as ambiguous genitals, salt wasting crisis, virilization, precocious puberty, and delayed pubertal development . Turner Syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality affecting one X chromosome. It has various clinical manifestations such as short stature, ovarian dysfunction, cardiovascular anomalies, hypertension, and hearing loss . Cushing's disease results from prolonged exposure to high levels of cortisol due to pituitary tumors secreting ACTH . AIS is an inherited disorder resulting from defects in androgen receptors. Patients have normal female external genitalia but develop male internal genital structures and testicles instead of uteri .

Doctors can diagnose this condition by conducting physical examinations of patients with their parents’ help. They may also order radiological studies such as X-rays, CT scans, MRI, ultrasound, and bone density testing to identify any unusual features in the bones. Genetic testing is another option for confirmatory diagnosis.

The medical term for this condition is Achondroplasia. It is an autosomal dominant disorder that results from mutations in the FGFR3 gene, leading to abnormal bone development and disproportionate features such as shorter limbs relative to the trunk, frontal bossing, midface flattening, and lumbar lordosis.

The condition where a person is born with dwarfism is known as achondroplasia (ACP). It is caused by mutations in the FGFR3 gene that lead to abnormal bone growth during fetal development. On the other hand, severe immunodeficiency can be caused by various genetic defects affecting different parts of the immune system, including SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency), WAS (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome) and XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). While some forms of ACP may have mild immune deficiencies, it is not considered an autoimmune disorder like SCID, WAS or XLA.

The acquired bleeding or clotting disorder that can develop later in life and cause easy bruising or excessive bleeding without an obvious reason is called idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). It is caused by antibodies against platelets.

The rare congenital condition known as Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (SCS) is characterized by craniosynostosis and limb anomalies such as polydactyly or syndactyly of the hands and feet . Cranial deformities caused by premature fusion of one or more sutures in SCS include brachycephaly with underdeveloped frontal bones, trigonocephaly, and plagiocephaly . Symptoms may vary depending on the age at which they appear; for example, infants may have feeding difficulties due to facial asymmetry, while older children may experience vision problems from flattening of their foreheads .

Catania syndrome is also known as oculoauriculovertebral dysplasia spectrum (OAVDS). It is a rare autosomal dominant disorder characterized by craniofacial malformations, vertebrae defects, hearing loss, eye abnormalities, and other systemic anomalies. The facial deformity includes micrognathia, short nose with depressed nasal bridge, low-set ears, and ear lobe atrophy. Other common manifestations include cervical spine fusion, rib fusions, spinal cord meningoceles, and sensorineural hearing loss. Infantile hypotonia may be present. Diagnosis can be made through clinical examination and confirmed by genetic testing for mutation in the PITX1 gene. Treatment involves management of associated conditions such as feeding problems, respiratory distress, and hearing impairments. Surgery may be required to correct skeletal and joint deformities.

Acromegaly is characterized by excess growth hormone (GH) levels due to pituitary tumors. In addition to enlarged hands and facial features, other common signs and symptoms include enlarged feet, soft tissue swelling in the tongue, jaw, and face, headaches, vision changes, sweating, fatigue, sleep apnea, carpal tunnel syndrome, high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, osteoarthritis, and decreased sexual function.

The inherited disorder known as acroosteolysis is characterized by resorption of the distal phalanges resulting in shortened fingers with tapered ends. It can be associated with other conditions such as osteogenesis imperfecta type V or dyschondrodysplasia. Symptoms include painless shortening of the fingers, especially the middle and ring fingers, which may lead to difficulty performing fine motor tasks. Other common features include blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss, and joint hypermobility .

The signs and symptoms of a severe adverse reaction to alcohol shortly after drinking include flushing, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, confusion, tremors, seizures, coma, abnormal heart rate, arrhythmia, hypotension, cardiac arrest, respiratory depression, pulmonary edema, cerebral edema, liver failure, pancreatitis, and death.

The rare intermittent condition you are referring to may be acute porphyria. Acute porphyrias are a group of rare genetic disorders characterized by an overproduction of heme in the liver due to defects in enzymes involved in heme biosynthesis. This can lead to neuropsychiatric manifestations such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, anxiety, panic attacks, seizures, psychosis, hypertension, tachycardia, autonomic instability, and respiratory failure .

Acute intermittent porphyrias (AIPs) are rare genetic disorders characterized by overproduction of heme due to deficiencies in enzymes involved in heme biosynthesis . AIPs can present with acute attacks known as porphyric crises, which may be triggered by various factors such as fasting, alcohol consumption, infection, or hormonal changes . The most common type of AIP is variegate porphyria (VP), followed by hereditary coproporphyria (HCP) and acute intermittent porphyria (AIP).

The typical signs and symptoms of this condition include involuntary jerking or twisting movements of one limb or multiple limbs at rest or during sleep, which may last for seconds to minutes and occur several times per day. These movements often worsen when the affected person is tired or stressed. It can also cause difficulties with balance, walking, writing, speaking, swallowing, and other activities of daily living. This condition can affect people of all ages but typically presents before age 20 years old.

The most common symptom associated with appendiceal malignancy is right lower quadrant pain that may be persistent or intermittent over several days to weeks. Other possible signs include nausea, vomiting, fever, weight loss, anorexia, diarrhea, constipation, palpable mass, and rectal bleeding .

The rare metabolic disorder you are referring to is called Methylmalonic Acidemia (MMA). It is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects 1 in 60,000 newborns worldwide . In MMA, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase enzyme activity is reduced due to genetic defects, leading to accumulation of toxic levels of methylmalonic acid in body tissues such as blood, urine, liver, heart, and brain. This can result in neurological symptoms including developmental delay, seizures, intellectual disability, cerebral edema, coma, and even death during infancy or early childhood.

The most common cause of these lesions is lipoma, which is benign and does not require treatment unless it becomes large enough to interfere with daily activities or grows rapidly. Lipomas can occur anywhere in the body but are more commonly found in the upper back, shoulders, neck, arms, thighs, buttocks, and hips. They may also develop from existing moles or birthmarks. Other possible causes include angiolipoma (a type of noncancerous tumor), sebaceous cyst, epidermal inclusion cyst, dermatofibroma, neurofibroma, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and mycosis fungoides. It is important for patients to consult their healthcare provider if concerned about any new or unusual growths.

The most common sign of Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is hypotonia in infancy. Other signs include feeding difficulties, growth retardation, poor weight gain, failure to thrive, hyperphagia, and obesity later in life. Behavioral problems may also occur, including autistic features, temper tantrums, obsessive compulsions, anxiety, and learning disabilities. Prenatal diagnosis can be made by detecting maternal disomy 15 or an interstitial deletion using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis after birth. Early recognition of PWS can help prevent complications related to malnutrition and excessive food intake.

The usual treatment for mild to moderate scoliosis in teenagers involves physical therapy exercises, corrective braces, and pain medication such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). If these methods fail, surgical correction may be necessary. Surgery typically involves fusing multiple vertebrae with rods and screws to straighten the spine. Other treatments include spinal traction, electrical stimulation, and acupuncture. Observation is usually reserved for very young children with small curves that have not yet reached skeletal maturity. Bracing is often used in combination with other therapies, especially before surgery.
The rare condition you are referring to is called Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD). It is classified as an autoinflammatory disorder rather than an autoimmune disease.

The yellowish buildup or spot you mentioned is called drusen. Drusen can cause age-related macular degeneration (AMD), which is one of the leading causes of blindness among older people worldwide. AMD occurs when there is damage to the cells of the eye's light-sensitive tissue known as the retina. There are two types of AMD: dry and wet. Dry AMD is more common than wet AMD but less severe. Wet AMD usually results from abnormal blood vessels under the retina that leak fluid and blood into the center of the macula. This leads to rapid and significant loss of vision.

Conditions that can lead to a person being born with very low blood clotting factors include congenital factor deficiencies such as hemophilia A (deficiency of Factor VIII) and B (deficiency of FIX). These conditions may also develop later in life due to acquired inhibitors against these factors. Unexplained bleeding could occur from other causes like autoimmune disorders, liver disease, certain medications, and some genetic diseases.

The term "pancreatic agenesis" refers to a congenital absence of all or part of the pancreas. It occurs in 1 out of every 20,000 births worldwide . Pancreatic agenesis may be partial (45%), total (37%), or complete (18%) .

Type I NIID is characterized by recurrent episodes of fever, headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, and lethargy. It can also present with developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, dystonic movements, and epilepsy.
