Biopsies involve removing small pieces of tissue from the suspected area using a needle under local anesthesia. These samples are then examined by pathologists who look for abnormal cells that indicate STS.

The most common types of sarcomas that can occur in children are rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and synovial sarcoma. RMS accounts for approximately 4% of all childhood cancers, with about half of these cases occurring in infants under one year old. Osteosarcoma typically affects adolescents aged 10 to 20 years old, while Ewing sarcoma occurs more frequently in younger patients, usually between five and 15 years old. Synovial sarcoma tends to affect individuals over age 30 but may also occur in children or young adults. Other less common types of pediatric soft tissue sarcomas include desmoplastic small round cell tumors, extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcomas, clear cell sarcomas, alveolar soft part sarcomas, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, liposarcomas, leiomyosarcomas, angiosarcomas, and fibrosarcomas.

Pediatric soft tissue sarcomas (STS) can be divided into two main categories: benign tumors that do not have malignant potential and malignant tumors with varying degrees of aggressiveness and metastatic potential. The most common types of STS in children include rhabdomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, Ewing’s sarcoma, osteosarcoma, lipoma, fibrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, and desmoid tumor .

In pediatric patients with solid tumors, treatment is determined by several factors including age at diagnosis, location and size of the tumor, stage or grade of disease, presence of metastasis, and other clinical characteristics. For most childhood cancers, multimodal therapy involving surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation is used to treat localized disease. Surgery may be performed as primary therapy for some tumors such as neuroblastoma, while others may require adjuvant surgical resection after initial chemotherapy (e.g., Wilms’ tumor). Chemotherapy is often given before or after surgery depending on the specific type of cancer. Radiation therapy may also play a role in the management of certain pediatric malignancies.

Doctors typically use several different diagnostic tests and procedures to evaluate for Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). These include physical examination, blood test such as complete blood count (CBC) with differential, biopsy of affected tissue or lymph node, CT scan, PET-CT scan, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, and fine needle aspiration (FNA) of lymph nodes . The diagnosis is confirmed by histopathological evaluation of cells obtained from these samples in addition to immunohistochemical staining to identify characteristic cellular markers. Imaging studies may also be used to stage the disease after diagnosis has been made.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is a form of blood cancer that originates from white blood cells known as B or T lymphocytes. It occurs when these cells undergo uncontrolled growth in the lymph nodes, causing them to become enlarged and swollen. NHL can also affect other parts of the body such as bone marrow, spleen, liver, and digestive tract. The exact cause of NHL remains unknown but certain risk factors have been identified including family history, age, exposure to radiation, autoimmune disorders, and viral infections. Symptoms may include fever, weight loss, fatigue, weakness, abdominal pain, coughing, difficulty breathing, and chest pain. Diagnosis involves a combination of physical examination, imaging tests, biopsy, and laboratory testing. Treatment typically includes chemotherapy, radiotherapy, stem cell transplantation, and targeted therapy depending on the stage and subtype of the disease. Regular follow-up with a healthcare provider is important for monitoring symptoms and detecting early signs of recurrence.

The prognosis depends on the specific subtype of NHL. In general, indolent types have a more favorable prognosis than aggressive types. For example, follicular lymphoma (FL) has an overall 5-year survival rate of approximately 80%, while diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) has an overall 5-year survival rate of around 40%. However, there can be significant variation in outcomes within each subtype depending on other factors such as age at diagnosis, stage of disease, and response to treatment.

Doctors use several methods to diagnose HIV-related cancers in people living with HIV (PLWH). Firstly, they conduct physical examinations and obtain detailed medical histories from patients to identify any suspicious signs or symptoms of cancer. Secondly, they order specific laboratory tests such as blood counts, viral load testing, CD4 cell count, liver function tests, and tumor markers to assess for anemia, inflammation, immune deficiency, and organ damage that may be associated with certain types of cancer. Thirdly, they perform imaging studies like CT scans, MRIs, PET scans, and ultrasounds to detect abnormalities in organs and tissues. Finally, they also collect biopsy samples from suspected areas for further examination under a microscope by pathologists who look for abnormal cells that indicate the presence of cancer .

Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCL) include a group of rare malignant disorders characterized by abnormal proliferation of mature skin T cells . The most common CTCL is mycosis fungoides (MF), which accounts for approximately 50% of all cases. Other types of CTCLs include Sézary syndrome (SS), atopic dermatitis-like acute lymphomatous CD4+ T cell leukemia, and various other unclassified forms .

Rare cutaneous skin lymphomas can be treated with topical corticosteroids or oral retinoids such as acitretin in early stages. For more advanced stages, systemic chemotherapy regimens may be prescribed along with radiation therapy to certain areas of the body.

Primary central nervous system lymphomas (PCNSLs) are rare but aggressive non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas that originate in the brain parenchyma, leptomeninges, or spinal cord . The incidence of PCNSL is 0.4 per 100,000 people annually , with an estimated 650 cases diagnosed each year in the United States alone .

Lymphoma can be diagnosed by taking a complete patient history, conducting physical examinations, and using imaging tests such as CT scans or MRI to check for swollen lymph nodes. A biopsy of the affected area may also be performed where a small tissue sample is removed from the body to examine under a microscope (histopathological examination) for abnormal cells. Immunohistochemistry stains are used to identify specific markers that help diagnose the type of lymphoma. Genetic testing may also be done to determine if there are any genetic mutations associated with certain types of lymphomas.

Lymphoma refers to a group of blood cancers that originate from cells of the immune system called lymphocytes. In children under 15 years old, non-Hodgkin's lymphomas (NHL) account for approximately 4% of all childhood cancers . The most common subtypes of NHL in children include Burkitt lymphoma, diffuse large B cell lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma, T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and lymphocytic lymphoma. These types of cancer may occur at any age but tend to be more aggressive in younger patients due to their rapid growth rate. Symptoms vary depending on where the tumor is located within the body; however, some common symptoms include swollen lymph nodes, abdominal pain or distension, fever, weight loss, bone pain, fatigue, difficulty breathing, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis typically involves biopsy of affected tissue followed by immunohistochemistry staining to determine the type of lymphoma present. Treatment often includes chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy, as well as supportive care measures such as antibiotics and nutritional support. Prognosis depends on several factors including age, stage of disease, and specific type of lymphoma.

The four stages of lymphoma in children according to Ann Arbor staging system are as follows: Stage I - localized lymph node involvement; Stage II - regional lymph nodes or extranodal organs (e.g., spleen); Stage III - disseminated disease involving two or more nodal regions or one region with extranodal organ involvement; Stage IV - diffuse bone marrow involvement .

Cancer of the genitals can be diagnosed through physical examination, laboratory tests (such as blood tests), imaging tests such as ultrasound or MRI scans, and biopsy. The type of test used will depend on the specific symptoms being experienced by the patient and where in the genital region the suspected cancer may have originated from. It's important to note that early detection of cancer increases chances for successful treatment. If you experience any unusual signs or symptoms related to your reproductive organs, it's recommended to consult with a healthcare provider right away.

There is no definitive evidence for specific lifestyle changes or interventions to reduce the risk of developing anal cancer. However, some factors such as smoking cessation, limiting alcohol consumption, maintaining a healthy body weight, practicing safe sex, and being vaccinated against HPV may be beneficial in reducing the overall risk of anal cancer (1).

Doctors typically perform neurological exams to assess brain function, followed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head to visualize any potential lesions or masses within the brain tissue. If necessary, computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), and cerebrospinal fluid analysis may also be performed to further investigate the presence of a tumor or other abnormality in the central nervous system.

The tonsils are lymphoid organs located in the back of the throat that play an important role in filtering out harmful bacteria and viruses from the air we breathe. They also help to maintain immune function by producing antibodies against foreign substances.

There are several ongoing clinical trials in pediatric patients with central nervous system (CNS) malignancies that include investigational therapies such as targeted agents, immunotherapies, and combination chemotherapy regimens. Some of these trials involve novel therapeutic approaches, while others aim to improve outcomes by optimizing existing treatment strategies.

Children with brain tumors may present with various signs and symptoms depending on the location of their tumor. Some common symptoms include headache, vomiting, seizures, visual disturbances, weakness in one arm or leg, numbness, dizziness, balance issues, speech difficulties, personality changes, irritability, social withdrawal, and loss of consciousness. These symptoms can occur gradually over time or suddenly. If any of these symptoms appear to worsen rapidly or if there is sudden confusion, convulsions, or loss of consciousness, it could indicate an emergency situation that requires immediate attention. It's important for parents to seek urgent medical care if they notice any of these warning signs.
The treatment approach typically involves surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible followed by chemotherapy and radiation therapy depending upon the location and size of the tumor.

The prognosis of children diagnosed with a rare rhabdoid tumor in the brain or central nervous system varies depending on several factors such as age at diagnosis, location of the tumor, extent of surgical resection, histological features, presence of metastasis, and response to chemotherapy and radiation therapy. However, overall survival rates remain poor despite aggressive treatment regimens.

Brain tumors can be caused by various factors such as exposure to radiation or certain chemicals, genetic mutations, viral infection, or unknown reasons (idiopathic). However, most childhood brain tumors occur for unknown reasons. The exact cause is not yet known.

The four grades (I-IV) of pediatric gliomas are defined by histological features such as cellularity, mitotic activity, nuclear atypia, and microvascular proliferation . Grade I pilocytic astrocytoma is considered low grade with slow growth rate and good prognosis. Grades II to IV diffuse astrocytoma, anaplastic astrocytoma, and glioblastoma multiforme are high grade malignant tumors that have increased cellularity, pleomorphism, and mitoses compared to grade I pilocytic astrocytoma. These higher grade tumors also exhibit more aggressive behavior and poorer outcomes than lower grade tumors.

The most common sign or symptom is headache, which may be present for several weeks before other symptoms develop. Other possible signs include vomiting, drowsiness, weakness, seizures, blurred vision, double vision, difficulty walking, numbness, tingling sensations, back pain, neck stiffness, and changes in personality or behavior.

Pediatric germ cell tumor is a rare type of cancer that originates from cells that develop into sperm or egg cells during fetal development. These tumors can occur anywhere in the body but most commonly arise in the testicles (in boys) or ovaries (in girls). In children, however, they usually originate in the brain or spinal cord. The exact cause of these tumors is unknown, but some risk factors have been identified such as exposure to certain chemicals or radiation, family history of cancer, and genetic conditions like Down syndrome. Symptoms may vary depending on where the tumor is located within the brain and include headaches, seizures, vomiting, vision problems, balance issues, and weakness or numbness in the arms or legs. Diagnosis typically involves imaging tests such as MRI and CT scans, as well as blood tests to measure tumor markers. Treatment often includes surgery, chemotherapy, and sometimes radiotherapy. Prognosis depends on several factors including age at diagnosis, location of the tumor, and whether it has spread beyond the primary site.

The prognosis of pediatric patients diagnosed with primary central nervous system (CNS) germ cell tumors depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, location within CNS, histology, extent of resection, presence of metastasis, and response to treatment . Overall survival rates have improved over time due to advances in diagnostic techniques, surgical procedures, chemotherapy regimens, and radiotherapy protocols.

A child with a brain tumor near the pituitary gland may experience various signs and symptoms depending on which part of the pituitary is affected. The most common presenting symptom in children is headache, followed by visual disturbances (such as decreased acuity, blurred vision, double vision), endocrine dysfunction (hormonal imbalances leading to growth retardation, delayed puberty, precocious puberty, skin changes, hair loss, etc.), and rarely, diabetes insipidus (excessive thirst and urination). Other less frequent symptoms include fatigue, weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, poor appetite, behavioral changes, and weight loss .

The usual treatment for a pediatric brain tumor depends on various factors such as type of tumor, location, size, age at diagnosis, and overall health status. In general, surgical resection is the primary modality used to treat most types of pediatric brain tumors. However, the extent of surgery varies depending on these same factors mentioned above. For example, if the tumor is located near an important part of the brain that cannot be removed without causing significant damage, then less aggressive surgery may be performed to remove only the necessary amount of tissue. Other treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation therapy may also be recommended before or after surgery, depending on the specific type and stage of the tumor. It is important to note that each case is unique, so the best course of action will vary from patient to patient.

The usual long-term prognosis depends on various factors such as age, type of tumor, size, location, grade, and whether it has metastasized to other parts of the body or not. Most children who undergo complete surgical resection have an excellent chance of survival without any further complications. However, if there was residual tumor left behind after surgery, this can increase the risk of recurrence in some cases. If the tumor recurs, additional treatment may be necessary which could include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or repeat surgery. In general, the earlier that the tumor is diagnosed and treated, the better the chances of recovery will be.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) can affect anyone; however, it most commonly occurs in men over 40 years old with chronic liver damage or cirrhosis from long-term exposure to hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), alcohol consumption, smoking tobacco products, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), obesity, diabetes mellitus, autoimmune disorders such as primary biliary cholangitis, and exposure to certain chemicals like thorotrast and vinyl chloride .

There are several ongoing clinical trials that may be relevant to patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)-associated periductal infiltrating carcinoma (PDIC) or PSC-related cholangiocarcinoma (CC). These include phase II trials evaluating the use of chemotherapy agents such as gemcitabine plus cisplatin (NCT03658741), FOLFOX (folic acid, 5-fluorouracil, oxaliplatin; NCT02902946), and irinotecan plus fluoropyrimidines (NCT03022487); a phase III trial comparing first-line treatment with either durvalumab plus cisplatin–gemcitabine or cisplatin–gemcitabine alone (NCT03666982); and a phase Ib/II study testing pembrolizumab plus gemcitabine versus gemcitabine alone (NCT03533383).

Biliary cancers include tumors that arise from the intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts. The most common type of biliary cancer is cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), which arises from the extrahepatic bile ducts. Diagnosis of CCA requires a combination of imaging studies and tissue biopsy for histological confirmation.

The most common types of childhood liver cancer include hepatoblastoma (HB), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (bile ducts) (CA), neuroblastoma (NBL), rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), and lymphomas . Hepatoblastoma is the most frequent form of primary malignant tumor in infants and young children under 4 years old, accounting for approximately half of all cases . It originates from immature cells found in fetal livers known as oval cells or small cleaved cells. These cells have characteristics similar to those of embryonic stem cells, which allow them to differentiate into various cell types such as hepatocytes, biliary epithelial cells, and mesenchyme-like cells .

The different stages of liver cancer refer to how far the cancer has spread within the liver or beyond. Staging is important because it helps determine treatment options for patients with liver cancer. There are several ways to stage liver cancer, including by using imaging tests such as computed tomography (CT) scans or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), by analyzing tissue samples from biopsies, and through blood tests that measure certain substances in the body.

There are several ways to prevent liver cancer from occurring or progressing. Firstly, maintaining a healthy body weight through regular exercise and proper dietary habits can reduce the risk of liver cancer. Secondly, avoiding alcohol consumption and quitting smoking can also lower the chances of developing liver cancer. Thirdly, getting vaccinated against hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection by receiving all three doses of Hepatitis B vaccine within 6 months after birth for those who were born to infected mothers can help prevent liver cancer caused by chronic HBV infection. Lastly, limiting exposure to environmental factors such as aflatoxin contamination can further decrease the likelihood of developing liver cancer.

The usual long-term prognosis of bone cancers depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, location of the primary lesion in the body, histological subtype, grade, metastatic status, response to treatment, etc. Generally speaking, low-grade benign bone tumors have an excellent prognosis with high cure rates while high-grade malignant bone tumors have poorer outcomes . For example, osteoid osteoma has a 95% cure rate after surgical excision whereas giant cell tumor of bone has a local recurrence rate of up to 40%. Similarly, Ewing sarcoma which is a highly aggressive type of bone cancer has a survival rate of about 65–70%, while chondrosarcomas have a better overall survival (OS) ranging from 83% for stage I to 21% for stage IIIB disease. Metastasis at presentation significantly reduces OS across all types of bone cancers.

Osteosarcoma can occur in any population but is more common in children and young adults. The highest incidence occurs between 10 to 25 years old with another peak around 60–70 years old. Risk factors include family history of osteosarcoma, certain genetic syndromes such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome, exposure to radiation (either from therapeutic use or atomic bomb survivors), and some chemicals including arsenic and nickel compounds.

Osteosarcomas are treated with chemotherapy in combination with surgery to remove the tumor . The most common treatment regimen is neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by limb-sparing or amputation surgery, then adjuvant chemotherapy . Neoadjuvant chemotherapy refers to chemotherapy given before surgery, while adjuvant chemotherapy refers to chemotherapy given after surgery.

Doctors use various methods to diagnose a slow-growing tumor in the stomach or intestine. These include blood tests, imaging tests such as CT scans, endoscopy with biopsy, and ultrasound. The type of test used depends on several factors, including the patient's symptoms, medical history, and risk factors for cancer. It is important to note that early detection of these types of cancers is crucial for successful treatment and improved survival rates.

Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) refer to a group of hematologic malignancies characterized by ineffective production of mature blood cells from the bone marrow due to genetic mutations or epigenetic changes in hematopoietic stem cells . The disease can affect all three lineages of blood cells, but most commonly affects red blood cell precursors called erythroblasts. This leads to anemia, which is often the main presenting symptom. Other symptoms include fatigue, weakness, frequent infections, bleeding and bruising, weight loss, and pain in the upper left side of the abdomen. Diagnosis involves a combination of clinical presentation, laboratory tests such as peripheral blood smear evaluation and bone marrow biopsy, and molecular testing for specific gene mutations associated with MDS. Treatment options depend on various factors including age, overall health status, and risk stratification based on prognostic scoring systems. Low-risk patients may be managed conservatively with supportive care measures while high-risk patients may require more aggressive treatments such as chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Chronic blood and bone marrow disorders can be treated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplantation, targeted therapies (such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors), immunomodulatory drugs, monoclonal antibody therapy, or supportive care measures such as red blood cell transfusions, iron chelation therapy, and growth factor support . The specific treatment plan depends on several factors, including the type of disorder, its stage, whether it has spread to other parts of the body, and the individual's overall health status.

Myelofibrosis (MF) is a rare chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by abnormal proliferation of fibroblasts within the bone marrow leading to extracellular matrix deposition, resulting in reduced hematopoietic activity . The disease can be primary or secondary to another cause such as radiation exposure or autoimmune disorders. MF causes anemia, enlargement of the spleen and liver, and progressive symptoms including fatigue, pruritus, early satiety, and weight loss. Diagnosis requires a combination of clinical features, laboratory tests, and bone marrow biopsy. Treatment options include supportive care, low-dose aspirin, hydroxyurea, ruxolitinib, and allogeneic stem cell transplant for patients with advanced disease who have failed other treatments.

Platelets play an important role in hemostasis by forming plugs at sites of vascular injury to prevent excessive bleeding . Thrombocytopenia is defined as a condition where there is a decrease in the number of circulating platelets below 150 × 109 per liter (platelets/L) of whole blood . The most common cause of thrombocytopenia is reactive thrombocytosis due to autoimmune diseases, viral infections, drug reactions, pregnancy, and surgery .
The chronic blood cancer in which one type of white blood cell becomes abnormally high is called myeloid leukemia.

Mixed bone marrow and blood cancers (myeloproliferative neoplasm) may present with symptoms such as anemia, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, fever, abdominal pain or discomfort, early satiety, bleeding or bruising, and enlargement of the spleen, liver, or lymph nodes . The disease is diagnosed by evaluating peripheral blood cells for increased white blood cell count, immature granulocytes, and blast cells; increased red blood cell mass; and elevated hemoglobin levels. Bone marrow aspiration confirms the diagnosis by showing hypercellularity in the medullary space due to myeloid precursors and extramedullary hematopoiesis .

The prognosis of AML depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, cytogenetic abnormalities, molecular mutations, response to initial therapy, and relapse status. In general, younger patients (<60 years old) have better outcomes than older ones. Patients with favorable-risk cytogenetics also tend to have better survival rates compared to those with intermediate- or adverse-risk features. Treatment can prolong life expectancy in many cases but may not cure the disease. Over time, most patients will experience recurrence and eventually succumb to their condition.

The treatment of rare leukemias in children is determined by the type of leukemia, risk stratification, age at diagnosis, and presence or absence of specific genetic mutations. In general, low-risk patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) receive induction chemotherapy followed by maintenance therapy consisting of oral mercaptopurine and methotrexate. High-risk AML patients typically undergo intensive chemotherapy regimens such as 7 + 3 or FLAG-IDA, followed by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). For intermediate-risk AML patients, there are several different approaches that can be taken depending on the patient's age, comorbidities, and availability of HSCT.

The term "myeloid sarcoma" refers to extramedullary tumors that arise from immature hematopoietic cells (blasts) in the context of either MDS or MPN. It can be present at diagnosis or develop during the course of the disease as an indicator of progression towards acute leukemia .

Gynecological cancers include cervical, ovarian, uterine (endometrial), vulvar, fallopian tube, placental trophoblastic, and other malignancies that affect female reproductive organs. The most common early symptom is abnormal vaginal bleeding, which may occur between periods or after menopause. Other possible symptoms include unusual discharge from the vagina, persistent pelvic pain or pressure, changes in bowel habits, urinary problems, swelling in legs or abdomen, weight loss, fatigue, indigestion, constipation, diarrhea, and nausea . It is important to note that these symptoms do not necessarily indicate cancer, but it is recommended for women who experience any of them to consult their healthcare provider.

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to uterine cancer treatment that are currently recruiting participants in various stages of disease progression (1). These include phase III trials evaluating different chemotherapy regimens as first-line treatments for advanced endometrial cancers, such as carboplatin plus paclitaxel versus carboplatin plus cisplatin (NCT03475268) and carboplatin plus SMILE (saracatinib, mitomycin C, irinotecan, liposomal doxorubicin, and etoposide) versus carboplatin plus pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD) (NCT03905889), and phase II trial comparing pembrolizumab with or without bevacizumab as second-line therapy for recurrent or metastatic endometrioid endometrial carcinoma (NCT04003680). Other phase I/II trials are investigating targeted therapies, including everolimus combined with PLD (NCT03003492) and niraparib alone or in combination with olaparib (NCT04165112). Additionally, there is an open label single arm study assessing the efficacy of d

The prognosis and course of rare cancers of the uterus vary depending on the specific type of cancer involved. In general, most types of endometrial cancer have a good prognosis with early diagnosis and treatment, while cervical cancer has a poorer prognosis but may be curable if diagnosed and treated in its early stages. Uterine sarcomas tend to have a worse prognosis than other types of uterine cancers due to their aggressive nature and tendency to recur.

Extragonadal germ cell tumors (EGCT) refer to malignant neoplasms that arise from primordial germ cells outside of the gonads during embryonic development . These rare cancers account for approximately 2%-3% of all childhood solid tumors with an estimated annual incidence rate between 0.15 and 0.4 per million individuals under the age of 19 years old . EGCT most commonly occur within the midline structures such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and pelvis but may also be found in other locations including the pineal region, presacral area, bladder, kidney, liver, omentum, and testicular tunics .

Germ cell tumours (GCTs) are rare malignancies that occur most frequently in adolescents and adults but can also be found in infants and children under 10 years of age . The incidence rate of GCTs in childhood is approximately 2–4 cases per million persons . In contrast to adult-onset GCTs, which have a male predominance, paediatric GCTs show an equal sex distribution .

Rare extragonadal germ cell tumors (GCTs) can occur in both males and females. However, they are more common in men than women. The highest incidence is seen in young adults aged 20 to 39 years old. There may be an association with family history or genetic syndromes such as Klinefelter syndrome, Yersinia enterocolitica infection, and cryptorchidism in males.

Extragonadal germ cell tumors (EGCT) can be treated with surgery, chemotherapy or radiation therapy depending upon the stage of disease at diagnosis. For patients diagnosed with localized EGCTs, surgical resection is recommended as primary treatment modality. Chemotherapy may also be used in combination with surgery for advanced cases. Radiation therapy alone or combined with chemotherapy is often used to treat metastatic lesions.

Doctors use several methods to diagnose mucosal melanomas including physical examination, biopsy, imaging tests such as CT scans or MRIs, endoscopy with tissue sampling, and laboratory testing of cells removed during biopsies. The diagnosis is then confirmed by pathologists who examine the samples under microscopes for abnormal cell growth patterns. Immunohistochemical staining can also be used to identify specific proteins that may indicate the presence of malignant cells.

Retinoblastoma (RB) is an ocular malignancy that usually affects infants and young children. It arises from the retinal cells and can spread to other parts of the body if left untreated. The main symptoms include leukocoria (white pupil), strabismus (crossed eyes), and ophthalmia nodosa (swollen eyelids). Prompt diagnosis and treatment are crucial for successful management of RB.

The prognosis depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, stage of disease, location within the brain, histologic subtype, and presence or absence of metastasis. In general, children with low-grade gliomas have better outcomes than those with high-grade tumors.

Women who have never been pregnant or had their first pregnancy after 30 years old, those with early menarche (before age 12), late menopause (after age 50) or hormone replacement therapy using estrogen only, history of ovarian cysts, endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, pelvic inflammatory disease, obesity, family history of breast or ovarian cancer in a first-degree relative, smoking, low parity, long oral contraceptive use, and diaphragm usage for birth control are all considered to be high-risk factors that may increase the likelihood of developing gynecological malignancies .

The prognosis of gynecological cancer depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, histology, grade, age, and other comorbidities. In general, early-stage disease has a better prognosis than advanced-stage disease. For example, the five-year relative survival rate for localized ovarian cancer is 92%, while that for distant metastatic ovarian cancer is only 30%. However, even patients diagnosed with late-stage disease may have good outcomes if they receive appropriate treatments. With advances in diagnostic techniques and multimodal therapies, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and hormonal therapy, many women with gynecological cancer achieve long-term disease control .

Germ cell tumors (GCTs) can cause various signs and symptoms depending on their location in the body. The most common sites of GCT origin include testicles, ovaries, mediastinum, retroperitoneal space, and brain.

There is an ongoing phase II trial of carboplatin plus paclitaxel chemotherapy in combination with bevacizumab (an anti-VEGF antibody) as first line treatment for patients with advanced epithelial ovarian cancer . The study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of this regimen compared to standard platinum-based therapy alone.

Borderline low malignant potential (BLMP) tumor is an uncommon type of ovarian epithelial neoplasm that has intermediate features between benign and malignant histology . The International Federation of Gynecologists and Obstetrics (FIGO) stage system for BLMP tumors is similar to that used for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer. It takes into account both clinical factors such as residual disease after surgery and pathological characteristics such as histologic grade, depth of invasion, lymph node involvement, and presence or absence of distant metastasis.

Women who have never been pregnant or had few pregnancies, women with a history of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), women over 50 years old, obese women, women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) or hormonal changes due to oral contraceptives, women with diabetes, and women with high levels of estrogen exposure from menarche age until menopause.

Cancer of the biliary tract can be diagnosed by several methods including blood tests such as CA 19-9 or imaging modalities like ultrasound, CT scan or MRI. A biopsy of the suspected area is also required for confirmation of diagnosis.

Men who have not been circumcised during childhood are more likely to develop penile cancer than those who were circumcised. Other risk factors include smoking, phimosis (inability to retract the foreskin), chronic inflammation or irritation of the penis due to tight-fitting clothing, excessive hygiene practices, lichen sclerosus, condylomata acuminata, human papilloma virus infection, and having a history of other cancers such as bowel cancer .

The prognosis of cancers in the genital areas depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, type of cancer, age, sex, lifestyle habits, etc. However, most types of cancers in this region are highly treatable if diagnosed early through regular screening tests or self-examination .

The prognosis depends on the severity of the condition at diagnosis. If treated promptly and effectively, most infants with IUGR have good outcomes. However, if left untreated or diagnosed late in gestation, there may be long-term health consequences such as developmental delays, learning disabilities, behavior problems, heart disease, and high blood pressure in adulthood.

The most common type of leukemia in adults is acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which affects cells that would normally develop into red blood cells, platelets or neutrophils. It can affect anyone at any age but is more common in older adults over 65 years old.

The treatment of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) depends on several factors such as age, location, number and size of lesions, organs involved, and whether it is single-system or multi-system disease. Treatment may include observation with regular follow-up exams if there is a solitary bone lesion in an adult; steroids alone or surgery plus steroid therapy for localized skin or bone lesions; chemotherapy for multisystem involvement; and stem cell transplantation for high-risk patients with organ dysfunction or multiorgan involvement.

Doctors use several methods to diagnose throat cancer. Firstly, they conduct physical examinations of the head and neck region to check for lumps or swellings in the neck area. They also perform flexible fiberoptic endoscopies with biopsy to examine the tissues inside the mouth and throat. In addition, doctors may order imaging tests such as CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, and ultrasounds to look for any abnormalities in the structures of the neck. Finally, they may recommend blood tests to rule out other diseases that have similar symptoms.

Oral cancers refer to malignant tumors arising from any part of the mouth, including the lips, gums, palate, tongue, buccal mucosa, floor of the mouth, and other areas within the oral cavity . Throat cancers include neoplasms originating in the pharynx (nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal, hypopharyngeal) as well as the larynx . These types of cancers may also be referred to collectively as head and neck cancers. The term “oropharyngeal” refers to cancers occurring in the back portion of the throat behind the tongue, which includes the tonsils and base of the tongue.

Doctors may use various methods to assess for potential signs of more serious conditions like throat cancer in patients presenting with symptoms of a severe sore throat or voice problems. These include taking a detailed patient history, conducting physical examinations including visualization of the throat using flexible endoscopes, ordering appropriate diagnostic tests (such as biopsies), and considering risk factors such as smoking, alcohol consumption, family history of head and neck cancers, and human papillomavirus infection.

There are several types of cancer that can occur in the oral cavity including tongue cancer, lip cancer, gingival (gum) cancer, buccal mucosa cancer, floor of the mouth cancer, alveolar ridge cancer, hard palate cancer, soft palate cancer, pharyngeal cancer, tonsil cancer, oropharynx cancer, nasopharynx cancer, salivary gland cancer, and lymphoma.

The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) has developed a staging system for cancers that arise in the lips and oral cavity. This staging system is used to determine prognosis and treatment options. There are four main categories of lip and oral cavity cancer staging: stage 0, I, II, III, and IV. Stage 0 refers to carcinoma in situ, which means that abnormal cells have only invaded the top layer of tissue in the mouth or lips. Stages I through IV refer to increasing levels of invasion and spread of the cancer beyond the surface of the lips or mouth. For example, stage I cancer may involve only one area of the lips or mouth, while stage IV cancer may involve more than one part of the lips or mouth as well as other areas of the body.

When the primary site of an advanced-stage cancer is unknown (i.e., “unknown primary”), it can make diagnosis and treatment more challenging for physicians. In such cases, imaging studies may help identify potential sites of origin. The most common type of cancer with an unknown primary site is metastatic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in the head and neck region, which often presents as nodal disease without an obvious primary lesion .

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) refers to malignant tumors arising from the epithelial cells of the nasopharynx. The incidence rate of NPC varies greatly worldwide, with higher rates reported in Southern China, North Africa, and Alaska . It has been estimated that there were approximately 130,986 new cases of NPC diagnosed globally in 2020, accounting for about 4% of all head and neck cancers .

Cancer of the nasopharynx (NPC) can be staged using the TNM system developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). The letters “T” stands for tumor size, “N” represents lymph node involvement, while “M” indicates distant metastasis. Each letter is followed by numbers that indicate different stages of severity. For example, T1 means the primary tumor measures 2 cm or less; N0 means no regional lymph nodes involved; M0 means there is no evidence of distant metastases.

The common symptoms that indicate a potential oral cancer include a persistent sore throat, difficulty swallowing, unexplained weight loss, white patches inside the mouth, red or black discoloration of the gums, tongue, or other areas of the mouth, ulcers or sores that do not heal within 14 days, and a lump or thickening in the neck.

There are several ongoing clinical trials that aim to improve treatment outcomes in patients with head and neck cancers (HNCs), including those affecting the oral cavity and pharynx. These include phase III trials evaluating the efficacy of induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone (NCT02987156) and the use of cetuximab as an adjuvant therapy after surgery (NCT03425050). Other trials are investigating novel radiation techniques such as proton beam therapy (NCT03574138) and intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT; NCT01228172). Immunotherapies such as pembrolizumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) have also been studied in recurrent or metastatic HNCs (NCT03006620). In addition, there is ongoing research into the development of targeted therapies such as vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors and tyrosine kinase inhibitors .

The prognosis of cancers originating from the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses varies depending on the location and stage at diagnosis. Generally speaking, tumours arising from the maxillary sinus have a better prognosis than those arising from other areas such as the ethmoid or sphenoid sinuses. Treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapies, and immunotherapies. The response to these treatments may vary depending on the type and stage of cancer, but overall, early-stage disease tends to be more responsive to treatment than advanced-stage disease. It is important to note that while some types of nasal or sinus cancer may initially respond well to treatment, they may eventually recur or progress over time. Therefore, ongoing monitoring and follow-up care are essential for patients with this condition.

Salivary glands cancer (SGC) is rare in children but more common in adults, with an incidence rate of 0.5 per 100,000 people under the age of 20 years compared to 3.7 per 100,000 people over the age of 80 years . The parotid gland is the largest major salivary gland and accounts for approximately one third of all SGCs.

The standard of care for head and neck cancers is surgical resection with adjuvant chemoradiation therapy (CRT) to prevent recurrence . Surgery involves removal of the tumour along with some healthy tissue around it, which may include part of the jawbone, teeth, tongue, soft tissues in the mouth, nose, throat, or lymph nodes. Depending on the size and location of the tumour, this procedure can be extensive and result in significant functional impairment, including speech problems, swallowing difficulties, facial deformity, and loss of mobility in the jaw, among others.

Abdominal glands include the pancreas, liver, gallbladder, stomach, spleen, and intestines. The incidence of developing cancer in these organs varies by age, sex, race, lifestyle factors such as smoking, alcohol consumption, dietary habits, physical activity, family history of cancer, and genetic mutations.

The standard of care for resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) includes surgical resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy consisting of either gemcitabine alone or in combination with FOLFIRINOX (fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin). For locally advanced PDAC that cannot be completely removed, neoadjuvant therapy may be given to reduce tumor size before surgery. Neoadjuvant therapy typically consists of chemotherapy or chemoradiation. If metastatic disease is detected at diagnosis, systemic chemotherapy is recommended as the first-line treatment.

The prognosis depends on various factors such as size, location, hormone secretion status, metastasis at diagnosis, and grade of malignancy . Generally, patients with non-functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (pNETs) have a better prognosis than those with functional pNETs or other types of pancreatic cancer .

The stages of kidney cancer range from stage I (confined to the kidneys) to stage IV (metastasized). Stage 0 is considered carcinoma in situ, which refers to abnormal cells confined to the surface layer of the kidney without invasion into deeper tissues. Stages I-IV refer to increasing degrees of tumor growth beyond the surface layer of the kidney with progressively more invasive properties.

Doctors may use several methods to diagnose cancer of the bladder or kidneys. These include physical examination, imaging studies such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and cystoscopy. Cystoscopy is a procedure where a thin tube with a camera at the end is inserted into the urethra through the bladder to examine the inside of the bladder for any abnormalities. A biopsy may also be taken during this procedure if an abnormality is found. Blood tests can help rule out other causes of blood in the urine. If there is still no diagnosis after these procedures, a laparotomy may be necessary to remove tissue from the bladder or kidneys for further testing. It is important to note that early detection of cancer is crucial for successful treatment, so it is recommended to seek medical attention promptly if you have symptoms such as blood in your urine.

Wilms tumor (WT) is a malignant neoplasm arising from renal blastemal cells during embryonic development . It accounts for approximately 6% of all pediatric cancers and occurs most commonly between ages five to nine years old . The exact cause of WT remains unknown; however, several genetic mutations have been identified as contributing factors, such as WT1 gene mutation , which leads to abnormal cellular proliferation and differentiation.

Pediatric cancer staging systems have been developed to help guide treatment decisions and predict prognosis in children with cancer. The most commonly used system is the International Classification of Childhood Cancer Stages (ICCC), which was first published in 1986 by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Union Against Cancer (UICC). This classification scheme divides childhood cancers into four main categories: localized disease, regional metastatic disease, distant metastatic disease, and unknown primary site .

There is no evidence that specific dietary changes can prevent the development of lung cancer. However, maintaining a healthy body weight throughout life may lower the risk of lung cancer later in life. Additionally, avoiding smoking tobacco products and exposure to secondhand smoke are the most effective ways to prevent lung cancer.

The classification of breast cancer is typically done using the Tumor-Node-Metastasis (TNM) system, which takes into account three factors: the size of the tumour (T), whether there has been invasion by nearby lymph nodes (N), and whether distant metastases have occurred (M). Based on these parameters, breast cancers are categorized as stage 0 to IV, with higher numbers indicating more severe disease.

A chest or breast lump can potentially be hereditary and may run in families. The BRCA1 gene mutation has been linked to an increased risk of developing breast cancer in men. Additionally, other genes such as TP53, PTEN, CDH1, PALB2, RAD50, CHEK2, ATM, NBN, BARD1, FAM175A, BLM, MRE11A, RECQL4, and XRCC6 have also been associated with an elevated risk of male breast cancer.

The usual treatment option for men who present with a breast or chest lump depends on various factors such as age, family history of cancer, previous medical conditions, size and type of tumor, hormone status (estrogen receptor), etc. Generally speaking, the first line of treatment is usually surgical excision followed by chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and targeted therapies depending upon the severity of the condition. If detected early, the prognosis can be good; however, in cases where it is detected late, the chances of survival may decrease significantly.
The five main steps in the progression of melanoma include (1) radial growth phase; (2) vertical growth phase; (3) regional metastasis; (4) distant metastases; and (5) death due to melanoma .

The ABCDE rule is used to identify melanoma warning signs: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variegation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution (changing over time). Other warning signs include sudden onset of itching or bleeding.

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to melanoma treatment. One of them is NCT03945782 which aims to evaluate the safety and efficacy of nivolumab plus ipilimumab in patients with unresectable stage IIIB-D or IV melanoma who have not been previously treated with immunotherapy. Another trial, NCT01611558, is evaluating the combination therapy of dacarbazine, cisplatin, and pembrolizumab as first line treatment for metastatic melanoma. The third study, NCT02224781, is investigating the effectiveness of combining nivolumab with radiation therapy in treating advanced melanoma that has spread to other parts of the body. Additionally, there is an ongoing phase 3 randomized controlled trial (NCT02905594) assessing the efficacy and safety of adjuvant nivolumab versus placebo after complete resection of high risk melanoma.

The long-term prognosis for Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) depends on various factors such as tumor size, depth of invasion, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis. MCC has been reported to have a high rate of nodal and distant metastases compared with other cutaneous malignancies. If left untreated, MCC can rapidly grow and spread to adjacent tissues and organs, resulting in significant morbidity and mortality.

Multiple Myeloma (MM) is a malignant disorder characterized by uncontrolled growth of clonal B-lymphocytes within the bone marrow (BM). It is considered as one of the most common hematological cancers with an incidence rate of 6 cases per 100,000 individuals worldwide . The estimated number of new MM cases diagnosed each year has been increasing steadily over time due to improved diagnostic techniques and increased life expectancy .

Multiple Myeloma (MM) is a malignant disorder of plasma cells in the bone marrow that produces monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains . The treatment plan depends upon several factors such as age, fitness status, disease stage, comorbidities, and patient preference.

Nerve tumors can be diagnosed by conducting physical examinations of children with symptoms such as pain, weakness, numbness, tingling, or swelling in specific areas of their body. The doctor may also ask about any family history of similar conditions to determine if there is an inherited risk factor for developing these types of tumors.

Neuroblastoma can affect children at any age but is more common among those under 5 years old. It occurs slightly more often in boys than girls. There are some known genetic syndromes associated with an increased risk for developing neuroblastoma, including Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), Hirschsprung disease (HD) and multiple endocrine neoplasia type I (MEN1). BWS is characterized by macrosomia, macroglossia, exophthalmos, ear creases, abnormalities of the genitourinary tract, omphalocele, hepatomegaly, hyperinsulinism, hypoglycemia, diabetes mellitus, and predisposition to cancer. HD is caused by a deletion in chromosome band 4p36.2 which leads to loss of function of the RET proto-oncogene. MEN1 is an autosomal dominant disorder resulting from mutations in the tumor suppressor gene menin. Patients with MEN1 have a higher incidence of pheochromocytomas, parathyroid adenomas, thyroid carcinomas, and medullary cell carcinomas of the breast. However, these conditions do not necessarily lead to neuroblastoma development. Most cases of neuroblastoma occur spontaneously without any identifiable cause or family

The prognosis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, age, overall health status, smoking history, histology type, tumor location, treatment received, etc. In general, NSCLC has an aggressive course with a poor prognosis. If detected early through screening tests like low dose computed tomography scans, the 5-year relative survival rate can be up to 83%. However, if diagnosed in later stages, the 5-year relative survival rates drop significantly to 16% in Stage IIIA and 4% in Stages IIIB and IIIC .

Fast-growing lung or chest cancers include small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) and non-small cell lung carcinomas (NSCLCs). The latter includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma, bronchogenic carcinoma, and other types of NSCLCs .

There are several ongoing clinical trials that aim to improve outcomes in patients with fast-growing or aggressive lung cancers. Some examples include the NCT03627549 trial (NCT number), which is evaluating the efficacy of pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone as first-line therapy for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring high tumor mutational burden (TMB). The NCT01846416 trial is investigating the use of nivolumab after progression on platinum-based chemotherapy in squamous NSCLC. Other ongoing trials include the NCT03519971 trial, which is assessing the safety and efficacy of atezolizumab plus carboplatin and paclitaxel compared to placebo plus carboplatin and paclitaxel as first-line therapy for metastatic squamous NSCLC; the NCT03359401 trial, which is comparing durvalumab plus platinum-doublet chemotherapy versus platinum-doublet chemotherapy alone as first-line therapy for metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC; and the NCT03774732 trial, which is examining the efficacy and safety of neoadjuvant durvalum

The parathyroid glands are four small endocrine glands located behind the thyroid gland in the neck that regulate calcium levels in the blood by secreting parathyroid hormone (PTH). Parathyroid disease can affect one or more of these glands and may result from hyperplasia (enlargement), adenoma (noncancerous tumor), carcinoma (cancer), inflammation, or other conditions.

Parathyroid cancer is typically treated surgically by removing all diseased tissue through total thyroidectomy plus complete parathyroidectomy (total resection of all four glands) . If there has been recurrence after initial surgery, additional surgeries may be necessary to remove any remaining tumor tissue. In cases where surgery cannot be performed due to advanced disease stage, chemotherapy and radiation therapy may also be used as palliative treatments .

Doctors will typically examine any new growth or lesion that appears in the genitals to rule out cancer. They may also ask questions about the patient's sexual history and perform a physical examination of other parts of their body. If there is a suspicion of cancer, they may recommend further testing such as biopsies, blood tests, imaging scans (e.g., CT scan), or surgery for diagnosis. The specific course of action depends on various factors including the type of symptoms being experienced by the patient, the size and location of the growth or lesion, and its appearance under visual inspection and with additional diagnostic tools. It is important to note that early detection of cancers in this region is crucial for successful treatment outcomes. Patients who experience changes in their genitals, even if they seem minor, should consult a healthcare provider immediately.

Pituitary tumors can be benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous). They may cause problems with hormones produced by the pituitary gland, which is called hypothalamic–pituitary axis dysfunction. The symptoms of these disorders vary depending on the type of hormonal deficiency or excess.

The classification of pituitary gland tumors is based on their histological features and clinical behavior. There are four main types of pituitary gland tumors: adenomas, carcinomas, prolactin-secreting tumors (PitNETs), and corticotrophin-secreting tumors (Cushing’s disease). Adenoma is the most common type of pituitary gland tumor, accounting for 60–75% of all cases. It can be further divided into nonfunctioning adenomas (NFAs) and functioning adenomas such as PitNETs and Cushing’s disease . NFAs account for about 35–40% of all pituitary tumors and are typically benign with low recurrence rates after surgical resection. However, some NFA may secrete other hormones that affect growth, thyroid function, or sexual maturation in children . Functioning adenomas produce excess amounts of one or more pituitary hormone(s); these include PitNETs, which cause hyperprolactinemia; acromegaly, which causes excessive production of growth hormone; and Cushing’s disease, which results from an overproduction of ACTH by the anterior pituitary gland . Carcinomas are rare, aggressive tumors that occur in less than 1% of patients

Prostate cancer can be detected through various methods including digital rectal examination (DRE), blood test called PSA (prostate-specific antigen) and biopsy of the prostate gland. If any of these tests show signs of possible cancer, further testing may include imaging such as ultrasound, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) or CT scan (computed tomography). A transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy is then performed to confirm the diagnosis.

Prostate cancer can affect men of any age but is more common in those over 50 years old. The highest incidence occurs between ages 60–70. It tends to be less frequent after 80 years of age due to higher mortality from other causes. Family history plays an important role; having a first-degree relative with prostate cancer increases the risk by about two times compared to general population. However, the majority of cases still occur spontaneously (randomly).

Doctors use various methods to diagnose GI diseases. The most common method of diagnosis involves taking a detailed history from patients about their symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, rectal bleeding, etc., followed by physical examination, laboratory testing (blood test), endoscopy, imaging studies like X-ray, CT scan, MRI, ultrasound, barium enema, capsule endoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, and biopsy for histopathological evaluation.

The correct medical terminology for this condition would be colorectal cancer (CRC). It refers to any malignant tumor that arises from either the colon or the rectum. Bowel cancer can also refer to CRC but may include other types of cancer such as stomach cancer, small intestine cancer, etc.

The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system is used for colorectal cancer. It classifies patients into four main categories based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, metastasis, and other factors. These include stage 0, I, II, III, and IV. Stage 0 refers to carcinoma in situ, which is noninvasive cancer that has not spread beyond the topmost layer of cells covering the inner wall of the colon or rectum. Stages I through III refer to invasive cancers with increasing degrees of spread. In stage I, the cancer has grown outside the inner most muscle walls but does not involve any lymph nodes. In stage II, there is invasion of the outermost muscle layers but no lymph node involvement. In stage III, there is spread to regional lymph nodes. Finally, stage IV indicates distant organ metastases .

Bowel cancer can occur in anyone at any age; however, certain individuals have an increased likelihood of developing this condition due to their genetic makeup (e.g., Lynch syndrome) or environmental exposures such as smoking, obesity, dietary patterns, and family history of colorectal cancer .

Doctors use various methods to detect potential growths or tumors in the intestine or bowels. The most common method is through screening colonoscopies, which involve inserting a camera into the rectum to examine the entire digestive tract for any abnormalities. Other diagnostic tools include blood tests, stool samples, imaging tests such as X-rays, CT scans, MRI, ultrasound, and endoscopy procedures like sigmoidoscopy and upper GI endoscopy. If an abnormality is detected during these screenings, further testing will likely be recommended, including biopsy of the tissue.

Thymic carcinoma is rare (1–2% of all lung cancers) and presents in patients aged 50 to 70 years old. It may present with non-specific symptoms like cough, dyspnea, chest pain, fever, weight loss, and night sweats. In advanced stages, it may cause superior vena cava syndrome, which includes facial swelling, headache, blurred vision, coughing, wheezing, and difficulty breathing due to obstruction of venous flow from the heart.

The standard of care for treating thymic carcinoma depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, age, performance status, comorbidities, and other health-related variables. For early-stage (I–IVA) thymic carcinomas that cannot be surgically removed, chemotherapy with cisplatin plus either doxorubicin or irradiation to the chest is recommended .

Urethral cancer can be divided into superficial (noninvasive) and invasive types. The noninvasive type includes carcinoma in situ (CIS), which involves only the top layer of cells lining the inside of the urethra, and papillary lesions, which involve small projections that extend from the surface of the urethra to the inner lumen. In contrast, the invasive type refers to tumors that have invaded beyond the mucosal layer of the urethra, such as squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs).

Doctors will first ask about any symptoms such as pain, bleeding, discharge, fever, chills, weight loss, fatigue, difficulty urinating, or abdominal swelling. They may also ask if there has been recent sexual activity with an infected partner. A physical examination of the affected area should be performed, including a pelvic exam for women and a rectal exam for men. The doctor may order blood tests (complete blood count, liver function test), imaging studies (ultrasound, CT scan, MRI) and biopsy to help diagnose cancerous lesions.

The ABCD criteria for stroke diagnosis include age (>40 years), blood pressure (systolic ≥140 mmHg and diastolic ≥90 mmHg or known hypertension), clinical presentation (acute onset of focal neurological deficit such as weakness, speech impairment, vision loss, or sensory disturbance), and duration of symptoms (<24 hours).

The name of the rare disorder you mentioned is known as bile acid malabsorption (BAM). BAM occurs when there is damage to the small intestine's ability to absorb bile acids, leading to their accumulation in the colon. This can cause diarrhea, weight loss, steatorrhea, and other symptoms. It may also interfere with the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, resulting in deficiencies that can lead to serious health problems such as osteoporosis or anemia.

The usual treatment for this condition involves supplementation with lipid soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) as well as medium chain triglycerides to help bypass the intestinal absorption problem. Medications such as bile acid sequestrants may also be prescribed to reduce the amount of bile acids reaching the colon and thus reducing their toxic effects. Dietary modifications include limiting consumption of foods high in fiber and increasing consumption of low-fiber foods. Other treatments may involve parenteral nutrition therapy if oral feeding becomes difficult due to malabsorption.

Congenital absence of the patella can result in knee instability, which may lead to pain or discomfort during physical activity. The affected limb may also be shorter than the unaffected one due to reduced growth potential. However, these individuals do not usually experience significant limitations in daily activities unless there is associated deformity or other complications such as patellar tendon rupture.

Yes, an extra or abnormal nerve in the leg or foot can cause tingling, numbness, pain, or difficulty lifting the foot. This condition is known as neurofibroma of the peripheral nervous system (PNS). It occurs when there is overgrowth of normal Schwann cells that surround axons within nerves. The exact mechanism leading to this growth is unknown but may be related to genetic mutations affecting cellular proliferation and differentiation. Neurofibromas typically present with a palpable mass along the course of a nerve, which may be associated with sensory changes such as paresthesia or numbness. In rare cases, large neurofibromas can compress surrounding structures, resulting in weakness or paralysis of affected limbs. Diagnosis is usually made through physical examination and imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT), although biopsy may also be necessary for confirmation. Treatment options include observation, surgical excision, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or targeted drug therapies.

The disease you are referring to is called hereditary hemochromatosis (HH). It is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder that causes excessive absorption of iron from the gut and its accumulation in various organs such as liver, pancreas, heart, and joints. HH can lead to impaired glucose metabolism and neurological symptoms if left untreated.

The sensation of feeling that food is stuck in the throat during swallowing is known as globus pharyngeus (GP). GP may occur with or without difficulty initiating swallowing. It has been associated with various conditions including anxiety disorders such as panic attacks, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), upper airway inflammation, and neurological diseases affecting the brainstem or cranial nerves.

The most common sign is blue sclerae (blue eyes) which can be seen at birth. Other signs include short stature, bowing deformities, joint laxity, and facial features like triangular face with high arched palate, midface flattening, micrognathia, and downslanted palpebral fissures.

The rare congenital bone growth disorder known as Caffey disease is characterized by painless swelling of one or more bones in newborns that resolves within 24 hours after birth without any treatment. It can affect long bones (most commonly) or flat bones. At birth, there may be no obvious deformity present, but later, radiographic examination reveals periosteal thickening with cortical expansion. There are no other associated symptoms or complications.

Dwarfism can result from various factors including genetics, hormonal deficiencies, metabolic disorders, in utero exposure to alcohol or radiation, and other rare conditions. The most common cause of dwarfism is idiopathic short stature (ISS), which has no known underlying cause. ISS may be associated with familial short stature but does not follow an inheritable pattern; therefore, if one parent is affected, there is only a 50% chance that their child will also have ISS. Inherited forms of dwarfism include achondrodysplasia, hypochondroplasia, and SADD syndrome, among others. These types of dwarfism are typically passed down through autosomal dominant inheritance patterns. New random genetic mutations can occur during meiosis, when cells divide to form gametes, resulting in changes to chromosomes. However, these changes do not always lead to disease development. It is possible for individuals without family history of dwarfism to develop certain types of dwarfism due to newly acquired genetic mutations.

Short-limbed dwarfism is caused by mutations in genes that regulate skeletal development during embryogenesis. The most common type of short-limbed dwarfism is called Achondroplasia (ACH), which accounts for 70% of all cases . ACH is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, meaning one copy of the defective gene is sufficient to cause the disease.

The usual treatment for anemia due to non-iron deficiency causes depends on the underlying cause. For example, if it is caused by vitamin B12 or folate deficiencies, then supplements of these vitamins may be prescribed. If it is caused by chronic disease such as cancer, then chemotherapy may be used. In some cases, blood transfusions may also be necessary. This type of anemia can become very serious if left untreated, leading to fatigue, weakness, paleness, shortness of breath, dizziness, chest pain, heart failure, and even death.

Severe zinc deficiency may cause anemia, leukopenia, impaired immune function, skin lesions (such as acne), appetite loss, delayed sexual maturity, hypogonadism in males, testicular atrophy, impotence, poor wound healing, alopecia, dermatitis, diarrhea, growth retardation, pneumonia, and increased susceptibility to infections .

The condition you are referring to is called acrocephalosandynechthesia (ACSA). It is a rare genetic disorder characterized by facial and hand swelling, thickened and wrinkled skin on the scalp, and white spots in one or both eyes. ACSA can be diagnosed through physical examination and imaging tests such as X-ray, CT scan, and MRI. Treatment typically involves supportive care, including medication for pain management and surgery for cosmetic purposes.

The most common sign of McCune Albright syndrome is premature pubarche in children under 5 years old. Other symptoms include irregular menstrual cycles, hyperthyroidism, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, and increased risk for cancer (particularly thyroid). Diagnosis requires histopathological examination of affected tissue to confirm the presence of brown tumors.

Excessive stress steroids can lead to Cushing's syndrome (CS). The most common symptom of CS is weight gain in the face, neck, chest, abdomen, and thighs with thinning skin. Other symptoms include irregular menstruation, osteoporosis, high blood pressure, mood swings, fatigue, weakness, headaches, dizziness, blurred vision, acne, hirsutism, easy bruising, poor wound healing, and darkening of the skin. Physical examination may reveal purple striae, edema, and muscle wasting.

The typical symptoms of acute febrile neutropenia (AFN) include high fever (temperature ≥100.4°F), chills, fatigue, weakness, decreased appetite, sore throat, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, headache, muscle aches, back pain, joint pain, skin changes such as bright redness, warmth, swelling, tenderness, pustules, blisters, ulcers, and discharge. These symptoms usually develop within one to three days after chemotherapy treatment starts. AFN is differentiated from other types of infections by blood tests showing low levels of white blood cells, specifically neutrophils.

The condition being referred to here is acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), which is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in the gene encoding hydroxymethylbilane synthase enzyme. AIP is characterized by recurring attacks of abdominal pain, usually starting around 10–25 years old, often accompanied by neurologic manifestations including seizures, psychosis, hypertensive crisis, and autonomic instability. Porphyrias can be classified into two types: hepatic and erythropoietic. Hepatic porphyrias include AIP, variegate porphyria, hereditary coproporphyria, and aminolevulinic acid dehydratase deficiency porphyria. Erythropoietic protoporphyria is the most common type of cutaneous porphyria.

Treatments for severe breathing or lung problems include medication to relax the muscles around the airways, bronchodilators to widen them, corticosteroids to reduce inflammation, antibiotics to treat infection, and supplemental oxygen therapy. In cases of acute respiratory failure, noninvasive ventilation such as continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) may be used first, followed by intubation with mechanical ventilation if necessary. If there is no response to these measures, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) can be considered.

The most common cause of an abnormal growth in the tooth or jaw area is a dentigerous cyst (DC), which accounts for 20% of all jaw tumors . DCs occur when epithelial remnants from the developing tooth crown become separated during tooth eruption and form a fluid-filled sac beneath the affected tooth. Other types of odontogenic cysts include ameloblastoma, glandular odontogenic cyst, and keratocyst. Nonodontogenic cysts such as osteofibrous dysplasia can also appear in this region but are less frequent than odontogenic cysts. Infections that affect teeth and their surrounding tissues may lead to periapical lesions, including radicular cysts and acute apical periodontitis. Odontogenic neoplasms like ameloblastic fibroma and amelobastoma are rare compared with benign cysts. Genetic disorders associated with jaw cysts include Gardner syndrome, neurofibromatosis type I, and familial trichoepitheliomatosis.

Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is a type of malignant tumor that originates from salivary gland-type cells found throughout the body. The name "adenoid" refers to its histological resemblance to normal salivary glands, while "cystic" indicates the presence of cysts within the tumor, which can be present at various stages of development. The suffix "-carcinoma" denotes this cancer's epithelial cellular origins.

The treatment of phenylketonuria (PKU) involves strict adherence to a low-phenylalanine (Phe) diet throughout life. This is supplemented with Phe-free amino acid mixtures that provide essential amino acids not restricted in the diet. In addition, patients may require other therapies depending upon their clinical presentation and response to therapy.

The diagnosis of lipedema is made through physical examination and patient history. It can be distinguished from obesity by the presence of pain in the subcutaneous adipose tissue, which is disproportionate to the amount of excess body mass. Lipoedematous limbs may also have an orange peel appearance (orange peeling) due to small bumps under the skin surface caused by localized accumulation of fat cells. Other diagnostic criteria include asymmetry between affected and unaffected areas, sparing of the torso, and lack of associated metabolic abnormalities such as diabetes mellitus or hyperlipidemia.

The most common sign of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is an abnormal spine curve that progresses over time. It can be detected by visual inspection using the forward bend test (also known as the Adam's Forward Bend Test). Other signs include unequal shoulder height, asymmetric rib cage prominence, and uneven hips. These signs may not always be present in patients with milder forms of scoliosis.

The condition you are referring to is called Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC). It is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in either of two genes that encode proteins involved in cholesterol transport into lysosomes . Clinically, it presents as progressive neurodegeneration characterized by cognitive decline, dystonia, ataxia, vertical gaze paresis, dysarthria, and epilepsy. Visceral involvement includes hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pulmonary hypertension, and ascites. Diagnosis involves detection of elevated levels of unesterified cholesterol in leukocytes or fibroblasts, along with characteristic findings on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET), followed by genetic testing for pathogenic variants in NPC1 or NPC2 genes. Treatment options include supportive care, such as symptom management and nutritional support, as well as specific therapies like miglustat, which aims to reduce lipid accumulation in affected tissues .

The condition you are referring to is called adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD). It can be triggered by various factors such as viral infections, exposure to certain drugs, or environmental triggers. However, there is no definitive cause of AOSD yet identified.

The yellowish buildup in the eye that develops later in life and affects central vision is called drusen. Drusen can be treated by reducing risk factors such as smoking cessation, maintaining healthy blood pressure, consuming a Mediterranean diet, and exercising regularly. If drusen progresses to geographic atrophy (GA), then antioxidant supplements may help slow down its development.

Treatments for disorders causing blood not to clot properly include anticoagulants such as heparin or warfarin (Coumadin), antiplatelet agents like aspirin, platelet transfusions, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, desmopressin, recombinant factor VIIa, and surgical intervention depending upon the cause of bleeding .

A baby being born with congenital malformations such as missing parts of organs in the abdomen could be caused by various reasons including environmental exposures (e.g., maternal medications), chromosomal abnormalities, gene mutation, or other unknown causes. These conditions may occur independently or together. However, most cases have no known cause.

The typical signs and symptoms of Aicardi-Goutieres Syndrome Type 2 (AGS) include severe encephalopathy with microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, cerebral atrophy, seizures, progressive neurological deterioration, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, skin rash, lymphadenopathy, leukocytosis, elevated liver transaminases, hypothyroidism, and increased levels of interferon alpha .

Aicardi-Goutieres Syndrome (AGS) is an autosomal recessive disease that causes severe encephalopathy with early-onset dystonia and spasticity . It was first described by French neurologists Françoise Aicardi and Jean Goutières in 1984 as a distinct clinical entity characterized by microcephaly, basal ganglia calcifications, intracranial hemorrhages, leukodystrophy, and progressive cerebral atrophy . The pathogenesis of AGS involves dysregulation of nucleic acid metabolism leading to increased production of type I interferons (IFN), which can cause neuroinflammation and neuronal damage .

Amyloidosis refers to a group of diseases characterized by the deposition of insoluble fibrillar protein aggregates known as amyloid deposits in various tissues and organs . These amyloid deposits can lead to organ dysfunction and failure, resulting in significant morbidity and mortality for patients with this condition. The term “amyloidosis” itself derives from the Greek word “amylon,” meaning starch, due to the appearance of these deposits under polarized light resembling starch granules .

The inherited condition that causes abnormal bone growth and body changes is called Achondroplasia (ACH).
