Doctors can use several methods to determine if nasal congestion is due to a more severe illness like cancer or a benign cause like an allergic reaction or sinusitis. Firstly, they will ask about any other symptoms that may be linked with these diseases, including fever, weight loss, difficulty swallowing, pain in the mouth, trouble breathing, coughing, hoarseness, sore throat, earaches, headaches, eye pains, toothaches, numbness of the face, neck, or jaw, swelling of the lymph nodes, discharge from the eyes, or vision problems . They will also conduct a physical examination to check for enlarged lymph nodes, nodules, masses, tenderness, redness, warmth, or other signs of inflammation .

Cancer of the head and neck can occur in various parts of the oral cavity (mouth), pharynx (throat), larynx (voice box) and nasal cavities. The most common types of head and neck cancer include squamous cell carcinoma, which is a type of skin cancer that starts in the flat cells lining an internal surface; adenocarcinomas, which start in glandular tissue; undifferentiated carcinomas, which do not resemble any normal type of cell; and sarcomas, which affect connective tissues such as bone, fat and muscle.

The stages of oral cavity cancers (OCs) are determined by the TNM system according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). T stands for primary tumors, N represents regional lymph nodes, and M refers to distant metastasis.

Pancreatic cancer refers to any malignant tumor that arises from cells of the pancreas. It can be divided into two main types: endocrine (insulinoma) or exocrine (adenocarcinomas). Adenocarcinomas account for about 90% of all cases of pancreatic cancer .

Stomach (gastric) adenocarcinoma is staged according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC)/Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM system. The T stage indicates the depth of tumor invasion into the gastric wall layers, while N refers to lymph node involvement and M as distant metastasis. Stage 0 represents in situ carcinoma without invasion beyond the mucosa; I denotes localized cancer with invasion limited to the submucosal layer; IIa involves deeper penetration into the muscularis propria layer but not through the serosa; IIb extends through the serosa and invades adjacent organs or structures; III describes perigastric lymph nodes being involved; IV signifies distant organ metastases.

Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) can originate from different parts of the body including the lungs, pancreas, stomach, intestines, rectum, appendix, and brain. Hormones produced by NETs include serotonin, insulin, glucagon, gastrin, somatostatin, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), parathyroid hormone related peptide (PTHrP), calcitonin, vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), and growth hormone (GH). The most common NET is small cell lung cancer (SCLC), which produces TSH and PTHrP. Gastric NETs produce VIP, while pancreatic NETs produce insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin. Rectal NETs secrete serotonin, whereas pituitary NETs produce GH .

Cancer of the urinary tract refers to any type of malignant neoplasm arising from tissues involved in the normal function of the bladder, urethra, prostate gland, renal pelvis, ureter, and kidneys. This includes cancers such as transitional cell carcinoma (TCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), adenocarcinoma, sarcoma, and other rare types of cancer. The term “cancer” itself refers to a group of diseases characterized by uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells that may invade adjacent tissue structures and organs .

Cancer in the ureter or renal pelvis can cause various symptoms depending on its location. The most common symptom is hematuria (blood in the urine), which may be visible to the naked eye or detected by laboratory tests for red blood cells in the urine. Other possible symptoms include abdominal or flank pain, especially when accompanied by fever or weight loss, frequent urination, painful micturition, and lower back pain that does not resolve after rest. It is important to note that these symptoms can also occur due to other conditions, so it is crucial to consult a healthcare professional if any of them persist.

There have been several ongoing clinical trials to evaluate novel therapies for patients with advanced UC of the bladder. The phase III IMvigor130 trial is evaluating atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone as first-line treatment for metastatic disease . Another phase III study, KEYNOTE-768, is comparing pembrolizumab monotherapy versus platinum-based chemotherapy as first-line therapy for locally advanced or metastatic UC .

The long-term prognosis of pediatric patients diagnosed with renal tumor depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, stage of disease, histological subtype, and presence of metastasis. Overall, the survival rate for pediatric patients with localized RCC ranges from 70% to over 95%, while it drops significantly to around 10% when the disease has spread beyond the kidneys .

Breast cancer can occur in any woman regardless of their age or family history. However, there are certain groups that have an increased risk compared to others. The main risk factor for developing breast cancer is having a first degree relative (mother, sister, daughter) who has been diagnosed with the disease. This increases the chance of getting breast cancer by about 50%. Other risk factors include early menarche before the age of 12 years old, late menopause after the age of 50 years old, nulliparity, obesity, high alcohol consumption, exposure to ionizing radiation during childhood or adolescence, use of oral contraceptives, smoking, and genetic mutations such as BRCA1 and BRCA2. Younger women under the age of 40 also tend to be at higher risk than those over the age of 60 due to delayed detection.

The long-term outlook depends on various factors such as the type of cancer diagnosed, stage at diagnosis, age, sex, lifestyle habits (smoking status, alcohol consumption), and treatment received . For instance, if breast cancer is detected early through regular screening mammograms, it can usually be cured with appropriate treatments such as surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted drug therapy, etc., resulting in 5-year survival rates of up to 90% . However, if breast cancer is not detected until symptoms appear, the 5-year survival rate drops significantly to around 27%. Similarly, the 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer patients diagnosed at an early stage is about 90%, but this decreases to approximately 14% when diagnosed at a late stage . It's important to note that these statistics may vary depending on the specific subtype of cancer involved. Regular checkups and screenings play a crucial role in detecting cancers at an early stage, which greatly increases chances of successful treatment and recovery.

Breast cancer is rare in men compared to women. The main risk factor for developing breast cancer in both sexes is increasing age. Other risk factors include family history of breast cancer (particularly first-degree relatives), genetic mutations associated with hereditary syndromes like BRCA1 and BRCA2, exposure to ionizing radiation at an early age, high body mass index, alcohol consumption, smoking, diabetes mellitus, chronic liver disease, testosterone levels, and low physical activity .

Male breast cancer is typically divided into four stages (0-IV) according to the TNM staging system used for most types of cancer. Stage 0 indicates that the tumor has not spread beyond the lobules or ducts where it started, while stage I indicates that it has spread to nearby tissue but not lymph nodes. Stages II and III indicate that the cancer has spread to lymph nodes under the arm or above the collarbone, as well as other parts of the body such as bone, liver, or brain. The final stage, IV, indicates that the cancer has metastasized to distant organs.

The prognosis of suspicious skin lesions depends on their histopathological diagnosis. Most benign neoplasms have an excellent prognosis with complete surgical excision. However, some malignant tumors such as melanoma may be fatal if not diagnosed early and treated appropriately. Therefore, regular follow-up examinations after treatment are essential to monitor any recurrence or metastasis.

Anyone can develop skin cancer due to sun exposure, but those with lighter skin (fair or very fair) have an increased risk compared to darker skins. The reason for this difference in risk is that melanin, which absorbs UV radiation, provides protection against sun damage. People with less melanin are more susceptible to sunburns and premature aging of their skin. In addition, they may also be more likely to develop skin cancer later in life.

The usual treatment for a suspicious skin lesion depends on its characteristics such as size, location, type of skin cancer, and stage at diagnosis. For non-melanoma skin cancers (NMSC), topical imiquimod may be prescribed to treat superficial basal cell carcinomas (BCCs) and actinic keratoses. Cryosurgery, laser therapy, photodynamic therapy, curettage, Mohs surgery, and excision are also effective in treating BCCs. Topical fluorouracil, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and 5-fluorouracil cream are commonly used to treat squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs). If NMSC cannot be cured by these methods, then surgical removal is recommended.

Doctors can use various methods to diagnose suspicious skin growths, including physical examination, visual inspection with magnification (dermoscopy), and removal of tissue for microscopic evaluation (biopsy). The type of biopsy performed depends on the size, location, and characteristics of the suspected skin lesion. A punch biopsy involves removing a circular piece of tissue using a special tool called a punch; shave biopsy removes part of the top layer of skin; excisional biopsy removes all layers of skin. If the doctor suspects melanoma, a wide local excision may be recommended, which involves removing not only the tumor but also some surrounding normal-appearing skin. After the sample is removed, it will be examined by a pathologist who will look for specific features under a microscope that indicate the presence of skin cancer.

The best way to prevent sun damage is by practicing good sun safety habits every day. This includes wearing protective clothing such as long sleeves shirts, wide brimmed hats, sunglasses, seeking shade whenever possible, avoiding the sun during peak hours (10 am – 4 pm), using broad spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen, and reapplying it every two hours or after swimming, sweating, etc. It’s also important to check your skin regularly for any changes in moles or birthmarks and see a doctor if you find anything unusual.

The stages or levels of progression in plasma cell neoplasms (PCN) are classified by the International Staging System (ISS). This system is used to stage newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM), which is the most common PCN . It uses three variables: serum beta-2 microglobulin level, albumin level, and presence of plasmacytomas . Based on these variables, NDMM patients are divided into one of three risk groups: ISS 1, ISS 2, or ISS 3. Patients with lower scores have better outcomes than those with higher scores .

Neuroblastoma is one of the most common cancers diagnosed in childhood. The clinical presentation varies depending on the location of the tumor within the body. Abdominal mass or pain may be present if the primary site is located in the abdomen. Fatigue, anemia from bone marrow involvement, fever, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy may also occur. Other possible symptoms include constipation, diarrhea, vomiting, weakness, numbness, seizures, jaundice, and palpable masses in the neck, chest, spine, or pelvis.

There are several ongoing clinical trials investigating novel therapies for high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNBL). One such trial is evaluating the efficacy of combining anti-GD2 antibody therapy with chemotherapy to improve outcomes in patients with HRNBL. Another study is examining the use of targeted agents such as ALK inhibitors and MEK inhibitors to treat relapsed or refractory tumors. Other promising approaches include immunotherapies that target specific molecular subtypes of NB, such as those involving chimeric antigen receptor T cells. These therapies aim to enhance the body's immune response against cancer cells by modifying immune system components to recognize and attack them.

Doctors typically use several diagnostic tools to identify potential signs of lung cancer in patients with suspicious symptoms. The initial test is often a physical examination by a primary care physician (PCP) followed by an X-ray or CT scan of the patient's chest. If these preliminary examinations reveal any abnormalities, further testing may be required, such as bronchoscopy, biopsy, PET scan, MRI, or ultrasound. These procedures can help physicians distinguish between benign and malignant tumors and determine their location within the lungs. It is important for individuals experiencing persistent respiratory issues to consult a healthcare professional promptly, especially if there is a history of smoking or exposure to carcinogens. Early detection through regular screening and timely diagnosis are crucial for effective treatment and improving overall prognosis.

Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is an aggressive type of neuroendocrine tumor that originates in the lungs. It accounts for approximately 15% of all lung cancers. SCLC cells have a characteristic morphology with round or oval nuclei and scant cytoplasm. They also express specific biomarkers such as synaptophysin and chromogranin A. The exact cause of SCLC remains unknown, but several risk factors have been identified including smoking, exposure to radon gas, family history of lung cancer, and certain genetic conditions.

Treatment of aggressive, fast-growing cancers in the chest typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and surgical resection. The specific treatment plan may depend on several factors, including the type of tumor, its stage at diagnosis, the extent to which it has spread within the body (metastasized), and the overall health status of the patient.

The rare gland cancer you are referring to is called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). It originates from cells of the C-cells in the thyroid gland and can affect the parathyroid glands and cause changes in calcium levels. MTC is not the same as throat cancer, which typically arises from squamous epithelial cells and includes conditions such as laryngeal cancer and esophageal cancer.

Parathyroid cancer (PC) is an extremely rare endocrine malignancy that originates from the parathyroids, which are four small glands located in the neck near the thyroid. PC can be divided into three main types based on its clinical presentation: type 1, type 2, and type 3 . Type 1 is characterized by hypercalcemia due to excessive production of parathyroid hormone (PTH), while type 2 presents with hypocalcemia caused by PTH resistance. Finally, type 3 exhibits no biochemical abnormalities but may present as a benign or malignant tumor .

The presence of any of these symptoms could be an indication of penile cancer: 1) A sore or bump that doesn’t go away; 2) Pain or discomfort in the penis; 3) Bleeding from the tip of the penis; 4) Discharge from the head of the penis; 5) Redness or swelling of the skin around the penis; 6) Persistent skin change such as rash, wart-like growths, or thickening of the skin.

There are several ongoing clinical trials that aim to improve treatment outcomes in patients with prostate cancer (PCa). These include studies evaluating novel systemic therapies such as immunotherapy, targeted agents, and combination approaches . Some of these trials involve combinations of immune checkpoint inhibitors, while others evaluate the use of PARP inhibitors in combination with other drugs. Other ongoing trials focus on improving localized therapy options for PCa, including radiation therapy techniques and brachytherapy .

The prognosis for patients with brain tumors depends on various factors such as type, size, location, grade, age at diagnosis, overall health status, and treatment received. Generally speaking, low-grade gliomas have a better prognosis than high-grade ones. Surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and targeted therapies may be used to treat brain tumors. However, some types of brain tumors may recur after initial treatment, leading to worse outcomes. It is important to note that every patient's situation is unique, so it is best to consult with a healthcare provider for personalized advice.

Pain during urination (dysuria), frequent urination, urgent need to urinate, cloudy or foul smelling urine, and difficulty initiating urine flow can all be indicative of a serious problem in men. These symptoms may also occur due to non-serious conditions such as benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) or an infection. However, if they persist for several days without improvement despite home remedies or over-the-counter medications, it is important to consult a healthcare provider. It is not possible to determine what specific symptom would warrant immediate attention, but any new or persistent urinary symptoms that do not resolve within a few days should prompt further evaluation by a healthcare professional.

There have been several recent developments in the treatment of prostate cancer and related urinary conditions. One such development is the use of focal therapy to treat localized prostate cancer. Focal therapy involves treating only the areas with cancer rather than the entire prostate gland. This can be done using various techniques including cryotherapy, high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), brachytherapy, and photodynamic therapy. Another area of research is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the diagnosis and management of prostate cancer. AI algorithms have shown promise in improving the accuracy of diagnosing prostate cancer from biopsies as well as predicting which patients will benefit most from specific treatments. In addition, there has also been progress in developing new drugs to treat advanced prostate cancer. These include new classes of hormonal therapies that target the androgen receptor pathway, such as enzalutamide and darolutamide, as well as inhibitors of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) proteins, such as olaparib and rucaparib .

The most common symptoms of a serious bowel condition include diarrhea, constipation, rectal bleeding, weight loss, anemia, abdominal pain, bloating, gas, and nausea. It is important to note that these symptoms can also be caused by other conditions unrelated to the bowels, so it is crucial for individuals experiencing any of them to consult with their healthcare provider for proper diagnosis and treatment.

There have been several recent advances in the treatment of colorectal cancer (CRC). In 2019, the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) approved two new drugs to treat CRC patients with specific genetic mutations. The first drug is encorafenib, which targets BRAF-mutant tumors . This was followed by the approval of cetuximab, an antibody that binds to EGFR, as a second line therapy for RAS wildtype CRC .

The prognosis and likelihood of recovery from cancer in the genital area depend on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, type of cancer, age, sex, lifestyle habits (smoking, alcohol consumption), and overall health status. Generally speaking, early-stage cervical cancers have a better chance of being successfully treated than later stages. For example, 92% of women diagnosed with Stage IA1 cervical cancer will survive for five years or more after treatment, while only 67% of those diagnosed with Stage IIIB cervical cancer will be alive for five years or more . Similarly, vulvar cancer has a relatively good prognosis if detected early; however, survival rates decrease significantly when diagnosed at later stages . Endometrial cancer also tends to have a favorable prognosis, especially during the first few years after diagnosis. However, long-term outcomes may vary depending on tumor characteristics and other risk factors .

There are several ways to reduce one's risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC), which is the third most common type of cancer in both men and women worldwide . These include maintaining a healthy weight, exercising regularly, limiting alcohol consumption, not smoking, eating plenty of fruits and vegetables, consumming whole grains instead of refined grains, drinking milk, avoiding red meat, especially processed meats, and consuming probiotics such as yogurt with live bacteria cultures . Additionally, it is important to get screened for CRC at least once every 10 years starting at age 45. Screening options include fecal occult blood testing (FOBT) by mail, sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, computed tomographic (CT) colonography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). People who have a first-degree relative diagnosed with CRC should start screening earlier than average age, typically around age 40 .

Symptoms such as severe pain (especially if it is constant), fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea lasting more than 3 days, bloody stools, and any signs of dehydration can be indicative of a more serious infection. It's important to seek immediate medical attention for these symptoms.

Thymomas and thymic carcinomas are both types of cancer that originate from cells found within the thymus gland. The main difference between these two cancers lies in their cellular origins. While thymomas arise from epithelial cells or B lymphocytes, thymic carcinomas develop from squamous cells (epidermoid) or neuroendocrine cells (small-cell carcinoma).

There are several ongoing clinical trials for thymic carcinoma (TC) that have been listed by ClinicalTrials.gov as of August 2021. These include phase I-III trials evaluating chemotherapy regimens such as cisplatin plus pemetrexed, carboplatin plus paclitaxel, and gemcitabine plus docetaxel. Other trials are investigating targeted therapies such as lenvatinib, an oral multikinase inhibitor, and nivolumab, an anti-PD-L1 antibody. Additionally, there is also a trial assessing immunotherapeutic agents like interleukin-2 and interferon alpha.

Urethral cancer has an overall 5-year survival rate of approximately 80%. The specific rates vary depending on the stage at diagnosis. Stage I tumors have a 96% 5-year relative survival rate, while stages II to IV range from 74% to 23%, respectively .

Persistent itching, burning, a sore or lump that does not go away, or abnormal bleeding can be signs of a serious vulvar or vaginal problem. If any of these symptoms occur along with other symptoms like pain during sex, urinating problems, discharge, or foul odor, this may indicate more than normal irritation. It is important to see a healthcare provider if you have any concerns about your symptoms.

The usual treatment option depends on the type of cancer and its stage at diagnosis. For example, penile cancers may be treated with chemotherapy, surgery, or both depending on their stages. Surgery is usually performed in combination with other treatments (such as radiotherapy) for vulvar cancer. Radiation therapy alone or combined with chemotherapy is used to treat vaginal cancer. Treatment decisions are made by a multidisciplinary team that considers various factors, including tumor size, location, grade, and staging system.

An abnormality in the structure of blood vessels around the heart is known as coronary artery anomaly (CAA). It occurs when there is an alteration in the normal pattern of development of the coronary arteries during embryogenesis. The most common type of CAA is the left circumflex artery from the right coronary sinus, which affects 0.2%-1.5% of the population . Other rare types include the right coronary artery originating from the pulmonary artery (Pulmonary-coronary artery fistula), double lumen coronaries, and ectopic coronary arteries.

The diagnosis of malabsorption is made by combining clinical history with laboratory testing. A thorough dietary history can help rule out lactose intolerance as a potential cause. Laboratory testing typically includes serum albumin levels, which may be low in cases of protein loss due to diarrhea; serum calcium levels, which may be low if there is an underlying problem with fat absorption; and fecal elastase levels, which measure pancreatic enzyme production and can indicate exocrine pancreas insufficiency (EPI). Other diagnostic tools include endoscopy with biopsy, which can identify inflammation or damage to the small bowel, and capsule enteroscopy, which allows for visualization of the entire small bowel.

A congenital absence or hypoplasia of one or more bones can be associated with various conditions such as fibular hemimelia (a condition characterized by underdevelopment of the calf muscles), anorectal atresia, tibial dyschondroplasia, and others. The most common sign is the presence of a shortened limb with a visible gap between the knee and ankle where the missing bone should be located. Other possible symptoms include weakness, pain, stiffness, and limited range of motion in the affected joints. Early complications may include delayed walking, difficulty maintaining balance, and increased risk for falls due to muscle imbalance and foot instability.

Rare metabolic disorders that cause an accumulation of toxic compounds due to impaired enzyme activity may present with various clinical manifestations including recurrent vomiting, diarrhea, seizures, developmental delay, intellectual disability, failure to thrive, hypotonia, macroglossia, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiomyopathy, ophthalmologic abnormalities, dermatological findings, and dysarthria . The specific symptoms depend upon the type of disorder and affected organ system. For example, maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is characterized by distinctive odor of sweat and urine resembling burnt sugar, which results from ketoacids produced when proteins are catabolized for energy. Other common features of MSUD include poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, vomiting, and coma. In addition, patients with organic acidurias such as propionic academia have increased levels of lactic acid in their blood, which causes nausea, vomiting, weakness, confusion, and seizures. Patients with urea cycle disorders exhibit excessive ammonia production leading to altered mental status, vomiting, and seizures.

The usual treatment for a painful, swollen extra bone or bony bump near the arch of the foot depends on its cause. If it's due to an injury or trauma, RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) therapy may be recommended. For soft tissue injuries such as tendinitis, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), physical therapy, or corticosteroids can help with pain management. Surgery may be necessary if conservative treatments fail or there is severe deformity.

Dysphagia is characterized by difficulty in swallowing that can lead to discomfort, pain, and other complications if left untreated. The most common symptom of dysphagia is the sensation of food getting stuck while swallowing (also known as globus sensation). Other symptoms include difficulty initiating swallowing, prolonged swallowing, sense of choking or suffocation during swallowing, coughing after eating, and regurgitation. Chest pain may also be experienced due to reflux of acidic contents from the esophagus into the stomach. In severe cases, aspiration pneumonia can occur due to food entering the airway instead of the esophagus. It is important for individuals experiencing these symptoms to seek medical attention promptly to determine the underlying cause and receive appropriate treatment.

The condition you are referring to is called Achondroplasia (ACH). It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the FGFR3 gene that leads to defective bone growth. Affected individuals have disproportionate short stature with characteristic rhizomelia of the limbs and trident acetabular roof. Other features include macrocephaly, frontal bossing, midface flattening, ptosis, high-arched palate, dental crowding, and hearing loss.

Achondrogenesis type I A (also known as Fraser syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by dwarfism, disproportionate limb shortening, and underdevelopment of the epiphyseal growth plates . It results from mutations in the gene encoding fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), which plays a crucial role in chondrocyte differentiation during endochondral ossification . The condition can be diagnosed prenatally or soon after birth through physical examination and radiographic imaging.

Short-limbed dwarfism is characterized by disproportionally short limbs with normal trunk size. The condition can be caused by various genetic mutations that affect skeletal growth during childhood. It may also occur due to certain environmental factors. Some individuals with this disorder have additional symptoms such as joint laxity, scoliosis, hernias, and intellectual disability.

Achondroplasia is a type of dwarfism that can be accompanied by an immune deficiency disorder called hypogammaglobulinemia primary immunodeficiency (HIGM). Hypo refers to low levels or production of antibodies, which are proteins produced by B cells that help fight off infection. The most common sign of HIGM is recurrent respiratory tract infections such as pneumonia, bronchitis, sinusitis, otitis media, and ear infections. Other signs include short stature, skeletal abnormalities, joint laxity, hearing loss, vision problems, delayed puberty, poor growth, and intellectual disability. Patients may also have autoimmune diseases such as thyroid disease, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and inflammatory bowel disease.

The medical term for this condition is idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). It is characterized by low platelet count with no identifiable underlying causes such as autoimmune disease or infection. Patients typically present with bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, and other signs of increased risk of bleeding. Treatment options include steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin therapy, and splenectomy.

The rare condition you are referring to may be Vitamin B12 deficiency. It can cause skin changes such as a red rash on the face, lips, tongue, diaper area, and other parts of the body. Other symptoms include failure to thrive, irritability, weakness, fatigue, pale skin, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting, poor appetite, and neurological issues like numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, balance difficulties, and memory problems.

The correct name of the disease is "costochondritis". It refers to inflammation in the cartilage that connects ribs to the breastbone (sternum). This can cause chest pain with movement or deep breaths. It should not be confused with costovertebral angle tenderness, which involves the joint between the ribs and vertebrae.

The rare congenital bone growth disorder you are referring to is known as Spondylocarpotarsal Synostosis Syndrome (SCTS). It is caused by mutations in the HOXD13 gene that lead to premature fusion of bones in the spine, carpals, tarsals, and vertebrae. This can result in short stature, deformities in the limbs and spine, and other skeletal anomalies. While this condition may be associated with some limitations in mobility and activities of daily living, it does not typically have any significant impact on life expectancy.

The condition being referred to is called Pierre Robin sequence (PRS). It can be isolated or associated with other anomalies. PRS is characterized by micrognathia (underdevelopment of the lower jaw), glossoptosis (backward positioning of the tongue), cleft palate, and airway obstruction. Other common features include facial asymmetry, ear deformity, hearing loss, swallowing difficulty, gastroesophageal reflux, and respiratory distress. Associated anomalies may involve the heart, genitourinary system, skeleton, nervous system, and muscles.

The condition you are referring to is leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LV). It can cause a high fever along with small, reddish-purple spots or bumps that may be tender when touched. These symptoms typically appear after exposure to certain triggers such as drugs, infections, or environmental factors. LV is not caused by a bacterial or viral skin infection but rather from damage to the skin's blood vessels due to immune system activation.

Typical symptoms of an acute porphyria attack include severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and neurologic manifestations including peripheral neuropathy, seizures, psychosis, hypertension, autonomic dysfunction, cerebral ischemia, and stroke . Dark urine may be present due to heme precipitation in the tubular lumen from excess porphyrin precursors . Confusion can occur but it is not a common symptom of acute porphyric attacks.

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is defined as acute hypoxemia accompanied by bilateral pulmonary opacities that cannot be explained by left heart disease or fluid overload . It is caused by an inflammatory process within the lung parenchyma leading to increased permeability of alveolar capillaries, resulting in protein-rich edema fluid accumulating in the alveoli and interstitium . This can occur due to various factors such as sepsis, trauma, aspiration, drowning, blood transfusions, and drug reactions .

The term "gum" refers to the gingiva, which is the soft tissue that surrounds the teeth. A lesion on the hard palate of the roof of the mouth would not be considered a gum problem. It's possible that you may have meant an oral ulcer or other type of oral mucosal condition rather than a gum issue.

Doctors can use several diagnostic tools to identify an abnormality in the lower abdomen. The most commonly used methods include physical examination, blood tests, ultrasound scans, CT (computed tomography) scan, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), laparoscopy, and biopsy.
The symptoms of this rare metabolic disorder include developmental delay, seizures, low energy levels, and behavioral changes. These symptoms typically manifest during infancy or childhood.

Painful fatty lumps under the skin can be hereditary in some cases. They may also develop spontaneously without any family history of similar lesions. The exact cause is unknown but it has been suggested that certain genetic factors may play a role in their development.

The condition you are referring to is called idiopathic scoliosis (IS). It is characterized by a lateral curvature of the spine with no clear etiology. IS can occur at any age but most commonly presents during childhood and adolescence. While some studies suggest that certain genetic factors may be associated with IS, there is currently no evidence for specific environmental causes.

The signs and symptoms of endocrine glands overproducing hormone include excessive sweating, heat intolerance, diarrhea, flushing, headaches, palpitations, tremors, weakness, fatigue, anxiety, depression, decreased libido, infertility, irregular menstrual periods, vaginal dryness, impotence, loss of body mass, osteoporosis, skin changes (thickening), and unexplained weight loss.

Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) is an inflammatory disorder that can affect people of all ages but most commonly occurs in adults aged 30 to 50 years old . The typical presentation includes high spiking fever, arthritis, skin rashes, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, serositis, leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated acute phase reactants, and abnormal liver function tests . AOSD may also be associated with other conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, dermatomyositis, Sjogren syndrome, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, and malignancies .

The development of yellow spots (lipofuscin) or blurred central vision at an older age may be due to various factors such as genetics, lifestyle, environmental exposure, or normal aging process. It could also indicate the presence of macular degeneration, which has both genetic and environmental risk factors. Therefore, while there may be some familial predisposition for developing these symptoms, they cannot solely be attributed to heredity.

A bleeding disorder can be either congenital (inherited) or acquired. Congenital disorders result from an intrinsic defect in one of the coagulation factor pathways. Acquired disorders may develop as a result of certain medications, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, or other conditions that interfere with normal blood clotting.

Congenital abdominal organ malformations can present with various symptoms depending on the type of anomaly involved. For example, pyloric stenosis may cause vomiting after feeds, while gastroschisis may result in abdominal distension and skin erosion at birth. Diagnosis is often made during prenatal ultrasound screening or postnatally through physical examination and imaging tests such as X-ray, CT scan, MRI, and ultrasound. Treatment options vary widely but may include surgery, medication, or monitoring. It is important for healthcare providers to be aware of these conditions and their potential presentation to ensure timely diagnosis and appropriate management.

The typical early indications of this illness include epilepsy, impaired developmental milestones (e.g., language delay), muscle rigidity, and temperature instability. Other potential symptoms may include ataxia, dystonia, spasticity, and intellectual disability.

The most common symptoms of Addison's disease include fatigue, weight loss, skin hyperpigmentation, muscle weakness, dizziness upon standing up (orthostatic hypotension), nausea or vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headaches, irritability, depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbances. When the condition is poorly managed, patients may experience severe dehydration, low blood pressure, salt wasting syndrome, electrolyte imbalances, and even shock.

The condition described is likely Diabetes Insipidus (DI), which can be caused by congenital or acquired factors such as trauma to the pituitary gland. Symptoms of DI include excessive thirst, frequent urination, nocturia, polydipsia, polyuria, headaches, lethargy, dehydration, weight loss, growth retardation, and developmental delay. It may also cause electrolyte imbalances due to fluid loss, including hyponatremia and hypokalemia.

The condition you are referring to may be Achondroplasia (ACH). ACH is an autosomal recessive genetic disease caused by mutations in the FGFR3 gene, resulting in impaired chondrogenesis during endochondral ossification. It leads to disproportionate dwarfism with rhizomelia of the limbs, short trunk, frontal bossing, midface flattening, trident acetabular roofs, lumbar lordosis, kyphotic deformity, genu varum, and other skeletal anomalies .

The patient is suffering from a very rare genetic disorder called Cockayne syndrome (CS). CS is an autosomal recessive disease that affects multiple organ systems in children. It can be caused by mutations in either of two genes involved in transcription, namely, RNA polymerase I or III subunit A (POLR1A) or POLR3B. Children with CS may present with features like small head size (microcephaly), short stature, intellectual disability, hearing loss, cataracts, hypopigmentation, and photosensitivity. Other common clinical manifestations include failure to thrive, alopecia totalis, retinal degeneration, and delayed bone age.

The sudden or gradual loss of all hair on the body (alopecia universalis) may be caused by several factors including autoimmune conditions such as alopecia areata, telogen effluvium, trichotillomania, certain medications, chemotherapy treatments, nutritional deficiencies, hormonal imbalances, infections, and psychological disorders. It is important for individuals experiencing this type of alopecia to consult with their healthcare provider to determine the underlying cause and appropriate treatment options.

The condition being referred to is known as Cockayne syndrome (CS). It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in either one of two genes, ERCC8 or ERCC6. CS can present at birth or later in childhood. Common features include growth retardation, microcephaly, intellectual disability, hearing loss, photosensitivity, cataracts, and bone abnormalities. Hair loss may be generalized or localized. Treatment options for this disease are limited but involve supportive care such as photoprotection, treatment of infections, and management of nutritional deficiencies.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) is an acute phase protein that plays a crucial role in regulating inflammation by inhibiting neutrophil elastase activity . AAT deficiency can lead to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hepatitis, cirrhosis, and liver cancer . The treatment of AAT deficiency depends on the severity of symptoms and whether there is associated COPD or liver disease .

Yes, some types of anemias can be inherited from parents to their children. These include thalassemias (a group of genetic conditions that affect hemoglobin), sickle cell disease (an abnormal hemoglobin structure), and RBC membrane defects such as spherocytosis.
The inherited condition causing kidney problems, which may also affect hearing and the eye, is known as Alport Syndrome (AS). It is classified as a syndrome rather than a familial disease.

The symptoms of this condition may include shortness of breath, wheezing, cough, fever, chest pain, and fatigue. Other complications that could arise from this disease are pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, arrhythmia, and death.

The dental condition you described is known as amelogenesis imperfecta (AI). AI can be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means that one copy of the affected gene is sufficient for disease expression but may manifest with varying severity depending on whether both copies of the gene are affected. Other forms of AI include recessive patterns of inheritance, such as autosomal recessive and X-linked recessive.

Treatments include fluoride varnish applications to strengthen tooth structure, sealants to prevent food from getting into pits and fissures of back teeth, and restoring teeth using crowns or veneers. Long-term options include fluoridated water consumption, use of fluoride mouth rinses, and topical gels containing fluoride.

The symptoms of MPS can vary depending on the specific type of MPS but may include short stature, joint pain or stiffness, hearing loss, vision impairment, skin changes (such as roughness), enlarged spleen or liver, heart valve disease, and intellectual disability. Early signs of MPS may be difficult to detect because they mimic other conditions, including growth failure, dysmorphism, and delayed motor milestones. It is important for healthcare providers to consider MPS when evaluating patients with these symptoms, especially if there is a family history of the disorder. Genetic testing is necessary to confirm an MPS diagnosis.

The exact cause of these fibrous bands is unknown but it has been suggested that they may be related to genetic factors, maternal health conditions such as diabetes or hypertension during pregnancy, infection, trauma, or other environmental exposures. They often form when there is an abnormal amount of amniotic fluid in the uterus (polyhydramnios) or too little amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios). These bands can tighten around the baby's body parts, leading to pressure against the skin, causing tissue death and injury.

The most common symptoms associated with corneal deposits include blurred vision, foreign body sensation, tearing, light sensitivity, burning sensation, itching, and pain. These can be caused by various conditions including Fuchs endothelial dystrophy (FED), pseudophakic bullous keratopathy (PBK), and other forms of corneal edema. It is important to note that these symptoms may also occur due to other causes unrelated to corneal deposits, so a thorough ophthalmic examination is necessary for proper diagnosis.

Hypotonia is characterized by low muscle tone, which can be present at birth (congenital) or develop later in life (acquired). In infants, congenital hypotonia may manifest as poor feeding, difficulty sucking, swallowing difficulties, breathing problems, weak cry, poor head control, decreased movement, and reduced reflexes. These symptoms typically do not worsen over time but may persist throughout childhood and adulthood. Acquired hypotonia can result from various causes including genetic disorders, prematurity, brain injury, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, and neuromuscular diseases. The management of hypotonia depends on its underlying cause and may involve physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology intervention, orthopedic surgery, medication, assistive devices, and other interventions to improve motor function and quality of life.

The diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is made through a combination of clinical history, physical examination, laboratory testing, electrodiagnostic studies, imaging, and genetic testing. It can be challenging to differentiate between ALS and other neurological disorders that present with similar symptoms, but there are several diagnostic criteria that can help guide the physician towards an accurate diagnosis.

An aggressive primary brain tumor that originates from glial cells is known as glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). GBM is classified as grade IV by the World Health Organization (WHO) classification system for central nervous system (CNS) tumors . Brain cancers include both primary and secondary types of tumors. Primary brain tumors originate within the brain itself while secondary ones arise elsewhere in the body before spreading to the brain through blood circulation or cerebrospinal fluid. The most common type of primary brain tumor is meningioma which usually develops from the outer membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. However, these tumors tend to be benign and do not metastasize easily unlike other forms of brain cancers like gliomas, medulloblastomas, ependymomas etc., which have high rates of recurrence after treatment due to their ability to spread rapidly throughout the CNS via white matter tracts .

The rare inherited neurological disorder you are referring to may be spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). SMA is an autosomal recessive neuromuscular disease characterized by degeneration of lower motor neurons in the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord. It causes muscle weakness and atrophy, particularly affecting the proximal muscles used for activities such as walking, sitting up, swallowing, and breathing. There are four types of SMA, with type 1 being the most severe and occurring before six months of age. Type 2 occurs between six months and two years of age, while type 3 presents from two to sixteen years old. Type 4 has adult onset and is less common than the others. SMA is not typically diagnosed until after birth because symptoms often appear later in life; however, some studies suggest prenatal diagnosis through genetic testing. While there is no cure for SMA, treatments exist to manage symptoms and improve quality of life.

The condition you are referring to is called congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). It occurs when there is a defect in one of the enzymes involved in cortisol production in the adrenal gland. This can lead to excess production of androgens and virilization of external genitalia in girls at birth.

The most common sign of a fetal brain anomaly is microcephaly (small head circumference). Other possible signs include asymmetry in skull formation, ventriculomegaly (enlarged fluid-filled spaces within the brain), agenesis of corpus callosum (lack of connection between two sides of the brain), and hypoplasia of cerebral hemispheres (underdevelopment of one side of the brain). These findings may be detected during routine ultrasonography at 18–20 weeks gestation or later. After delivery, additional imaging studies including computed tomography (CT) scan or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may reveal further details about the nature and extent of the brain defects.

The condition you are referring to is called Ohtahara Syndrome (OS). It is a severe form of early-onset epileptic encephalopathy characterized by suppressed background activity in electroencephalography (EEG), hypotonia, and abnormal eye movements . OS has been associated with mutations in genes involved in neuronal migration during neurodevelopment, such as ALX4, CASK, CDK5RAP2, CHD3, DCHS1, KIAA0986, MED13L, MED13, MEF2C, NCKAP1L, PCDH19, POGZ, SLC6A1, SYNGAP1, TCF4, and TTN .

Cerebral angiopathy is a rare condition that affects the brain's blood vessels and coverings. The most common symptom of cerebral angiopathy is severe headache, which may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, vision loss, weakness, numbness, speech impairment, and seizure-like episodes. Behavior changes, including depression, anxiety, aggression, personality changes, and cognitive decline, may also occur. It typically begins in childhood but can develop at any age.

The condition described is known as oculoanal anomaly syndrome (OAS), which is a rare congenital malformation that affects the eyes and anus. It was first reported in 1968 by Dr. Robert Klein of Columbia University Medical Center . OAS occurs when there is abnormal development during embryogenesis, resulting in fusion between the upper and lower eyelid margins due to tissue bands called symblepharon. This leads to partial or complete closure of both eyes. In addition, the anal canal may be atresic, meaning it has no opening for feces to pass through.

An impacted or fused tooth is when one tooth has failed to erupt properly due to physical obstruction from another tooth. Symptoms include pain, swelling, infection, and discomfort during biting or chewing. A typical tooth problem may be caused by decay, trauma, or other issues. To differentiate between them, it's important to consider the patient's history, clinical examination, radiographic findings, and professional judgment.

The condition of congenital absence or severe hypoplasia of nails is known as oligodactyly. It can be associated with other anomalies such as shortened limbs, syndactlylized toes, and cleft palate. Oligodactyly may occur in isolation or in association with other conditions such as Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and Fanconi anemia.

A child with anophthalmia (the absence of eyeballs) may have other birth defects that affect their brain, heart, kidneys, bones, teeth, ears, nose, throat, intestines, skin, muscle, or nervous system. They may also experience vision loss, hearing impairment, balance issues, seizures, developmental delays, intellectual disabilities, behavioral disorders, and social difficulties.

The most common symptom of inherited thrombophilia is venous thromboembolism (VTE), which includes deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). Other symptoms include unexplained localized pain, swelling, redness, warmth at a specific site, and fatigue. Inherited thrombophilias can be diagnosed through laboratory tests that measure levels of coagulation factors involved in the coagulation cascade. These tests may also detect antibodies against certain proteins associated with thrombotic disorders. Genetic testing for mutations in genes responsible for these conditions may also be performed to confirm diagnosis.

The usual treatments for autoimmune diseases that affect the muscles and lungs include corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and in some cases, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) infusions. Oxygen supplementation may be necessary if there is hypoxia present due to lung involvement. Physical therapy may also be prescribed depending on the severity of muscle weakness. In general, most patients with myasthenia gravis experience improvement within 12 months after starting appropriate treatment, although relapses can occur throughout their lifetime. Patients with dermatomyositis typically have an excellent prognosis, especially when treated early before significant muscle damage occurs. However, they often require long-term follow-up care to manage any residual symptoms or complications from the disease.

The condition you described is called Crouzon syndrome (CS). It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 gene (FGFR2) that results in craniofacial malformations including microcephaly, hypertelorism, midface retrusion, exophthalmos, maxillary hypoplasia, and external ear anomalies such as low-set ears. Other features include fusion of bones in the hands and feet, syndactyly, and joint laxity. In children with CS, there may be feeding difficulties due to upper airway obstruction, hearing impairment from conductive loss, and vision problems from corneal clouding. Children with CS also have cognitive delays and learning disabilities. During adolescence and adulthood, individuals with CS continue to experience progressive ocular protrusions, facial asymmetry, and jaw deformities. They may develop respiratory issues from obstructed breathing and require tracheostomy. Individuals with CS often need orthodontic treatment for their dental malocclusion. Surgeries are commonly required throughout childhood and into adulthood to correct these physical manifestations.

A baby being born with an area of skin that did not form properly or is missing (known as cutis aplasia) may be caused by genetic factors such as mutations in genes involved in embryonic development, exposure to certain medications during pregnancy, or environmental factors such as radiation therapy or trauma. It can also occur due to chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 13 or 18. Cutis aplasia can sometimes be associated with other birth defects such as skeletal malformations or neurological disorders.

Aldosterone is a hormone produced in the adrenal glands that helps regulate sodium levels in the body. Too much aldosterone can lead to hypertension (high blood pressure), which is one of the most common causes of heart disease and stroke worldwide. Other symptoms associated with high levels of aldosterone include weakness, headache, muscle cramps, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, and fatigue. In addition, long-term exposure to excess aldosterone may cause fluid retention, leading to swelling in the legs, ankles, and feet; weight gain; and abdominal pain due to liver enlargement. It is important for individuals experiencing these symptoms to consult their healthcare provider, who may recommend further testing to determine if they have hyperaldosteronism.

This condition may be caused by an allergic reaction to certain ingredients found in soaps, shampoos, detergents, deodorants, perfumes, bath oils, bubble baths, and other personal care products. It could also be due to chlorine in swimming pools or hot tubs. To treat this type of itchiness, one should avoid using these types of products and instead use hypoallergenic soaps or fragrance-free body washes. Over-the-counter antihistamines like diphenhydramine (Benadryl) or hydroxyzine (Atarax) might provide some relief for mild cases. For more severe cases, prescription topical corticosteroids or oral antihistamines might be helpful.
reference_answers: Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose adult ALL. The following tests and procedures may be used: - Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as infection or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patient's health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken. - Complete blood count (CBC) with differential : A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following: - The number of red blood cells and platelets. - The number and type of white blood cells. - The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells. - The portion of the blood sample made up of red blood cells. - Blood chemistry studies : A procedure in which a blood sample is checked to measure the amounts of certain substances released into the blood by organs and tissues in the body. An unusual (higher or lower than normal) amount of a substance can be a sign of disease. - Peripheral blood smear : A procedure in which a sample of blood is checked for blast cells, the number and kinds of white blood cells, the number of platelets, and changes in the shape of blood cells. - Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy : The removal of bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone or breastbone. A pathologist views the bone marrow, blood, and bone under a microscope to look for abnormal cells. The following tests may be done on the samples of blood or bone marrow tissue that are removed: - Cytogenetic analysis: A laboratory test in which the cells in a sample of blood or bone marrow are looked at under a microscope to find out if there are certain changes in the chromosomes of lymphocytes. For example, in Philadelphia chromosome positive ALL, part of one chromosome switches places with part of another chromosome. This is called the Philadelphia chromosome. - Immunophenotyping : A process used to identify cells, based on the types of antigens or markers on the surface of the cell. This process is used to diagnose the subtype of ALL by comparing the cancer cells to normal cells of the immune system. For example, a cytochemistry study may test the cells in a sample of tissue using chemicals (dyes) to look for certain changes in the sample. A chemical may cause a color change in one type of leukemia cell but not in another type of leukemia cell.

Key Points - Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes abnormal myeloblasts (a type of white blood cell), red blood cells, or platelets. - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - There are different subtypes of AML. - Smoking, previous chemotherapy treatment, and exposure to radiation may affect the risk of adult AML. - Signs and symptoms of adult AML include fever, feeling tired, and easy bruising or bleeding. - Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose adult AML. - Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes abnormal myeloblasts (a type of white blood cell), red blood cells, or platelets. Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. This type of cancer usually gets worse quickly if it is not treated. It is the most common type of acute leukemia in adults. AML is also called acute myelogenous leukemia, acute myeloblastic leukemia, acute granulocytic leukemia, and acute nonlymphocytic leukemia. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the bone marrow makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a white blood cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - White blood cells that fight infection and disease. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. In AML, the myeloid stem cells usually become a type of immature white blood cell called myeloblasts (or myeloid blasts). The myeloblasts in AML are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells. Sometimes in AML, too many stem cells become abnormal red blood cells or platelets. These abnormal white blood cells, red blood cells, or platelets are also called leukemia cells or blasts. Leukemia cells can build up in the bone marrow and blood so there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. When this happens, infection, anemia, or easy bleeding may occur. The leukemia cells can spread outside the blood to other parts of the body, including the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), skin, and gums. This summary is about adult AML. See the following PDQ summaries for information about other types of leukemia: - Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia/Other Myeloid Malignancies Treatment - Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia Treatment - Adult Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia Treatment - Hairy Cell Leukemia Treatment There are different subtypes of AML. Most AML subtypes are based on how mature (developed) the cancer cells are at the time of diagnosis and how different they are from normal cells. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a subtype of AML that occurs when parts of two genes stick together. APL usually occurs in middle-aged adults. Signs of APL may include both bleeding and forming blood clots.

Key Points - Once adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. - There is no standard staging system for adult AML. Once adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. The extent or spread of cancer is usually described as stages. In adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the subtype of AML and whether the leukemia has spread outside the blood and bone marrow are used instead of the stage to plan treatment. The following tests and procedures may be used to determine if the leukemia has spread: - Lumbar puncture : A procedure used to collect a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the spinal column. This is done by placing a needle between two bones in the spine and into the CSF around the spinal cord and removing a sample of the fluid. The sample of CSF is checked under a microscope for signs that leukemia cells have spread to the brain and spinal cord. This procedure is also called an LP or spinal tap. - CT scan (CAT scan): A procedure that makes a series of detailed pictures of the abdomen, taken from different angles. The pictures are made by a computer linked to an x-ray machine. A dye may be injected into a vein or swallowed to help the organs or tissues show up more clearly. This procedure is also called computed tomography, computerized tomography, or computerized axial tomography. There is no standard staging system for adult AML. The disease is described as untreated, in remission, or recurrent. Untreated adult AML In untreated adult AML, the disease is newly diagnosed. It has not been treated except to relieve signs and symptoms such as fever, bleeding, or pain, and the following are true: - The complete blood count is abnormal. - At least 20% of the cells in the bone marrow are blasts (leukemia cells). - There are signs or symptoms of leukemia. Adult AML in remission In adult AML in remission, the disease has been treated and the following are true: - The complete blood count is normal. - Less than 5% of the cells in the bone marrow are blasts (leukemia cells). - There are no signs or symptoms of leukemia in the brain and spinal cord or elsewhere in the body. Recurrent Adult AML Recurrent AML is cancer that has recurred (come back) after it has been treated. The AML may come back in the blood or bone marrow.

Signs and symptoms of chronic lymphocytic leukemia include swollen lymph nodes and tiredness. Usually CLL does not cause any signs or symptoms and is found during a routine blood test. Signs and symptoms may be caused by CLL or by other conditions. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following: - Painless swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin. - Feeling very tired. - Pain or fullness below the ribs. - Fever and infection. - Weight loss for no known reason.

Key Points - Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a disease in which the bone marrow makes too many white blood cells. - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - Signs and symptoms of chronic myelogenous leukemia include fever, night sweats, and tiredness. - Most people with CML have a gene mutation (change) called the Philadelphia chromosome. - Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose chronic myelogenous leukemia. - Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a disease in which the bone marrow makes too many white blood cells. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (also called CML or chronic granulocytic leukemia) is a slowly progressing blood and bone marrow disease that usually occurs during or after middle age, and rarely occurs in children. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the bone marrow makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a white blood cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. - Granulocytes (white blood cells) that fight infection and disease. In CML, too many blood stem cells become a type of white blood cell called granulocytes. These granulocytes are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells. They are also called leukemia cells. The leukemia cells can build up in the blood and bone marrow so there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. When this happens, infection, anemia, or easy bleeding may occur. This summary is about chronic myelogenous leukemia. Key Points - After chronic myelogenous leukemia has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread. - Chronic myelogenous leukemia has 3 phases. - Chronic phase - Accelerated phase - Blastic phase After chronic myelogenous leukemia has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread. Staging is the process used to find out how far the cancer has spread. There is no standard staging system for chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). Instead, the disease is classified by phase: chronic phase, accelerated phase, or blastic phase. It is important to know the phase in order to plan treatment. The information from tests and procedures done to detect (find) and diagnose chronic myelogenous leukemia is also used to plan treatment. Chronic myelogenous leukemia has 3 phases. As the amount of blast cells increases in the blood and bone marrow, there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. This may result in infections, anemia, and easy bleeding, as well as bone pain and pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs on the left side. The number of blast cells in the blood and bone marrow and the severity of signs or symptoms determine the phase of the disease. Chronic phase In chronic phase CML, fewer than 10% of the cells in the blood and bone marrow are blast cells. Accelerated phase In accelerated phase CML, 10% to 19% of the cells in the blood and bone marrow are blast cells. Blastic phase In blastic phase CML, 20% or more of the cells in the blood or bone marrow are blast cells. When tiredness, fever, and an enlarged spleen occur during the blastic phase, it is called blast crisis.

Signs and symptoms of hairy cell leukemia include infections, tiredness, and pain below the ribs. These and other signs and symptoms may be caused by hairy cell leukemia or by other conditions. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following: - Weakness or feeling tired. - Fever or frequent infections. - Easy bruising or bleeding. - Shortness of breath. - Weight loss for no known reason. - Pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs. - Painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin.

Key Points - There are different types of treatment for patients with hairy cell leukemia. - Five types of standard treatment are used: - Watchful waiting - Chemotherapy - Biologic therapy - Surgery - Targeted therapy - New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials. - Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. - Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. - Follow-up tests may be needed. There are different types of treatment for patients with hairy cell leukemia. Different types of treatment are available for patients with hairy cell leukemia. Some treatments are standard (the currently used treatment), and some are being tested in clinical trials. A treatment clinical trial is a research study meant to help improve current treatments or obtain information on new treatments for patients with cancer. When clinical trials show that a new treatment is better than the standard treatment, the new treatment may become the standard treatment. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. Some clinical trials are open only to patients who have not started treatment. Five types of standard treatment are used: Watchful waiting Watchful waiting is closely monitoring a patient's condition, without giving any treatment until signs or symptoms appear or change. Chemotherapy Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells or by stopping them from dividing. When chemotherapy is taken by mouth or injected into a vein or muscle, the drugs enter the bloodstream and can reach cancer cells throughout the body (systemic chemotherapy). When chemotherapy is placed directly into the cerebrospinal fluid, an organ, or a body cavity such as the abdomen, the drugs mainly affect cancer cells in those areas (regional chemotherapy). Targeted therapy Targeted therapy is a treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells without harming normal cells. Monoclonal antibody therapy uses antibodies made in the laboratory from a single type of immune system cell. They may be used alone or to carry drugs, toxins, or radioactive material directly to cancer cells. A monoclonal antibody called rituximab may be used for certain patients with hairy cell leukemia. Signs and symptoms of childhood AML, childhood CML, JMML, or MDS include fever, feeling tired, and easy bleeding or bruising. These and other signs and symptoms may be caused by childhood AML, childhood CML, JMML, or MDS or by other conditions. Check with a doctor if your child has any of the following: - Fever with or without an infection. - Night sweats. - Shortness of breath. - Weakness or feeling tired. - Easy bruising or bleeding. - Petechiae (flat, pinpoint spots under the skin caused by bleeding). - Pain in the bones or joints. - Pain or feeling of fullness below the ribs. - Painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, groin, or other parts of the body. In childhood AML, these lumps, called leukemia cutis, may be blue or purple. - Painless lumps that are sometimes around the eyes. These lumps, called chloromas, are sometimes seen in childhood AML and may be blue-green. - An eczema -like skin rash. The signs and symptoms of TMD may include the following: - Swelling all over the body. - Shortness of breath. - Trouble breathing. - Weakness or feeling tired. - Pain below the ribs.
