One study is evaluating the efficacy of nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab or pembrolizumab as first-line treatment for advanced KS . Another study is investigating the use of crizotinib in patients with advanced KS who progressed after at least one prior line of therapy . Additionally, there is an open-label phase 2 trial examining the safety and efficacy of lenvatinib in patients with metastatic KS who were previously treated with anthracycline chemotherapy .

The prognosis of childhood rhabdomyosarcoma depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, tumor location, histologic subtype, metastasis status, response to treatment, etc. In general, patients with localized disease have a good chance of cure (5-year survival rate > 80%), while those with metastatic or recurrent disease have poorer outcomes (<30%) .

Childhood soft tissue sarcomas can occur in any child age group but most commonly affect children between 1 and 4 years of age . The exact cause of childhood soft tissue sarcomas is unknown, but certain factors may increase the risk of developing these tumors. These include exposure to ionizing radiation , genetic syndromes such as neurofibromatosis type I or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome , and prior history of cancer . Additionally, some studies have suggested that obesity may be associated with an increased risk of childhood soft tissue sarcomas .

There have been several ongoing studies of childhood soft tissue sarcomas in recent years. The National Cancer Institute has conducted a phase 1 study of the combination of pazopanib with temozolomide and irinotecan hydrochloride lipid suspension (IHL) as second-line treatment for children and young adults with recurrent or refractory solid tumors . Another study by the Children's Oncology Group evaluated the efficacy of doxorubicin plus ifosfamide versus vincristine plus dactinomycin as first-line therapy for patients with localized embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma .

There have been several recent studies published regarding childhood vascular tumors. One study investigated the use of sirolimus in patients with infantile hemangioma who were refractory to steroid therapy or had intolerable side effects from steroids . The results showed that 67% of patients responded to treatment with sirolimus, but there was also an increase in adverse events such as mucositis, diarrhea, vomiting, pneumonia, and leukopenia . Another study looked at the effectiveness of propranolol in treating infantile hemangiomas and found that it was effective in reducing the size of the lesions, especially when used early in the course of disease . A third study examined the long-term outcomes of children with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome and found that most patients developed normal blood counts within one year of diagnosis, although some may require multiple treatments including splenectomy .

The prognosis of adult Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) has significantly improved over time due to advances in treatment and better understanding of disease biology. With modern chemotherapy regimens such as ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine), 5-year overall survival rates have reached around 80% . However, there remains significant heterogeneity among patients with different risk factors affecting their outcomes. Patients who present with advanced stage or unfavorable histologic features may still have poorer long-term survival despite these improvements .

There are currently several ongoing studies related to adult non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). These include phase I/II clinical trials of new drugs or drug combinations in relapsed or refractory NHL patients, as well as phase III randomized controlled trials comparing different treatment regimens.

The stages of adult non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) are classified using the Ann Arbor staging system . This system classifies NHL into four stages based on the extent of disease at diagnosis: stage I involves one region or organ; stage II involves two regions or organs in the same area (called an “area”); stage III involves three or more areas in the same area; and stage IV is disseminated throughout the body.

The prognosis of ARL depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, stage of disease, type of lymphoma, treatment received, and immune status (CD4 cell count). In general, patients with higher CD4 counts have better outcomes than those with lower counts. Treatment options include chemotherapy alone or in combination with antiretroviral therapy (ART) .

Mycosis fungoides (MF) is a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that typically presents as patches or plaques on the skin . The diagnosis of MF requires a combination of clinical features, histopathological examination of skin biopsies, immunohistochemical staining for specific markers such as CD3, CD4, and Ki67, and genetic testing using molecular techniques such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Primary central nervous system lymphomas (PCNSLs) are rare types of non-Hodgkin's lymphomas that originate in the brain or spinal cord . PCNSL can occur at any age but is more common among adults aged 50 to 79 years old. The incidence rate for PCNSL has been increasing over time due to advances in neuroimaging techniques such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which allows earlier detection of small lesions not visible with other methods like computed tomography scans.

The standard treatment for primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) is high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy combined with whole brain radiotherapy . Other options include immunotherapy or stem cell transplantation in certain cases.

The prognosis of childhood Hodgkin lymphoma has significantly improved over time due to advances in treatment. With modern chemotherapy regimens such as ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) and advanced imaging techniques, 90% of children with localized disease can be cured . However, the cure rate drops to around 85% when the disease presents with metastasis at diagnosis or relapses after initial therapy . Long-term survival rates are generally high but may be affected by late effects from cancer treatments such as secondary malignancies, cardiovascular disease, infertility, and cognitive impairment .

The most common symptom of childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma is an enlarged painless lymph node that can be found in any area of the body, including the neck, underarm, groin or behind the ears . Other symptoms include fever, weight loss, fatigue, abdominal pain, vomiting, coughing, difficulty breathing, bone pain, skin changes (such as rashes), swelling in the face, jaw or legs, bleeding and bruising .

The treatment of childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and stem cell transplantation depending on the type and stage of the disease . For localized NHL, chemotherapy alone is often sufficient to achieve remission. However, in cases where the tumor has spread or is resistant to initial chemotherapy, additional therapies such as radiation therapy may be recommended. In some cases, bone marrow transplantation may also be necessary if the cancer has affected other parts of the body beyond the primary site.

The prognosis of anal cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor size, lymph node involvement, histologic grade, and patient age . In general, early-stage disease (Stage I or II) has a good prognosis with 5-year survival rates exceeding 80%. However, advanced-stage disease (Stage III or IV) carries a poorer prognosis, with 5-year survival rates dropping to around 60% .

An adult central nervous system tumor refers to any type of cancer that originates in the brain or spinal cord of an individual aged 18 years or older . These types of cancers include gliomas, meningiomas, pituitary adenomas, craniopharyngiomas, ependymomas, astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, medulloblastomas, schwannomas, hemangiopericytomas, and other rare types of CNS tumors. The most common type of primary brain tumor is glioma, which accounts for approximately half of all cases. Meningioma is another common type of brain tumor, accounting for about one-third of all cases.

The prognosis of adult central nervous system (CNS) tumors depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, type of tumor, grade or histology, location within the CNS, extent of surgical resection, adjuvant therapy received, and patient performance status . Generally speaking, low-grade gliomas have better outcomes than high-grade gliomas. For example, patients with diffuse astrocytoma (WHO Grade II), oligodendroglioma (WHO Grades II and III), ependymoma (WHO Grade II), pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO Grade I), and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA; WHO Grade I) tend to have longer survival rates compared to those diagnosed with anaplastic astrocytoma (WHO Grade III), glioblastoma multiforme (GBM; WHO Grade IV), medulloblastoma (WHO Grade IV), or other types of malignant brain tumors .

The exact cause of childhood brain tumours is unknown; however, several risk factors have been identified that may contribute to their development. These include exposure to ionizing radiation (such as X-rays or CT scans), certain genetic conditions such as neurofibromatosis type 1, and family history of cancer . Additionally, some studies suggest that environmental exposures such as pesticides and solvents may also play a role in the development of these tumours .

The treatment of childhood brain tumors depends on several factors, including the type of tumor, its location in the brain, whether it is low-grade or high-grade, and whether there has been spread to other parts of the body (metastasis).

Childhood astrocytoma is a type of brain tumor that arises from glial cells called astrocytes. The diagnosis of childhood astrocytoma typically involves a combination of imaging studies, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), along with other diagnostic tests, including blood tests, spinal fluid analysis, and biopsy.

Childhood central nervous system atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (AT/RTs) are highly malignant brain tumors that occur in infants and young children . They arise from undifferentiated cells of the neural tube or its derivatives, such as the cerebellar vermis, hindbrain, spinal cord, and optic nerve . AT/RTs are characterized by specific genetic alterations, including loss-of-function mutations in SMARCB1 (also known as INI1), which encodes a component of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex . These mutations lead to aberrant activation of various signaling pathways, including Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch, PI3K/AKT, and RAS/MAPK , resulting in uncontrolled cell proliferation, invasion, and migration .

The stages of childhood central nervous system atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (AT/RTs) are as follows: 1. Clinically silent period before symptoms appear; 2. Symptomatic stage with signs such as headaches, vomiting, seizures, or visual disturbances; 3. Diagnostic imaging stage where magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals an enhancing intra-axial mass lesion in the posterior fossa; 4. Surgical intervention to remove the tumor; 5. Postoperative adjuvant therapy including chemotherapy and radiation therapy; 6. Monitoring for recurrence and long-term follow-up .

Childhood brain stem gliomas (BSGs) can occur in both children and adults of any age group, but they are most commonly diagnosed between 3 and 10 years old . The exact cause of childhood BSGs remains unknown, but there are several factors that may contribute to their development.

There have been several ongoing studies related to childhood brainstem gliomas in recent years. Some of these include phase I/II clinical trials evaluating new chemotherapy regimens or targeted therapies such as temozolomide, irinotecan, bevacizumab, cediranib, and others . Other studies have focused on developing novel imaging techniques for early diagnosis and monitoring treatment response , as well as exploring potential biomarkers that could help predict prognosis and guide personalized treatment strategies . Additionally, there has also been interest in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying tumorigenesis and identifying therapeutic targets using genomic profiling approaches .

Diagnosis of childhood central nervous system (CNS) embryonal tumors typically involves a combination of clinical symptoms, imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and pathological examination of tissue biopsy samples obtained during surgery or other invasive procedures.

The stages of childhood central nervous system germ cell tumors (GCNTs) were developed by the Children's Oncology Group in 2016 to provide a standardized approach for risk stratification and treatment planning . GCNTs can be classified into four groups based on their location within the CNS and histologic features:

There have been several ongoing studies in recent years to investigate childhood central nervous system germ cell tumors. These include phase I/II clinical trials of chemotherapy regimens such as cisplatin, etoposide, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, ifosfamide, carboplatin, paclitaxel, irinotecan, temozolomide, topotecan, and bevacizumab. Other studies have focused on molecular profiling and targeted therapies using drugs such as mTOR inhibitors, MEK inhibitors, PARP inhibitors, and immune checkpoint blockade agents. Some examples of these studies include the Children's Oncology Group study A9372, which evaluated the efficacy of adding everolimus or placebo to standard therapy for newly diagnosed medulloblastoma; the Pediatric Brain Consortium study 14-086, which investigated the use of pembrolizumab in recurrent high grade gliomas; and the Children's Oncology Group study AHN-1531, which assessed the safety and efficacy of trametinib in patients with recurrent low grade gliomas.

A childhood craniopharyngioma is a rare brain tumor that typically occurs in children aged 5-14 years old . The diagnosis of this condition involves several steps, including imaging tests such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT), blood testing, and genetic testing.

An ependymoma is a type of brain tumor that arises from cells called ependyma, which line the ventricles in the brain and spinal cord. These tumors can occur anywhere along the spine or within the brain, but most commonly arise in the posterior fossa region of the brain.

The most common symptom of adult primary liver cancer is pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastric area that worsens with lying down. Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, weight loss, fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, light stool color, abdominal mass, palpable liver, ascites (fluid buildup in the peritoneal cavity), and enlarged lymph nodes .

The treatment of adult primary liver cancer depends on several factors such as the stage of disease at diagnosis, overall health status, and patient preferences. For early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), surgical resection is recommended . If surgery is not possible, other options include local ablation therapies or transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) . In cases where HCC has metastasized to other parts of the body, systemic therapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitors may be used in combination with TACE or sorafenib alone if TACE is contraindicated .

The prognosis of bile duct cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor location, extent of liver involvement, presence or absence of metastasis, and overall health status. Generally speaking, patients with early-stage localized cholangiocarcinoma have better survival rates than those with advanced disease. However, even in cases where surgery may be an option, there is still a high risk of recurrence and poor long-term outcomes .

There are several known risk factors that have been associated with childhood liver cancer. These include exposure to certain chemicals such as vinyl chloride or pesticides, genetic disorders such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), infections such as hepatitis B virus or hepatitis C virus, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency, primary sclerosing cholangitis, glycogen storage diseases type I, hemochromatosis, autoimmune hepatitis, and exposure to high doses of radiation .

The treatment of childhood liver cancer typically involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy depending on the specific type and stage of the tumor . For localized tumors that have not spread to other parts of the body, surgical resection is often the primary treatment option. Chemotherapy may also be used before or after surgery to help shrink the tumor and reduce the risk of recurrence. In cases where the cancer has metastasized to other organs, systemic chemotherapy is typically recommended as the first-line treatment. Depending on the specific type of liver cancer, radiation therapy may also play a role in the overall treatment plan. It's important to note that the treatment approach varies significantly by age group and depends on several factors such as the size and location of the tumor, whether it is malignant or benign, how far along the disease is at the time of diagnosis, and the child's overall health status.

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials related to liver cancer that aim to evaluate new treatments or combinations of existing therapies. These include studies evaluating immunotherapy agents such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, durvalumab, ipilimumab, tremelimumab, and combination therapy with chemotherapeutic drugs like cisplatin and gemcitabine. Other ongoing trials involve targeted therapies such as lenvatinib, regorafenib, cabozantinib, sorafenib, and ramucirumab in combination with other agents. Additionally, there are also trials investigating novel treatment approaches including radiopharmaceuticals, peptides, and gene-based therapies .
The stages of Ewing sarcoma were classified by the Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Study Group (IRSG) in 1987 . This classification is based on the presence or absence of metastasis at diagnosis.

The most common symptom of osteosarcoma is pain in or around a bone that worsens at night and may be associated with swelling, redness, and tenderness . Other possible signs include limping, weight loss, decreased appetite, and weakness.

There have been several ongoing studies related to osteosarcoma and malignant fibrous histiocytoma of bone. One such study is the Children's Oncology Group (COG) trial ACCT0831, which aims to evaluate whether adding pembrolizumab to standard chemotherapy can improve progression-free survival in patients with relapsed or refractory osteosarcoma . Another study by the COG, AO2014, is evaluating the efficacy of combining nivolumab with irinotecan and temozolomide as second-line therapy for recurrent osteosarcoma .

The prognosis of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors depends on various factors such as the location of the primary tumor, stage at diagnosis, grade, and presence or absence of metastasis. In general, patients with localized disease have an excellent prognosis, while those with advanced disease have poorer outcomes . Surgery remains the mainstay treatment option for resectable tumors, but systemic chemotherapy may be used in combination with surgery or alone for unresectable or metastatic disease .

The treatment of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) depends on several factors such as age, overall health status, genetic mutations present in the blood cells, risk classification, and whether the patient is eligible for stem cell transplantation .

Polycythemia vera (PV) is a rare myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an overproduction of red blood cells due to clonal proliferation of erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow . PV is associated with increased risk for thrombosis and cardiovascular disease, as well as progression to acute myeloid leukemia or fibrotic transformation into primary myelofibrosis . The diagnosis of PV requires the presence of all three criteria: elevated hemoglobin level greater than 16 g/dL in men and greater than 16.5 g/dL in women; bone marrow biopsy showing markedly enlarged erythroblasts without ring sideroblasts; and JAK2 mutations or abnormalities in other genes that activate the Janus kinase pathway .

The main symptoms of primary myelofibrosis (PMF) include fatigue, abdominal pain or discomfort due to an enlarged spleen, weight loss, early satiety, and signs of anemia such as weakness, dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath, and chest pain . Other common symptoms include night sweats, fever, bone pain, itching, skin rashes, and sexual dysfunction.

The prognosis of essential thrombocythaemia (ET) depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, platelet count, presence or absence of constitutional symptoms, and history of thromboembolic events. In general, ET has an indolent course with a median survival of 15 to 20 years . However, patients who have high-risk features may experience more aggressive disease progression and shorter survival rates.

The symptoms of chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL) can vary depending on the degree to which the bone marrow is infiltrated by eosinophils . Some patients may have no or minimal symptoms, while others may experience more severe symptoms due to organ involvement from the disease process.

The treatment of myeloid dysplasia/myeloproliferation neoplasm (MDS/MPN) depends on several factors such as age, comorbidities, risk stratification, bone marrow blast percentage, and genetic mutations. For low-risk MDS patients who do not require transfusions or have mild anemia, supportive care is recommended . This includes iron supplements to treat iron deficiency, erythropoietin stimulation in case of anemia, antibiotics if there is infection, and blood transfusion when necessary.

The treatment of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) is determined by factors such as age, comorbidities, risk stratification, and availability of supportive care options . For patients with low-risk CMML who are not eligible for or decline allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (alloHCT), hypomethylating agents (HMAs) are recommended first-line therapy . Azacitidine has been shown to improve overall survival in this population compared to intensive chemotherapy . Venetoclax plus azacitidine was recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of CMML after failure or intolerance to HMAs .

Atypical chronic myeloid leukaemia (aCML) is a rare type of blood cancer that develops from cells in the bone marrow. It is characterized by an accumulation of immature white blood cells called myeloblasts, which can lead to bone marrow failure and other complications such as infection or bleeding .

The symptoms of MMN-U can vary depending on the specific type of blood cell that is affected by the disease. Some common symptoms include fatigue, weakness, weight loss, abdominal pain or discomfort, frequent infections, easy bruising or bleeding, paleness, and enlargement of the spleen or liver .

The diagnosis of endometrial cancer typically involves a combination of clinical symptoms, physical examination, imaging tests such as ultrasound or MRI, and histopathological evaluation of tissue biopsies obtained through procedures such as dilation and curettage (D&C) or hysteroscopy.

Uterine sarcomas are rare types of cancer that originate from cells in the uterus. They account for less than 1% of all female reproductive cancers . There are two main subtypes of uterine sarcoma: leiomyosarcoma, which develops from smooth muscle cells, and endometrial stromal sarcoma, which arises from the stromal layer of the endometrium. Leiomyosarcomas are more common than endometrial stromal sarcomas, accounting for approximately 80–90% of cases .

The most common type of uterine sarcomas is leiomyosarcoma (LMS), which can be divided into three subtypes based on their stage at diagnosis: 1) low-grade LMS that develops from benign smooth muscle tumors such as leiomyomas; 2) high-grade LMS that occurs de novo without any precursor lesions; and 3) undifferentiated uterine sarcoma .

The exact cause of childhood extracranial germ cell tumors is unknown. However, several factors have been identified that may contribute to their development. These include genetic predisposition, exposure to certain environmental agents such as pesticides or chemicals found in tobacco smoke, and hormonal imbalances .

The stages of childhood extracranial germ cell tumors (EGCTs) were first described by the International Pediatric Germ Cell Cancer Consortium in 2013 . There are four main categories of EGCTs: mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT), testicular NSGCT, ovarian NSGCT, and miscellaneous sites of NSGCT. Each category is divided into three stages based on their metastatic potential.

The most common symptom of extragonadal germ cell tumor is abdominal pain or mass in women . In men, it can present with testicular cancer symptoms such as lump or swelling in the scrotum, pain or discomfort in the lower abdomen or testicles, a feeling of heaviness in the scrotal sac, or a change in the size or appearance of the testicles . Other nonspecific symptoms include weight loss, fever, nausea, vomiting, weakness, fatigue, anemia, constipation, diarrhea, dysuria, hematuria, urinary frequency, and pelvic pressure or pain .

The prognosis of uveal melanoma depends on several factors, including tumor size, location within the eye, genetic mutations, and treatment received. Overall, uveal melanoma has a relatively good prognosis compared to other types of melanomas. However, it can metastasize to distant organs such as the liver, lungs, bone, or brain in 20%-35% of cases .

Yes, retinoblastoma is typically inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, meaning that both copies of the RB1 gene have a mutation. Most cases occur due to two independent genetic events (de novo), with no family history. Less commonly, it can be inherited from one parent who has a germline RB1 mutation or deletion.

Retinoblastoma is a malignant tumor that arises from retinal cells in children. It can be divided into two types: hereditary (accounting for 40% of cases) or non-hereditary (60%) . The disease usually presents within the first year of life with leukocoria, strabismus, ocular pain, hyphema, iris heterochromia, proptosis, phthisis bulbus, optic disc swelling, and metastatic disease to bone marrow, liver, brain, and other organs .

No, ovarian epithelial cancer is not typically considered to be hereditary or familial in nature. However, there may be some genetic predisposition for certain types of ovarian cancers, such as Lynch syndrome (also known as hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) which has been associated with mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes .

The stages of ovarian epithelial cancer (OEC) are determined using the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging system . Stage I is limited to the ovary(s), while stage II extends beyond one fallopian tube or ovary but remains localized within the peritoneum. Stages IIIA-B involve regional lymph node metastasis with or without extension outside the abdominal cavity, whereas stage IV involves distant metastases.

Diagnosis of ovarian germ cell tumor (GCT) is usually made through imaging studies such as ultrasound or CT scan followed by laparoscopy with biopsy for histopathological examination. Imaging may reveal solid masses with cystic areas and calcifications. Ultrasound can also detect elevated blood flow in these lesions. Serum markers like alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), beta chorionic gonadotropin (βhCG) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) should be checked preoperatively to aid diagnosis and post operatively to monitor response to treatment.

An ovarian low malignant potential tumor (LMPT), also known as an atypical proliferative lesion of the ovary or an atypical proliferative tumor of uncertain malignant potential (ATUMOP), is a rare type of ovarian tumor that has some features of both benign and malignant tumors . These tumors have been found to be associated with an increased risk of developing ovarian cancer in the future , but they do not typically metastasize outside of the pelvis .

The treatment of ovarian low malignant potential tumor typically involves surgical removal of the affected ovary and any other involved tissues or organs. In some cases, chemotherapy may also be recommended depending on the specific type and stage of the tumor.
