Other diagnostic procedures such as CT and MRI scans help identify any abnormalities that may indicate the presence of liver cancer. PET scanning uses radioactive tracers to detect metabolic activity in tumor cells. A biochemical analysis of the blood can also provide information about the stage of the disease.

Bile duct cancer, also known as cholangiocarcinoma, refers to any malignant tumor that arises from the epithelial cells lining of the intrahepatic or extra-hepatic biliary tree . The exact cause of this condition remains unknown; however, several risk factors have been identified. These include primary sclerosing cholangitis, liver fluke infection, hepatitis C virus infection, alcoholic cirrhosis, obesity, tobacco smoking, diabetes mellitus, and genetic predisposition such as familial adenomatous polyposis . Early symptoms can be vague and nonspecific, making diagnosis challenging. Common signs may include abdominal pain, jaundice, pruritus, fatigue, weight loss, dark urine, clay-colored stools, nausea, vomiting, and pale feces . Diagnosis typically involves imaging studies such as ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biopsy, and blood tests for serum carbohydrate antigen 19–9 (CA 19–9). Treatment options depend on various factors, including stage at diagnosis, location of the tumor, presence of metastasis, and overall health status. Surgery is often recommended when possible,

There are several ongoing phase II or III clinical trials that are testing different combinations of chemotherapy drugs in patients with advanced cholangiocarcinoma. Some examples include the combination of gemcitabine plus cisplatin, which is currently being evaluated as first-line treatment for metastatic disease; the combination of FOLFOX (fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin) plus irinotecan, which is being studied as second-line therapy after progression on gemcitabine monotherapy; and the combination of capecitabine plus temozolomide, which is also being investigated as second-line treatment .

In children, the most common symptom is pain in the right upper quadrant (RUQ). Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, weight loss, fatigue, abdominal mass or distension, jaundice, palpable spleen, ascites, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, anemia, pallor, easy bruisability, bleeding disorders, fever, chills, diarrhea, constipation, pruritus, dark urine, clay-colored stools, and decreased appetite .

There are several ongoing clinical trials for childhood liver cancer in children at present. The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is conducting a phase II trial of sorafenib mesylate for pediatric patients with recurrent hepatoblastoma not amenable to surgical resection or chemotherapy (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01345296). Another study by Children’s Oncology Group is evaluating the efficacy of cisplatin plus doxorubicin versus cisplatin plus vincristine as first-line therapy for localized hepatoblastoma (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03876552). A third study by St Jude Children's Research Hospital is investigating the effectiveness of combining pembrolizumab with azacitidine and venetoclax for relapsed or refractory solid tumors including hepatoblastoma (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03506910).

Ewing Sarcoma (ES) is a malignant bone tumor that arises from undifferentiated mesenchymal cells. It most commonly occurs in children and young adults but can also occur at any age group. The exact cause of ES remains unknown; however, certain genetic mutations have been identified as contributing factors to its development.

The standard of care for localized Ewing Sarcoma is multimodal therapy consisting of chemotherapy, surgical resection, and radiation . Chemotherapy regimens include vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide (VDC), or ifosfamide instead of cyclophosphamide (VIDE) alternating with ifosfamide and etoposide (IE). For metastatic disease, chemotherapy alone may be used in patients who have no symptoms from their tumors and whose lesions can be monitored radiographically without surgery.

Osteosarcomas can be detected by X-ray or CT scan. MRI is also used to detect soft tissue extension. The diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy with microscopic examination. In contrast, malignant fibrous histiocytomas (MFH) have nonspecific symptoms such as pain in the affected area, swelling, and limited range of motion. Diagnosis requires a biopsy for pathological evaluation.

Carcinoid tumor is a type of slow-growing neuroendocrine cancer that can occur anywhere in the body but most commonly develops in the small intestines (70%), followed by the appendix (15%) and colon (12%). It occurs more often in men than women and typically affects people over 50 years old.

Carcinoid tumors can be divided into two main types based on their location in the digestive system: foregut (esophagus), midgut (small intestine), or hindgut (large intestine). The most common type is midgut carcinoids, which account for about 50% of all cases.

Chronic Myeloproliferative Neoplasms (MPNs) are a group of rare blood cancers that arise from mutations in hematopoietic stem cells or progenitor cells leading to uncontrolled cell growth . These disorders cause overproduction of one or more types of blood cells such as red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets . The most common MPNs include polycythemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythemia (ET), primary myelofibrosis (PMF), chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), and chronic neutrophilic leukemia (CNL). PV is characterized by an increase in red blood cells due to bone marrow overproduction, while ET causes excessive production of platelets. PMF results in fibrotic changes within the bone marrow, which leads to decreased function of the organ. CNL involves elevated levels of immature neutrophils in the peripheral blood. Although these diseases have different clinical features, all MPNs share some common characteristics including increased risk for thromboembolism, splenomegaly, and progressive cytopenias .

Polycythemia vera (PV) is characterized by an overproduction of red blood cells due to clonal proliferation of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow. The most common presenting symptom of PV is fatigue, which can be attributed to the increased hematocrit level. Other typical signs include pruritus, headaches, dizziness, visual disturbances, palpitations, dyspnea, weight loss, and early satiety . Less commonly, patients may present with thrombosis, splenomegaly, arterial hypertension, hyperviscosity syndrome, and abdominal pain .

The overall prognosis of primary myelofibrosis (PMF) varies depending on several factors such as age at diagnosis, risk stratification, comorbidities, and treatment response. According to the Transformational Healthcare Institute's 2018 report, the median survival rate in PMF patients was approximately five years . However, some studies have reported that the median survival rates can range from two to seven years or even longer .

Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an increase in platelet count above 450 × 109 cells per liter with bone marrow hypercellularity and increased numbers of enlarged megakaryocytes . The mainstay of ET management involves low-dose aspirin therapy to reduce cardiovascular risk, as well as cytoreductive agents such as hydroxyurea or interferon alpha to control hematocrit levels and prevent progression to acute myeloid leukemia .

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL) is a rare type of myeloid malignancy characterized by sustained eosinophilia in peripheral blood and bone marrow involvement with immature eosinophils . The current standard of care for CEL involves upfront allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), which can lead to complete remission and potentially cure . However, HSCT may not be feasible due to advanced age or comorbidities, unavailability of matched donors, or lack of access to transplant centers . In these cases, chemotherapy regimens such as cladribine plus cytarabine , fludarabine-based regimens  and high-dose cytarabine monotherapy  have been used with variable success rates. Other treatments include corticosteroids, interferon alpha, hydroxyurea, anti-IL5 antibodies, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and radiolabeled anti-CD25 antibody .

Chronic Myelomonocytic Leukemia (CMML) is a type of cancer that affects blood cells in the bone marrow. It causes an overproduction of monocytes and granulocyte precursors, which accumulate in the bone marrow and spleen. The symptoms include fatigue, weight loss, fever, abdominal pain, and splenomegaly. CMML can be diagnosed by examining the patient's blood and bone marrow samples under a microscope.

Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) is a rare type of blood cancer that affects children. It is caused by genetic mutations in cells of the bone marrow that lead to an overproduction of monocytes and other abnormal white blood cells . JMML typically develops between 6 months and 2 years of age, but it can also occur at older ages. The symptoms include fever, bruising, bleeding, weakness, fatigue, weight loss, enlarged spleen or liver, and recurrent infections. Diagnosis involves a physical exam, blood tests, bone marrow aspiration, imaging studies such as ultrasound or MRI, and genetic testing. Treatment options for JMML include chemotherapy, stem cell transplantation, targeted therapy with small molecule inhibitors, and supportive care measures such as antibiotics and blood transfusions .

Atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) is a rare subtype of CML that accounts for approximately 5% to 10% of all cases . It is characterized by an unbalanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, resulting in Philadelphia chromosome-positive cells. The clinical presentation of aCML can be similar to other types of CML, with some unique features.

Myelodysplastic/Myeloproliferative Neoplasm (MDS/MPN) is a rare blood cancer that develops from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow . It can be classified into two types depending on whether there is an increase or decrease in one type of blood cell count. The first type is MDS which causes a reduction in red blood cells, platelets, or white blood cells while the second type is MPN which increases certain types of blood cells such as neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, or platelets .

Endometrial cancer has a good overall 5-year survival rate of around 80%. The specific prognosis depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, histologic type, grade, age, and other comorbidities. Patients with early-stage disease have a high chance of being cured by surgery alone, while those diagnosed in advanced stages may require additional chemotherapy or radiation therapy.

Uterine sarcomas can occur in any woman regardless of age or race; however, they are more common among women over 50 years old. Women with certain genetic conditions such as Lynch syndrome may be at increased risk for developing this type of cancer. Additionally, those who have had radiation therapy to the pelvic area, including brachytherapy, are also considered high-risk patients.

The standard of care for treating low-grade endometrial stromal sarcomas is surgery followed by adjuvant hormonal therapy with progestins or aromatase inhibitors . For high grade undifferentiated uterine sarcomas, chemotherapy regimens containing doxorubicin and ifosfamide have been used as first line treatments .

Childhood extracranial germ cell tumors (EGCTs) are rare malignant neoplasms that originate from cells with embryonic origin in organs outside of the brain and central nervous system . The most common sites for EGCTs to develop include the gonads, mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and testis. Although these tumors can occur anywhere in the body, they have been found more frequently in males than females, particularly in adolescents aged 15–19 years old .

The treatment of choice for most extracranial germ cell tumors in children is surgical resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy . Chemotherapy regimens typically include bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP) or similar agents such as vinblastine instead of bleomycin . Radiation therapy may be used if complete surgical resection cannot be achieved but should generally be avoided due to its potential long-term side effects .

Extragonadal germ cell tumors (EGCTs) can be detected by various imaging techniques such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), or biopsy. The most common presenting symptoms of EGCTs include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, weight loss, weakness, fatigue, fever, lymphadenopathy, and scrotal swelling in males .

Intraocular or uveal melanoma refers to a type of cancer that originates from the pigment-containing cells called melanocytes located within the eye's uvea layer. The term "intraocular" indicates that the tumor remains confined within the eyeball at the time of its discovery. Uveal melanomas can occur anywhere inside the eye but most commonly develop in the choroid, which lies between the sclera and retina. This form of ocular cancer is rare, accounting for only 3% of all melanomas, with an annual incidence rate of approximately one case per million individuals worldwide .

Intraocular or uveal melanoma is a rare type of cancer that originates from pigment-containing cells called melanocytes found within the eye. It can occur anywhere inside the eye but most commonly develops in the choroid layer under the retina. The disease has been divided into five distinct clinical stages based on its location, size, cellular atypia, and metastatic potential .

Retinoblastoma can affect anyone regardless of age, gender or ethnicity. However, certain factors may increase the likelihood of developing this condition. These include having a family history of retinoblastoma or another type of cancer (such as osteosarcoma), being born with a genetic mutation in one or both copies of the RB1 gene, exposure to high levels of radiation during childhood, or having a parent who has had an unsuccessful pregnancy due to chromosomal abnormalities. Children under 5 years old are most likely to develop retinoblastoma, but it can also occur in older children and adults.

Retinoblastoma is treated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or enucleation (surgical removal of the eye). The treatment plan depends on several factors such as the size and location of tumors in both eyes, whether it has spread to other parts of the body, and the patient's age. Chemotherapy can be used alone or in combination with other therapies. It works by stopping cells from dividing and growing. Radiation therapy uses high-energy X-rays or protons to kill cancer cells. Enucleation may be recommended if the tumor cannot be controlled with other treatments or if it has grown into the optic nerve.

Ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancers cannot be completely prevented due to their unknown etiology. However, there are several steps that women can take to reduce their risk of developing these types of cancers. These include maintaining a healthy body weight, limiting alcohol consumption, practicing safe sex, using oral contraceptives for at least five years, undergoing tubal ligation or hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (removal of both fallopian tubes and ovaries), eating a diet rich in fruits and vegetables, and avoiding smoking cigarettes . Additionally, it is important to regularly screen for these cancers through pelvic examinations, transvaginal ultrasounds, and CA-125 blood tests .

The standard of care for patients with advanced stage epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancers is cytoreductive surgery followed by platinum-based chemotherapy . Platinum agents such as carboplatin or cisplatin in combination with paclitaxel have been shown to be effective treatments for these types of cancers . Other chemotherapeutic agents that may also be used include gemcitabine, docetaxel, topotecan, irinotecan, and pegylated liposomal doxorubicin . Targeted therapies such as olaparib (PARP inhibitor) and bevacizumab (antiangiogenic agent) have also demonstrated efficacy in treating recurrent disease .

The prognosis of ovarian germ cell tumor depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, histologic subtype, age, and surgical treatment. Patients with early-stage (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics stages IA to IC) disease have an excellent prognosis, with 5-year overall survival rates exceeding 90%. However, advanced-stage (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics stages IIIC or IV) disease has a poorer prognosis, with 5-year overall survival rates ranging from 38% to 67%, depending on the histological type.

Ovarian LMP tumors typically do not cause any specific or unique symptoms or signs. They may present with nonspecific symptoms such as bloating, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, urinary frequency, irregular menstrual cycles, or infertility. These tumors can be diagnosed through pelvic ultrasound and further evaluation to determine their exact nature (such as biopsy) is often recommended.

Ovarian LMP tumors (also known as benign cystic teratoma) are rare, accounting for only 2-3% of all ovarian neoplasms . They typically occur in young women under the age of 40 years and have been associated with germ cell neoplasm precursor lesions such as dysgerminomas and yolk sac tumors . The diagnosis is often made by ultrasound imaging, which shows a unilocular mass containing echogenic foci that can mimic functional cysts . However, these masses may also contain solid components, which can make it difficult to differentiate them from other types of ovarian cancer .

Gallbladder cancer (GBC) refers to malignant tumors that arise from the epithelial cells of the gallbladder. It is also known as cholecystocarcinoma or carcinoma of the gallbladder. GBC is a rare type of biliary tract cancer with an estimated incidence rate of 1 per 50,000 people in the United States . The most common symptom of GBC is acute cholecystitis, which can be mistaken for benign inflammation of the gallbladder. Other symptoms include abdominal pain, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, fever, and dark urine. Diagnosis typically involves imaging tests such as ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, and PET scans, along with tissue biopsy for confirmation. Treatment options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Prognosis depends on several factors including stage at diagnosis, size of the tumor, lymph node involvement, and resectability.

The stages of gallbladder cancer (GBC) are determined by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC), which uses the TNM system for staging GBC. This system takes into account three factors: tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and metastasis (M).

Testicular cancer is typically treated with surgery, chemotherapy or radiation therapy depending on the stage of disease at diagnosis. Surgery involves removing the tumor from the testicle (orchiectomy) followed by retroperitoneal lymph node dissection to remove any metastasized cells in the abdomen. Chemotherapy may be used before or after surgery if there is evidence of spread beyond the testicles. Radiation therapy can also be used as an alternative to surgery but is generally reserved for patients who cannot undergo surgery due to health reasons. The specific treatment plan will depend on factors such as age, overall health status, and whether the cancer has spread outside of the testicles.

Gestational trophoblastic diseases (GTD) include hydatidiform mole, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblast tumor, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors. GTD is more common in younger women aged 16–49 years old, especially those who have had multiple abortions, miscarriages, molar pregnancies, and assisted reproductive technologies such as IVF. Women with a history of GTN are also at an increased risk for developing recurrent GTN.

Gestational trophoblastic diseases (GTD) refer to a group of pregnancy-related disorders that arise from abnormal proliferation of placental cells after conception. GTD includes hydatidiform mole, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, epithelioid tumor, and placental site trophoblast tumors . The most common type of GTD is molar pregnancy, which occurs in approximately 1 out of every 800 pregnancies .

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) can be diagnosed with a combination of clinical features, laboratory testing, and imaging studies. The diagnosis requires characteristic multisystem findings along with tissue biopsy showing typical histopathological characteristics.

Hypopharyngeal cancer refers to malignant tumors that arise from the lining of the hypopharynx. The hypopharynx is part of the pharynx, which is divided into three regions: nasopharynx, oropharynx, and hypopharynx. It extends from the base of the tongue to the esophageal entrance and includes several structures such as the soft palate, tonsils, pyriform sinuses, posterior third of the tongue, glottic region (voice box), piriform sinus, postcricoid area, and the upper portion of the esophagus.

Hypopharyngeal cancer can be divided into four main subtypes based on their anatomical location: (1) supraglottic (above the vocal folds), (2) glottic (between the false vocal fold and true vocal fold), (3) pyriform sinus (located in the valleys between the arytenoids), and (4) posterior pharynx (posterior to the true vocal cords). The classification system used for hypopharyngeal cancer is similar to that used for other head and neck tumors, which includes TNM staging.

Laryngeal cancer refers to any type of malignant tumor that arises from cells in the larynx, which is a structure composed of nine small tubular organs located at the back of the throat. These include three regions of the glottis (the vocal folds, supraglottic region, and subglottic region), as well as the epiglottis, arytenoids, pyriform sinuses, ventricles, posterior pharyngeal wall, and intrinsic thyroid cartilage.

Laryngeal cancer is classified into four main stages (I-IV) according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system. Stage I represents an early stage tumor that has not extended beyond the true vocal fold or thyroid cartilage, while Stage IV indicates advanced malignancy with extension to tissue outside the neck. The usual progression of laryngeal cancer begins as a small growth called a polyp or nodule, which may develop into a squamous cell carcinoma over time if left untreated. As it grows deeper into the larynx, it can invade surrounding tissues such as muscles, nerves, bones, and cartilages. It can also spread to nearby lymph nodes in the neck region. Early symptoms include hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, pain in the throat, cough, and voice loss.

The most common sign of oral cancer is a white patch called leukoplakia that appears on the mucosa of the mouth. Other signs include red patches (erythroplasia), sores that do not heal, lumps or thickening, pain, numbness, difficulty swallowing, bleeding, and loosening of teeth. It can also cause swelling of the jaw bone which may lead to facial deformity.

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to head and neck cancers that include patients with lip and oral cavity cancer. Some of these trials involve immunotherapy agents such as pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-975), nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NCT03816242) and nivolumab plus chemoradiotherapy (NCT03906521). Other trials focus on targeted therapies such as cetuximab plus radiotherapy (NCT03514018) and erlotinib plus radiotherapy (NCT02648301). Additionally, there is an ongoing trial evaluating the use of photodynamic therapy in combination with surgery for early stage tumors (NCT02649700).

Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the neck with an unknown primary site can be staged according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition cancer staging system for head and neck SCCs . The AJCC staging system takes into account several factors such as the size of the primary tumor, lymph node involvement, presence or absence of distant metastasis, and other clinical features.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a type of head and neck cancer that originates from the epithelial cells lining the nasopharynx. The most common symptoms include nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, otitis media, hearing loss, pharyngalgia, dysphagia, odynophagia, and cervical lymphadenopathy . These symptoms can be nonspecific and may not always indicate NPC; therefore, it is important for patients who experience any of these symptoms to consult with their healthcare provider.

There are several ongoing phase I-III clinical trials that aim to evaluate novel therapeutic agents in combination with chemotherapy (either cisplatin alone or cisplatin plus 5-fluorouracil) as first-line treatment of patients with recurrent or metastatic NPC. These include the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab, and atezolizumab; antibody drug conjugates such as enfortumab vedotin and sacituzumab govitecan; targeted therapies such as apatinib, everolimus, and lenvatinib; and other small molecule drugs such as cabozantinib, capecitabine, and temsirolimus. The results of these trials have shown promising outcomes in terms of overall response rate, progression-free survival, and overall survival compared to standard chemotherapy alone. However, it is important to note that these trials are still ongoing, and further evaluation is needed before these agents can be recommended as part of routine care for patients with advanced NPC.

The prognosis of oropharyngeal cancer depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, age, overall health status, and type of treatment received. In general, early-stage cancers have better outcomes with 5-year relative survival rates ranging from 80% to over 90%. However, advanced-stage cancers have much lower survival rates, with less than 20% chance of surviving five years after diagnosis . Long-term survival also varies depending on the specific subtype of oropharyngeal cancer. For example, HPV-positive tumors tend to be more responsive to treatment and have higher survival rates compared to HPV-negative tumors.

Paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity cancers occur most frequently in men over 60 years of age who have been exposed to tobacco smoke, alcohol consumption, occupational exposure to wood dust, formaldehyde, nickel compounds, asbestos, chromium salts, soot, coal, and iron fumes .

The treatment of paranasal sinus and nasal cavity cancers depends on several factors such as stage, location, size, grade, histology, patient age, general health status, and personal preferences. In most cases, surgery is combined with radiation therapy (RT) or chemoradiation therapy (CRT). Surgery may involve endoscopic resection, partial maxillectomy, mandibulectomy, orbital exenteration, cranial resections, and total nose removal. RT involves external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), brachytherapy, or both. CRT typically includes platinum-based chemotherapy agents administered concurrently with RT. Other systemic therapies include targeted molecular therapies, immunotherapies, hormonal therapies, and other cytotoxic drugs.

Salivary Gland Cancer Diagnosis: The diagnosis of salivary gland cancer involves several steps that include physical examination, imaging studies such as CT or MRI scans, biopsy, and histopathological analysis to confirm the presence of malignant cells.

The best way to prevent oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancers is by practicing good oral hygiene habits such as brushing your teeth at least twice daily with fluoridated toothpaste, flossing once per day, eating a healthy diet low in sugar and alcohol consumption, avoiding smoking tobacco products and using smokeless forms of tobacco, limiting alcohol intake, and getting regular dental check-ups. Additionally, vaccination against human papillomavirus (HPV) infection may also help reduce the risk of developing these types of cancers .

Pancreatic cancer can be diagnosed through several methods including physical examination, blood tests, imaging tests such as ultrasound (US), computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS), and biopsy of tissue from the pancreas. The most common diagnostic test for pancreatic cancer is an abdominal US which may detect any tumors in the pancreas. A CT scan provides more detailed images than a US but cannot distinguish between benign and malignant lesions. An MRI uses radio waves to produce detailed images of soft tissues like the pancreas. It is often used when other tests have not provided enough information about the size or location of a tumor. EUS allows doctors to examine the pancreas closely with a thin tube inserted into the mouth that produces a small camera at its tip. This procedure can also help guide fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsies, where cells are removed from a suspicious area using a very thin needle and examined under a microscope by a pathologist. FNA is considered the gold standard for diagnosing pancreatic cancer because it can provide evidence of whether a mass is likely to be cancerous or not.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (pNETs) are rare neoplasms that originate from cells of the endocrine system within the pancreas. These tumor cells produce hormones such as insulin or glucagon, which can cause symptoms like hypoglycemia or diarrhea . The exact mechanism by which these tumors arise is not well understood but may involve genetic mutations leading to uncontrolled cell growth and proliferation .

The standard of care for resectable pancreatic islet cell tumors is surgical resection with curative intent. For non-resectable or metastatic disease, first line systemic therapy includes somatostatin analogues such as octreotide long acting repeatable (LAR) in combination with street stabilizing agents like everolimus or sunitinib .

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials for renal cell carcinoma (RCC). One such trial is evaluating the efficacy of nivolumab plus ipilimumab in patients with previously untreated advanced RCC. Nivolumab is an anti-PD1 antibody that has shown promising results as monotherapy in treating metastatic RCC. Ipilimumab is also an immunotherapeutic agent that blocks CTLA4 from binding to its ligands B7.1 and B7.2. By blocking both PD1 and CTLA4 pathways, this combination therapy may provide enhanced antitumor activity compared to either agent alone.

Transitional cell carcinomas (TCCs) can occur in any part of the urinary tract system, including the kidney, renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, prostate gland, and urethra. TCCs that originate from the renal pelvis or upper ureter are known as upper urinary tract urothelial carcinomas (UTUC). The staging of UTUC follows the same guidelines as for bladder cancer, which is described by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) classification .

The most common symptom of Wilms tumor is an abdominal mass or pain. Other symptoms include fever, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, weight loss, decreased appetite, weakness, fatigue, hypertension, and anemia. Less frequent symptoms can be associated with urinary tract obstruction such as hematuria, dysuria, and flank pain.

The Children's Oncology Group (COG) is conducting several ongoing clinical trials for pediatric solid tumors, including Wilms tumor. These include AEWSO1832, which evaluates whether upfront chemotherapy with vincristine, doxorubicin, and dactinomycin can reduce the need for nephrectomy in patients with localized Wilms tumor; AEWS0161, which compares two different dosing schedules of vincristine, doxorubicin, and dactinomycin as upfront therapy for localized Wilms tumor; and AEWO1721, which examines the efficacy of adding irinotecan to standard chemotherapy in high-risk Wilms tumor. Other COG trials underway include AEWSO1934, which investigates the use of targeted therapies such as mTOR inhibitors and tyrosine kinase inhibitors in relapsed or refractory solid tumors; AEWSO1925, which assesses the role of antiangiogenesis agents in metastatic rhabdomyosarcoma; and AEWS1922, which tests the effectiveness of combining immunotherapies with radiation therapy for newly diagnosed stage 4 sarcomas. Additionally, there are several trials being conducted

The most common symptom of breast cancer is a painless lump or thickening under the armpit or in one of the breasts that lasts for more than two weeks . Other possible symptoms include changes to the shape or size of the breast, redness or rash around the nipple, dimpling of the skin, a change in the position of the nipple, fluid discharge from the nipple, and a feeling of heat in the breast . It is important to note that these symptoms may also be caused by other conditions such as an infection or benign tumor; however, it is recommended to consult a healthcare provider for further evaluation.

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials for breast cancer treatment in various stages of development. Some examples include a phase III trial evaluating the efficacy of adding atezolizumab to nab-paclitaxel as first-line therapy for metastatic triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) (IMpassion130), a phase II study assessing the safety and efficacy of combining pembrolizumab with olaparib in patients with germline BRCA mutated advanced TNBC (KEYNOTE-192), and a phase Ib/IIa trial investigating the combination of durvalumab plus olaparib versus chemotherapy alone for HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer (DUO). Additionally, there is an ongoing phase 3 trial comparing abemaciclib plus endocrine therapy vs placebo plus endocrine therapy in postmenopausal women with hormone receptor positive advanced breast cancer that has progressed on or after prior nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor therapy (MONARCH 3). These are only some examples of the many ongoing clinical trials for breast cancer treatment. It is important to note that these trials may have specific eligibility criteria and should be discussed with a healthcare provider to determine if they would be appropriate options for individual patients.

Male breast cancer can be detected by self-examination of the breasts for any lumps or changes in the skin. It may also be found during routine screening mammograms. A physical examination should include an inspection and palpation of both breasts by a healthcare provider. If there is a concern about a potential mass or other abnormality, further imaging such as ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be ordered. Biopsy is necessary for definitive diagnosis.

There are several factors that increase an individual's risk for developing skin cancer including fair skin color, family history of skin cancer, excessive sun exposure (both intentional and unintentional), increased number of moles or freckles, certain types of scar tissue, older age, smoking, chronic UV radiation exposure, immunosuppression, personal history of other cancers such as melanoma, xeroderma pigmentosa, basal cell carcinomas, actinic keratoses, and precancerous lesions such as Bowen’s disease and dysplastic nevi .

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials for melanoma treatment that involve immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors (either alone or in combination), targeted therapy using BRAF and MEK inhibition, as well as other novel therapies such as vaccines and adoptive cellular therapy . For non-melanoma skin cancers, there is also active investigation into systemic chemotherapies, topical agents, photodynamic therapy, and other approaches to improve outcomes .

Melanoma is one of the most aggressive forms of skin cancer with an estimated 5-year relative survival rate of approximately 21% in all stages combined (American Cancer Society). The overall incidence of metastatic disease at diagnosis ranges from 8 to 40%, depending on tumor thickness . If detected early through regular self-skin examinations and physician checks, the five-year survival rate approaches nearly 99%. However, if diagnosed late as stage IV, the five-year survival rate drops to around 23% .

Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is an aggressive skin cancer that occurs most frequently in older white men with fair skin who have prolonged sun exposure or actinic damage . It can also occur in organ transplant recipients receiving immunosuppressive therapy  and patients with viral infections such as HIV , Hepatitis B virus , and Human papillomavirus (HPV) .

The standard treatment for Merkel cell carcinoma is surgical excision of the primary tumor with wide margins (at least 1 cm). Lymph node dissection may be performed if there is evidence of nodal involvement or if the risk of metastasis to regional lymph nodes is high. Adjuvant radiotherapy may also be recommended in some cases after surgical resection. In advanced disease, systemic chemotherapy using cisplatin-based regimens is often used as first-line treatment. Radiation therapy can also be considered as palliative care for patients who have recurrent or metastatic disease that cannot be treated surgically.

Plasma cell neoplasms can be diagnosed by biopsy of bone marrow or extramedullary plasmacytomas. Imaging studies such as X-ray, CT scan, MRI, PET scan, and SPECT scans may also be used to evaluate for presence of tumor burden in patients with multiple myeloma.

Neuroblastoma (NB) is a pediatric solid tumor that arises from immature cells called neuroblasts in the adrenal medulla or along sympathetic nerve fibers . It can occur at any age but most commonly affects children under 5 years old. NB is classified as either low-risk or high-risk depending on its stage, histology, amplification status of MYCN gene, ploidy level, and other molecular markers. Low-risk patients typically have localized disease with favorable outcomes while high-risk patients often present with metastatic disease to bone marrow, lymph nodes, liver, skin, and bone, and have poor prognosis without intensive therapy .

Neuroblastoma (NB) is a pediatric tumor that arises from immature cells called neural crest cells during embryonic development . It can occur anywhere along the sympathetic nervous system but most commonly in the abdomen near the adrenal gland or within the neck near the base of the skull . NBs are divided into two main categories based on their clinical presentation: localized disease with no evidence of metastasis to other organs (localized NB), which accounts for approximately 40% of cases; and disseminated disease involving distant sites such as bone marrow, liver, lung, and lymph nodes (metastatic NB), which comprises about 60% of all diagnoses .

Non-smokers who have been exposed to secondhand smoke for long periods of time are at an increased risk of developing NSCLC. Other factors include exposure to radon gas, asbestos, coal dust, nickel chromate compounds, arsenic, cadmium, and air pollution. Smoking is by far the largest contributor to the development of NSCLC.

The standard first line treatment option for patients with non small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who have good performance status is chemotherapy in combination with either immunotherapy or targeted therapy depending upon the molecular profile of their tumor. For those with poor performance status, palliative care measures such as pain management and oxygen therapy may be recommended.

Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) can be diagnosed by taking a biopsy of tissue from the lungs using bronchoscopy, thoracentesis, or surgery. Imaging such as CT scan may also help to confirm the diagnosis. SCLC cells have specific features that allow them to be distinguished from other types of lung cancer under a microscope.

There are several things you can do to reduce your chances of developing lung cancer. Firstly, it is important to quit smoking if you currently smoke as this is one of the leading causes of lung cancer. Secondly, try to limit exposure to secondhand smoke from others who smoke around you. Thirdly, make sure to eat healthy foods such as fruits and vegetables which contain antioxidants that may help protect against lung cancer. Fourthly, exercise regularly as physical activity has been shown to lower the risk of lung cancer. Finally, get screened for lung cancer by having a chest X-ray taken every year.

Parathyroid cancer can be difficult to diagnose due to its rarity and non-specific symptoms. The most common diagnostic test for parathyroid cancer is ultrasound of the neck, which may show an enlarged gland with irregular margins and microcalcifications within it. However, this finding alone cannot confirm the presence of malignancy. If there is still suspicion for parathyroid cancer after ultrasound, further testing such as CT scan, MRI, PET scan, or FDG-PET (positron emission tomography) may be performed to look for local invasion or distant metastasis. In addition, laboratory tests including serum calcium levels and imaging studies should also be done to assess the extent of disease.

Penile cancer refers to any malignant tumor that arises from cells of the male genital organ known as the penis. The most common type of penile cancer is squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), which originates from the flat, scaly-like skin covering the external surface of the penis called the glans penis. Other types of penile cancers include adenocarcinomas, basal cell carcinomas, sarcomas, melanomas, and Paget's disease .

Penile cancer is classified into four clinical stages (I–IV) according to the TNM staging system for malignant tumors. The TMN classification system was developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC), which provides standardized guidelines for diagnosing, treating, and reporting outcomes in patients with cancer.

Pituitary tumors may present with various clinical manifestations depending on their size, location within the sella turcica, hormonal production, and secretion patterns . The most common presenting symptom is headache in 50% to 60% of patients , followed by visual impairment (38%) and hypopituitarism (27%) . Other less frequent symptoms include acromegaly, Cushing’s disease, diabetes insipidus, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, erectile dysfunction, loss of libido, weight gain or loss, fatigue, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, polyuria, polydipsia, anorexia, constipation, diarrhea, and skin changes such as hyper- or hypo-pigmentation .

There is ongoing research into novel treatment options for patients with pituitary adenomas. Some of these include targeted therapies such as somatostatin analogues (SSAs) in acromegaly, mTOR inhibitors in corticotrophinomas, and MEK inhibition in non-functioning pituitary adenoma (NFPMA). Other emerging therapeutics include peptides that target the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor (GnRH-II), which may be effective against both functioning and NFMPA .

Prostate cancer is classified into four main stages (I-IV) according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). The staging system takes into account both the pathological stage of the tumor as well as its anatomic location within the prostate gland. Stage I refers to a localized disease confined to one side of the prostate gland or less than 5% of the tissue involved; this is considered the earliest stage of prostate cancer. As the disease progresses, it can spread beyond the prostate capsule but remains contained in the pelvic region (Stage II), or outside the pelvis but still within the abdomen (Stage III). Finally, if the cancer has metastasized beyond the abdominal area, such as in the bones, lungs, liver, etc., it is considered Stage IV.

Colon cancer refers to malignant tumors that occur in the inner wall of the large intestine or colon. It arises from abnormal cell growth in the tissues of the colon. The exact cause of most cases of colon cancer remains unknown; however, several factors have been identified as increasing the risk of developing this disease. These include age (most commonly diagnosed between 50 and 70 years old), family history of colorectal cancer, certain types of inherited syndromes such as familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), long-term smoking, high alcohol consumption, obesity, lack of physical activity, diet low in fiber and high in fat, and chronic inflammatory bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease .

Colon cancer is divided into four main stages (0-IV) according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). Stage 0 refers to carcinoma in situ or intramucosal cancer, which has not yet invaded the muscular layer of the intestine wall. This stage is considered noninvasive but may develop into invasive cancer over time.

Rectal cancer is one of the most prevalent cancers worldwide . The incidence rate has been increasing in recent years due to various factors such as lifestyle changes, dietary habits, and environmental exposure . Early detection of this disease is crucial for effective treatment and improved survival rates. Therefore, it is important to understand its clinical presentation and associated risk factors.

There are several ongoing clinical trials for rectal cancer treatment that have been registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (https://clinicaltrials.gov). Some of them include phase III trial comparing neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy with capecitabine to standard fluorouracil-based regimen (NCT01475238), phase II study evaluating the efficacy of bevacizumab plus capecitabine as first line therapy for metastatic disease (NCT01691531) and phase Ib/II trial assessing the safety and activity of pembrolizumab alone or combined with radiation therapy prior to surgery for locally advanced rectal cancer (NCT02531272).

Small intestinal cancers refer to malignant tumors that arise from any of the three major types of cells in the lining of the small intestine (enterocytes, neuroendocrine cells, or Paneth cells). The most common type is adenocarcinoma, which arises from enterocyte cells and accounts for about 50% of all cases. Other less common types include carcinoid tumor, sarcoma, squamous cell carcinoma, undifferentiated carcinomas, and lymphoma .

The stages of small intestinal cancer (also known as small bowel or jejunal cancer) are defined by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). There are four stages for small intestinal adenocarcinoma: Stage I is limited to the wall of the small intestine; Stage II has spread into nearby tissues but not beyond the small intestine; Stage III has spread to regional lymph nodes near the small intestine; and Stage IV has spread to distant parts of the body such as the liver, lung, bone, etc.

The long-term prognosis of thymomas depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor size, histologic subtype, invasion into adjacent structures, and resection status . Thymic carcinomas have an overall 5-year survival rate of approximately 30% to 40%, which is significantly lower than that of thymomas . However, it should be noted that there has been a recent increase in the number of patients with advanced disease who undergo complete surgical resections, resulting in improved outcomes .

Urethral cancers are rare in women but more commonly seen in men. The most common site for urethral cancer to occur is the penile urethra (90%). Early signs and symptoms include dysuria, painful micturition, urinary retention, hematuria, or a palpable mass at the tip of the penis. It may also present with a foul-smelling discharge from the meatus. In advanced stages, patients may have lower extremity edema due to pelvic lymph node involvement.

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to urethral cancer that aim to evaluate new treatments such as chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, and other therapies. These include phase II and III randomized controlled trials comparing different treatment regimens with standard of care (chemotherapy) alone or in combination with radiotherapy. The National Cancer Institute Clinical Trials Network has a list of active clinical trials for urothelial carcinoma at https://clinicaltrials.gov/. It is important to note that these results should be interpreted carefully due to potential bias and limitations associated with clinical trial data.

Vulvar cancer can be staged using the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) system or the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). The FIGO stage classifies vulvar cancer into four stages, while AJCC divides it into five stages. Both systems use similar criteria to determine the stage of vulvar cancer.

People with an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) may not have any specific symptoms until it ruptures. The most common symptom of AAA is pain in the back or abdomen that does not go away. Other possible symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, fever, palpitation, weakness, dizziness, shortness of breath, loss of appetite, weight loss, dark urine, and pale stools . It is important to note that these symptoms can also be caused by other conditions, so if you experience any of them, it's essential to see your doctor right away for further evaluation.

Abetalipoproteinemia (ABL) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the MTP gene that encodes microsomal triglyceride transfer protein involved in chylomicron assembly . It can also be acquired due to homozygous deletion of the MTP gene as seen in some populations such as Inuit Eskimos .

The typical symptoms of Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome include intellectual disability, hypotonia, hyperlaxity of joints, skin laxity, and facial dysmorphism (flat midface with high nasal bridge). Common signs include short stature, macrocephaly, and congenital contractures in hands or feet. Unusual features can include dental malocclusion, ptosis, strabismus, hearing loss, and seizures.

Acanthosis Nigricans (AN) is a common skin condition that presents as areas of velvety hyperpigmentation with well-defined borders typically found in body folds such as the axillae, neck, and groin . AN may be associated with endocrine disorders or medications but most commonly occurs without an underlying cause . The treatment of AN depends on whether there is an underlying cause. If there is no identifiable cause, topical corticosteroids are often used to treat AN. Other options include cryotherapy, chemical peels, laser therapy, and surgical excision . In some cases, AN may resolve spontaneously over time .

An accessory navicular bone is typically asymptomatic but may cause pain at the medial aspect of the midfoot during weight-bearing activities. It can also lead to swelling and tenderness around the area. The pain is often described as a dull ache that worsens with activity and improves with rest.

Aceruloplasminemia (ACP) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding ceruloplasmin (Cp), which leads to iron accumulation in multiple organs including the brain . Diagnosis of ACP can be made through clinical presentation, laboratory findings, genetic testing, and imaging studies such as MRI and CT scans.

Achalasia is a condition in which food does not pass through the esophagus due to abnormal contractions of the lower esophageal sphincter muscle. Treatment options include medication with calcium channel blockers or nitrates, pneumatic balloon dilation (also known as Heller myotomy), surgical myotomy, and botulinum injection into the lower esophageal sphincter. All these treatments aim to reduce the pressure at the gastroesophageal junction, thereby improving swallowing by allowing food to pass from the throat down into the stomach.

Achondrogenesis is an autosomal recessive disorder in which both parents carry one mutated gene for this condition. Therefore, there is a 25% chance that their child will have the disease if neither of them has any family history of a similar genetic abnormality.

Achondrogenesis type 2 is an extremely rare genetic disorder that affects bone development during embryonic life. It results in severe dwarfism with distinctive facial characteristics such as large ears, short neck, small jaw, depressed nasal bridge, wide mouth, and widely spaced teeth. The limbs may be relatively longer than the trunk or equal to the trunk length. Joints can have limited mobility due to ligamentous hyperlaxity. Other common features include herniation (bulging) of abdominal organs into the thoracic cavity through the diaphragm muscle, which causes breathing difficulties; genitalia malformation; bowing of long bones; and underdeveloped breast tissue in females.

Achondroplasia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene that affect bone development. The most common treatment option for children with achondroplasia is surgical limb lengthening, which involves gradually elongating one or more bones to improve height and mobility. This procedure can be performed multiple times throughout childhood and adolescence as new bone growth occurs. Other treatment options include physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, orthodontic care, and psychological support to help individuals with achondroplasia manage their condition and achieve optimal health outcomes.

Acquired hemophilia (AH) refers to the development of bleeding disorders in previously healthy individuals without any family history or genetic predisposition for such conditions. It can be classified into two types: AH type I, which presents with factor VIII deficiency; and AH type II, which presents with factor IX deficiency . The exact cause of AH remains unknown but may involve autoimmune processes that result in the production of antibodies against coagulation factors. This condition has been associated with various underlying diseases including lymphoproliferative malignancies, systemic autoimmune diseases, pregnancy-related complications, drug reactions, and viral infections .

Acrocapitofemoral dysplasia (ACFD) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by short stature, coxa vara deformity, genu valgum, and hip subluxation . The most common clinical features include short stature with normal or reduced upper limb length, coxa vara deformity, genu valgus, and hip subluxation . Other associated findings may include scoliosis, kyphosis, and intellectual disability in some cases .

Scoliosis is not typically associated with achondroplasia. However, if an individual with achondroplastic has scoliosis, they may experience back pain or difficulty breathing due to restricted lung capacity. The spine's abnormal curvature can lead to uneven shoulders, hips, rib cages, and other skeletal deformities.

Acromegaly is a rare endocrine disorder caused by excess growth hormone (GH) secretion from the pituitary gland after puberty . It can lead to enlargement of hands and feet, coarse facial features, skin changes, jaw protrusion, carpal tunnel syndrome, sleep apnea, high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, cardiomyopathy, osteoarthritis, and colon polyps . The most common cause of acromegaly is a benign tumor of the pituitary called an adenoma that secretes GH continuously throughout life instead of only during childhood .

Acromesomelic Dysplasia (AMMD) is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects bone growth in the hands and feet. The most common features include shortened limbs with tapered fingers and toes, thumbs that lack opposing ability, and limited movement of joints. Other possible symptoms may include respiratory problems, hearing loss, intellectual disability, and facial abnormalities such as flat faces or small chins. AMMD is caused by mutations in the gene for alpha-3 beta-glucuronidase, which breaks down mucopolysaccharides in the body. Diagnosis is typically made through genetic testing and imaging studies such as X-rays to assess skeletal deformities.

Acute alcohol sensitivity is also known as systemic allergic reaction to alcohol or idiosyncratic alcohol intolerance. It refers to an adverse reaction that occurs after consuming even small amounts of alcohol in people who drink regularly. The symptoms can range from mild to severe and may include skin flushing, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rapid heart rate, liver enlargement, abdominal pain, fatigue, weakness, tremors, confusion, anxiety, depression, and seizures .

Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis (AFND) is an uncommon skin condition that causes small red bumps or papules to form on the skin during a feverish episode. The rash typically appears 1-3 days after the onset of fever and lasts about one week .

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) can be diagnosed by measuring urine levels of heme precursors such as delta-aminolevulinic acid (δ-ALA), porphobilinogen (PBG), or uroporphyrins I (UPI). A δ-ALA level greater than 30 mg/dL in a fasting state strongly suggests AIP . The diagnosis may also require genetic testing to identify specific mutations associated with this condition.

ADCY5-related dyskinesia (also known as DYT14) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder characterized by involuntary muscle contractions that cause repetitive movements of the face, neck, trunk, or limbs . It can also be associated with other symptoms such as speech dysfunction, swallowing difficulties, sleep disturbances, anxiety, depression, and cognitive impairment . The condition typically begins in childhood or adolescence but may not be diagnosed until adulthood due to its variable presentation .

Yes, adenocarcinoma of the appendix is a type of cancer that begins in cells lining the inside surface of the appendix. It can be considered as one of the most common types of malignant tumors arising from the gastrointestinal tract.

No, Adenoid Cystic Carcinomas (ACCs) do not appear to be inherited or have an increased risk of occurring within families. The development of ACC is thought to be due to random genetic mutations that occur during cellular differentiation .

Adiposis dolorosa is an uncommon condition characterized by painful lipomatous masses that develop in adulthood. The exact cause of this disease remains unknown but may be related to trauma or inflammation . It typically affects middle-aged women with no family history of similar conditions.

ADNP syndrome (also known as Angelman-Davis neurogenetic phenotype) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations or deletions of the chromosome 15q13 region that affect the expression of UBE3A gene. The condition was first described in 2014 by Dr. David Z. Davis and colleagues at Vanderbilt University Medical Center .

Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is not thought to be caused by genetic factors alone but rather involves complex interactions between multiple genes and environmental factors . A family history of AIS has been found to increase the risk of developing this condition, with siblings of those affected having an approximately 18% chance of also developing AIS compared to less than 3% for children without an affected sibling . However, even if there is no family history of AIS, any individual still has about a 2-4% chance of developing the condition during childhood or early adulthood . Therefore, while genetics may play some role in determining who will develop AIS, other factors such as growth patterns and biomechanical stresses on the spine likely also contribute to its development.

Typical symptoms of Down syndrome include cognitive impairment, intellectual disability, learning disabilities, developmental delays, congenital heart defects, vision problems, hearing loss, muscle hypotonia, joint laxity, short stature, poor motor skills, slurred speech, decreased muscle strength, delayed puberty, reduced bone density, recurrent middle ear infections, sleep apnea, and premature aging (Albert et al., 2019). These symptoms can vary from person to person with Down syndrome. In adults, some additional symptoms may be observed such as Alzheimer’s disease or dementia, leukemia, seizures, thyroid disorders, hearing loss, vision problems, and other health issues related to age (Molloy & Hesketh, 2018; Albert et al., 2019).

Adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD) is an inherited retinal disease that affects central vision in adults aged 30 to 65 years old. The most common symptom of VMD is gradual loss of central vision over several months or years. Patients with VMD may experience distorted or wavy straight lines, difficulty reading small print, trouble distinguishing colors, and decreased night vision. In some cases, patients may also have a blind spot in their central field of view. Vision can appear normal at first but then gradually deteriorate as the condition progresses.

Afibrinogenemia is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by deficiency or absence of circulating fibrinogen due to genetic mutations in one of three genes encoding its subunits (FGA, FGB, and FGG). It typically presents with bleeding tendencies such as epistaxis, menorrhagia, hematuria, easy bruising, and spontaneous skin hemorrhages. Patients may also experience recurrent venous thromboembolism events. The diagnosis can be made through laboratory tests including measurement of plasma fibrinogen levels, coagulation factor assays, mixing studies, and molecular testing for gene mutations. Treatment involves replacement therapy with fresh frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate transfusions during acute episodes and prophylactic antifactor Xa treatment.

Total intestinal aganglionosis is a rare congenital disorder characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the entire gastrointestinal tract from the esophagus to the rectum. The most common sign and symptom of this condition is chronic constipation that can lead to bowel obstruction or Hirschsprung's disease. Other possible signs include abdominal distention, vomiting, poor feeding, failure to thrive, and bloody stools due to secondary cow milk allergy.

Aicardi-Goutieres Syndrome (AGS) is an autosomal recessive genetic disease that affects the central nervous system and causes inflammation in the brain due to abnormal activation of innate immune cells . AGS can be classified into three types depending on the underlying cause or gene mutations involved in its pathogenesis. Type I is caused by mutations in genes encoding ribonucleases RNASEH2A, RNASEH2B, and RNASEH2C which play a role in degrading nucleotides present in RNA. Mutations in these genes lead to increased levels of interferons and proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), interleukin 6 (IL-6), and IL-8 in blood plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). These elevated levels result in neurodegenerative symptoms including microcephaly, spasticity, dystonia, seizures, and intellectual disability .

The typical symptoms of Aicardi-Goutieres Syndrome (AGS) include encephalopathy with microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, basal ganglia calcification, leukodystrophy, cerebral atrophy, hydrocephalus, seizures, spasticity, dystonia, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, interstitial lung disease, panniculitis, and skin rash .

Ainhum is an acute inflammatory disease of the skin that affects children under 10 years old. It is characterized by painful vesicles or blisters that form along the lines of Langerhans cells on the palms and soles (palmoplantar). The name "ainhum" comes from the Spanish word for "shoe," as these lesions can resemble shoe imprints.

Alagille syndrome (ALGS) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in JAG1 gene that codes for Jagged-1 protein involved in Notch signaling pathway . ALGS involves congenital heart defects such as peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis or atresia, biliary tract abnormalities including intrahepatic cholestasis with pruning of major ductus hepatis branches, skeletal anomalies like butterfly vertebrae, craniofacial features including posteriorly rotated ears, short nose, deep set eyes, facial asymmetry, growth retardation, intellectual disability, and characteristic eye movement disorders . The diagnosis of ALGS requires meeting two criteria: 1) presence of three out of four major diagnostic findings; or 2) having one major finding plus any minor feature along with positive family history of ALGS .

The cause of AHO is an autosomal dominant mutation in the GNAS1 gene that results in decreased production of cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) . This leads to abnormal bone mineralization due to impaired osteoblast function and increased osteoclastic activity . It is considered a genetic condition because it follows Mendelian inheritance patterns with a high penetrance rate of 90%-100%.

Moyamoya syndrome is a rare cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis or occlusion of large intracranial arteries such as the internal carotid artery and middle cerebral artery, leading to compensatory proliferation of small distal vessels with puff-of-smoke appearance on angiography . The name "moyamoya" means "puffy of smoke" in Japanese. It was first described in 1957 by Japanese physician Kawase Takeshi while studying pathological changes associated with stroke in children .

Alopecia universalis (ALO) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by total loss of scalp and body hair . It can be classified as either congenital or acquired. Congenital ALO presents at birth while acquired ALO develops later in life. The exact cause of ALO remains unknown but it may have genetic links to other forms of alopecia such as familial primary hypothyroidism with myxedema coma .

Alopecia Universalis (AU) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by complete loss of body hair . The exact cause of AU remains unknown; however, it has been associated with certain genetic mutations such as those in the IL-23R gene . Treatment options include topical corticosteroids, immunosuppressive agents, phototherapy, low-level laser therapy, and stem cell transplantation . However, these treatment methods have limited efficacy and may not be suitable for all patients due to potential side effects .

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is an inherited disorder caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene that encodes AAT protein. It is not acquired but rather present at birth. The most common mutation associated with severe AAT deficiency is Glu342Lys (PI*Z), which results in decreased synthesis of functional AAT protein . Other less frequent mutations include PI*S (Glu678Lys), PI*M (Met35Thr), PI*K (Gln290His), and PI*V (Val362Ile). These genetic variations lead to impaired folding of AAT protein within the endoplasmic reticulum, resulting in its accumulation as misfolded polymers in hepatocytes and neutrophils. This leads to reduced levels of circulating functional AAT protein, predisposing affected individuals to early development of lung disease due to uncontrolled proteolytic activity of neutrophil elastase during inflammation .

Alpha thalassemia refers to a group of genetic disorders caused by defects in one or more of the four α-globin genes located on chromosome 16 (HBA1, HBA2, HBBP1, and HBGD). These mutations can lead to abnormal production or function of hemoglobin, resulting in decreased oxygen transport capacity in red blood cells. The severity of symptoms depends on the number of affected genes and whether they occur in combination with other globin gene mutations such as beta thalassemias.

Alpha-Thalassemia X-Linked Intellectual Disability Syndrome (ATXIDS) is an inherited blood disorder caused by mutations in the X chromosome gene that codes for the protein hemoglobin beta chain . ATXIDS can cause severe physical and mental health problems such as intellectual disabilities, short stature, abnormal facial features, heart defects, and skeletal deformities . The most common sign of ATXIDS is developmental delay or intellectual disability, which usually becomes apparent during childhood. Other signs include short stature, microcephaly, small head size, low birth weight, weak muscle tone, delayed bone age, joint laxity, hearing loss, vision impairment, seizures, cardiac anomalies, and skeletal malformations such as butterfly vertebrae and flared iliac wings .

Alport syndrome is an inheritable genetic disorder that occurs due to mutations in one of three genes (COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5) encoding for type IV collagen chains . It typically runs in families with autosomal dominant inheritance; however, de novo cases have been reported where both parents were phenotypically normal but carried a pathogenic variant in one of these genes . The disease manifests as early as infancy and presents with hematuria, proteinuria, renal failure, sensorineural hearing loss, ocular abnormalities such as lenticonus, and posterior subcapsular cataracts .

Ambras Syndrome (also known as Hyperhidrosis Papulosa Congenita) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by hyperhidrosis or excessive sweating in specific areas of the body such as palms, soles, axillae, and face. It was first described by Dr. Ambras in 1948 . The exact cause of this condition remains unknown but may be related to abnormalities in the sweat glands or their innervation.

Amelogenesis imperfecta is an inherited condition that occurs due to genetic mutations in genes responsible for enamel formation during tooth development. It cannot occur spontaneously without these genetic factors.

The typical presentation of X-linked hypoplastic/hypomaturational amelogenesis imperfecta (XLHHAII) is characterized by delayed tooth eruption with malformed teeth that may be brown or yellowish in color. Other common signs include enamel defects such as thinning, pitting, and discoloration. Patients with this condition often have poor oral hygiene due to their difficulty maintaining proper dental care. They also tend to avoid eating hard foods like fruits and vegetables because they cause pain when chewing them.

Amniotic band syndrome (ABS) occurs when an amniotic band wraps around a fetus during pregnancy, resulting in various injuries to the fetus at birth or after delivery . The exact mechanism of ABS remains unknown; however, there are several theories that may explain its development. One theory suggests that the amniotic bands can cause compression of blood vessels, leading to decreased oxygen supply and tissue damage. Another theory proposes that the tension caused by the amniotic bands can lead to skin abrasions, bruising, and other forms of injury.

Amyloid A (AA) amyloidosis is an autoimmune disorder in which chronic inflammation causes deposition of insoluble fibrils composed of serum amyloid A protein in various tissues and organs . It can be classified as primary or secondary depending on whether there is an underlying cause for its development. The most common cause of secondary AA amyloidosis is long-standing hematologic malignancies such as multiple myeloma, lymphomas, leukemia, and other plasma cell dyscrasias; however, it may also occur due to nonmalignant conditions including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, tuberculosis, hemochromatosis, chronic infection, trauma, burns, and osteomyelitis .

Amyopathic dermatomyositis (ADM) is a rare subtype of dermatomyositis that lacks muscle involvement but presents with characteristic cutaneous findings such as heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules or sign, shawl sign, V-sign, and mechanic's hands . The pathogenesis of ADM remains unclear; however, it may be related to autoimmune dysfunction in peripheral blood vessels without myocyte involvement .

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects motor neurons in both the brain and spinal cord. The exact cause of ALS remains unknown; however, several factors have been identified as potential contributors to its development. These include genetics, environmental exposures such as heavy metals or pesticides, traumatic head injury, and certain viruses . Genetic mutations account for approximately 10% of all cases of ALS, with C9orf72 being the most common genetic variant associated with this condition . Environmental risk factors may also play a role in the development of ALS, particularly exposure to heavy metals and pesticides . Traumatic head injuries have also been linked to an increased risk of developing ALS, although the mechanism behind this association is not fully understood . Finally, certain viruses, including West Nile virus and Japanese encephalitis, have been implicated in the development of ALS, although their precise role remains unclear . It is likely that multiple factors contribute to the development of ALS, with genetic predisposition playing a significant role.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons in both the brain and spinal cord, leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, cramps, dysarthria, dysphagia, and respiratory failure . Parkinson's disease (PD) is caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra pars compacta, resulting in bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, postural instability, gait disturbance, mask-like facial expression, micrographia, and difficulty initiating movement . Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is associated with cognitive impairment, visual hallucinations, parkinsonian features, autonomic dysfunction, and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder .

An anaplastic ganglioglioma is a rare, malignant brain tumor that arises from mature glial cells with neuroectodermal differentiation. It is characterized by large pleomorphic nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli, and increased mitotic activity compared to low grade gangliogliomas.

Andersen-Tawil syndrome (ATS) is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects the heart, kidneys, and skeletal muscles. The most common symptoms include ventricular arrhythmias such as supraventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, hypokalemic periodic paralysis, muscle weakness, myalgia, and fatigue. Other less frequent manifestations may be hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, and chronic kidney disease. Diagnosis requires meeting two major criteria or one major criterion with two minor criteria. Major criteria include having both ATS-associated arrhythmia and paralytic attacks, or having a pathogenic variant in KCNJ2, SCN4A, or CACNA1C gene. Minor criteria include having either ATS-related arrhythmia or paralytic episodes, or carrying a pathogenic variant in KCNJ2, SCN4A, or CACNA1C gene.

Sideroblastic anemia is characterized by fatigue, weakness, pale skin, light stools or black tarry stool, and bruising. Spinocerebellar ataxia presents with unsteady gait, clumsiness in speech, difficulty swallowing, double vision, muscle cramps, numbness, tingling, pain, weakness, and loss of sensation in hands and feet.

Anencephaly is characterized by absence or incomplete development of brain structures, including the cerebral hemispheres, corpus callosum, thalamus, and midbrain . It can be diagnosed prenatally via ultrasound or at birth through physical examination. Newborns with anencephaly may appear pale, blue colored (cyanotic), have bulging fontanels, absent eyes, and no evidence of movement or muscle tone.

Angelman syndrome is caused by a random mutation in chromosome 15q11-q13 that occurs during early embryonic development. The condition is not hereditary and typically occurs spontaneously without any known family history of the disease.

Aniridia is a congenital ocular disorder characterized by complete or partial iris hypoplasia with potential associated structural defects of the anterior segment. The treatment and management options depend on the severity of the disease. For patients who have no other complications besides aniridia, regular follow-up examinations including visual acuity testing, intraocular pressure measurement, slit lamp examination, dilated fundus examination, and corneal topography are recommended to monitor the progression of the condition and detect any complications early.

Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is considered to have a genetic component as certain genes such as HLA-B27 may predispose individuals to developing AS . However, having one of these genes does not necessarily mean that someone will develop AS. It has been estimated that 10% of people with HLA-B27 will go on to develop AS , suggesting that other factors besides genetics play a role in its development.

Anonychia congenita refers to the absence or underdevelopment of one or more nails at birth . It can affect one or multiple fingers or toes. The cause of this condition is unknown but may be related to genetic factors such as mutations in genes involved in nail development .

Anophthalmia-plus syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by bilateral absence or small eyes (anophthalmos) with additional ocular anomalies such as coloboma, microphthalmos, cataracts, and retinal detachment . It can also be associated with systemic abnormalities including craniofacial defects, cardiac malformations, sensorineural hearing loss, renal dysplasia, cerebral anomalies, and mental retardation . The severity of these manifestations varies from patient to patient, but most individuals have severe vision impairment or blindness due to eye underdevelopment or degenerative changes in the optic nerve.

Anterior polar cataracts (APC) can present with various visual disturbances depending on their location within the lens. APC Type II is located at the anterior pole of the lens, which may result in glare, halos, starbursts, and night driving difficulties due to light scattering. Patients typically report difficulty seeing at night while maintaining good daytime vision.

Antisynthetase syndrome (ASS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by myositis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud's phenomenon, fever, arthritis, and mechanic hands. It is caused by antibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that catalyze the attachment of specific amino acids to their cognate tRNAs during protein biosynthesis . The exact cause of ASS remains unknown but may be related to genetic susceptibility or environmental triggers such as viral infections or exposure to certain drugs or chemicals .

Aortic arch anomalies can be associated with various congenital syndromes that present with characteristic facial features and intellectual disabilities. Peculiar Facies – Intellectual Disability Syndrome is one such condition characterized by a combination of aortic arch abnormalities (most commonly coarctation of the aorta), peculiar facies, and intellectual disability.

Aplasia cutis congenital is a rare skin disorder that occurs during fetal development in which certain areas of the scalp fail to develop properly, resulting in thin or absent skin with visible skull bone . It can be associated with other birth defects such as brain malformations, eye abnormalities, heart defects, kidney problems, limb deformities, and spinal cord issues. The condition may also affect other parts of the body besides the head, including the back, palms, soles of feet, and genitals. Treatment typically involves protective dressings and topical ointments to prevent infection and promote healing. In severe cases, surgery may be necessary to reconstruct affected areas.
